title: Experimental Design and Data Analysis for the Advancement of Mutant Populations
text:
Welcome
This manual accompanies the Regional Training Course on Experimental Design and Data Analysis for the Advancement of Mutant Populations (IAEA project RER5030), held at the Faculty of Agricultural Sciences and Food, Skopje, North Macedonia, 9–20 November 2026.

title: Experimental Design and Data Analysis for the Advancement of Mutant Populations
text:
How to use this manual

Each chapter matches one or more sessions of the agenda.
Every chapter follows the same structure: learning objectives, key concepts, a worked demo in R, interpretation for breeding decisions, an exercise and key takeaways.
All code uses the shared datasets in the data/ folder of the course repository.
Slides for each session are condensed versions of the chapters.

title: Experimental Design and Data Analysis for the Advancement of Mutant Populations
text:
Setup
Start with Getting started: it explains how to download the course project, install the packages and get the updates. Run R/install_packages.R once to install all course packages. Participants with older computers can use Posit Cloud.

title: Getting started: install and update the course materials

What you need
This page takes about 10 minutes. Do it once, on the first day, and keep it open: you will use the update steps again every time new content is added to the course.
crumbs: Getting started: install and update the course materials

title: Getting started: install and update the course materials
text:
A computer with R 4.3 or newer and RStudio (already prepared for the course).
Git, a free program that downloads the course files and their updates. You do not need a GitHub account, a username or a password.
An internet connection for the first download and for each update.
crumbs: Getting started: install and update the course materials

title: Getting started: install and update the course materials
text:
Step 1: install Git (once)



Computer
What to do




Windows
Download from https://git-scm.com/download/win, run the installer and accept all the default options.


Mac
Open the Terminal and type git --version. If Git is missing, the Mac offers to install it: click Install. Or download it from https://git-scm.com/download/mac.



Close RStudio completely and open it again, so that it finds Git.
crumbs: Getting started: install and update the course materials

title: Getting started: install and update the course materials
text:
Step 2: download the course project (once)

In RStudio, choose File, then New Project, then Version Control, then Git.
In Repository URL, paste:
https://github.com/lfdelgadom/rtc-mutant-breeding-2026.git
Leave the project directory name as it is. Under Create project as subdirectory of, choose a folder you will remember, for example Documents.
Click Create Project. RStudio downloads everything and opens the project.
crumbs: Getting started: install and update the course materials

title: Getting started: install and update the course materials
text:
Step 3: install the R packages (once)
In the RStudio Console, run:
source("R/install_packages.R")
Wait until every package shows OK. This can take several minutes. If a line says FAILED, run the command again, and if it still fails, ask an instructor.
crumbs: Getting started: install and update the course materials

title: Getting started: install and update the course materials
section: Step 4: create your own work folder (once)
text:
Step 4: create your own work folder (once)
In the RStudio Console, run:
dir.create("my-work")
Put your own scripts and copies of exercises there.
crumbs: Getting started: install and update the course materials

title: Getting started: install and update the course materials
section: Every time new content is added: update
text:
Every time new content is added: update
Open the course project in RStudio, then use one of these two ways.

Button: open the Git tab (top right panel) and click the blue arrow Pull.
Terminal: open the Terminal tab and type git pull.

New chapters, slides and data files appear in the project. The online version of the book, at https://lfdelgadom.github.io/rtc-mutant-breeding-2026/, is updated at the same time.
crumbs: Getting started: install and update the course materials

title: Getting started: install and update the course materials
text:
If the update fails
The most common cause is that a course file was edited. In the Terminal, type:
git stash
git pull
git stash sets your changes aside and git pull then brings the new content. Your edits are not lost, but from now on do your work in my-work.
crumbs: Getting started: install and update the course materials

title: Getting started: install and update the course materials
section: If Git does not work on your computer
text:
If Git does not work on your computer
Some computers do not allow installing programs. In that case, open https://github.com/lfdelgadom/rtc-mutant-breeding-2026, click the green Code button, choose Download ZIP, and unzip it. Repeat this each time the instructors announce new content, into a new folder.
If you only want to read the book, no installation is needed: use the online version.

title: 1  Getting Started with R and RStudio
text:
1.2 Installing the software
R has become one of the most widely used programming languages for data science applied to plant breeding. For beginners, learning how to set up and use R is an important first step, regardless of the operating system they use. This tutorial provides a practical guide to installing R on three major platforms: Windows 10, macOS, and Ubuntu Linux.

1.2.1 Installing R on Windows 10
Installing R on Windows 10 is a simple and process. The recommended approach is to download and install R directly from CRAN (The Comprehensive R Archive Network). To begin, visit the CRAN downloads page and follow the installation steps demonstrated in the video below.



How to download R for Windows OS


Once the download is complete, run the .exe file and follow the default installation steps by clicking Next until finished.


1.2.2 Installing RStudio
After installing R, install RStudio for a better environment to write and run R scripts. It includes a console, plotting tools, and workspace management. Simply visit the RStudio downloads page and follow the installation steps (watch video below).



How to download RStudio for Windows OS




1.2.3 Installing the course packages
R is extended through packages: collections of functions written by the community. We will use about 30 packages during the course. Instead of installing them one by one, run the installation script included in the course repository. Open RStudio and type in the Console:

source("R/install_packages.R")

The script installs only the packages that are missing and prints OK or FAILED for each one. Installation can take 10–20 minutes the first time. If a package shows FAILED, copy the error message and bring it to the session.






TipInstalling a single package



You can always install and load one package manually:

install.packages("dplyr")   # once per computer
library(dplyr)              # every time you start R





1.2.4 Posit Cloud: the alternative for older computers
If your computer has less than 4 GB of RAM or you cannot install software (for example, without administrator rights), use Posit Cloud, which runs RStudio in the web browser:

Create a free account at https://posit.cloud/plans/free.
Click New Project → New RStudio Project.
Upload the course files with the Upload button in the Files pane.
Run source("R/install_packages.R") as above.

The free plan has limited memory and hours per month, which is enough for the course exercises. You need a stable internet connection.


1.2.5 Before the session
Please check that you have:

R and RStudio installed (or a Posit Cloud account).
The course packages installed without FAILED messages.
Downloaded the course repository (datasets and scripts).
Created free accounts in at least two AI assistants (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek or Qwen). We will use them in week 2.

title: 1  Getting Started with R and RStudio
text:
1.3 The RStudio interface
When you open RStudio you will see four panes:







Pane
What it is for




Source (top left)
Scripts and Quarto documents: where you write and save your code


Console (bottom left)
Where R runs the code and prints the results


Environment / History (top right)
Objects you have created (datasets, results)


Files / Plots / Packages / Help (bottom right)
Your folders, graphs, installed packages and help pages






R Studio (IDE: integrated development environment)


Always write your code in a script (File → New File → R Script) rather than directly in the Console. A script is a record of your analysis that you can save, correct and run again. To run a line, place the cursor on it and press Ctrl + Enter (Windows) or Cmd + Enter (macOS).
crumbs: 1  Getting Started with R and RStudio

title: 1  Getting Started with R and RStudio
section: 1.4 RStudio projects and the working directory
text:
1.4 RStudio projects and the working directory
R reads and saves files in a folder called the working directory. The most common error for beginners is cannot open file 'data.csv': No such file or directory, which means R is looking in the wrong folder.
The best way to avoid this problem is to work inside an RStudio project. A project is a folder that contains all the files of one analysis, and RStudio automatically sets it as the working directory.
To create a project: File → New Project → New Directory → New Project, choose a name (e.g., rtc-course) and a location, and click Create Project. Inside the project, use this folder structure:
rtc-course/
├── rtc-course.Rproj   # double-click to open the project
├── data/              # raw data files (never edit them by hand after saving)
├── R/                 # your scripts
└── output/            # tables and figures produced by the scripts
You can check the working directory at any time:

getwd()







WarningAvoid setwd()



Scripts that start with setwd("C:/Users/maria/Desktop/analysis") only work on one computer. Inside a project, use relative paths such as "data/precourse_trial.csv", which work on any computer.
crumbs: 1  Getting Started with R and RStudio

title: 1  Getting Started with R and RStudio
text:
1.5 Objects and data structures

1.5.1 Objects and functions
Everything in R is an object. You create objects with the assignment operator <- (shortcut: Alt + -). You use functions to do something with objects. A function has a name followed by parentheses with its arguments.

plot_area <- 6          # plot area in m2
grain_kg  <- 2.7        # grain weight harvested in the plot
yield_t_ha <- grain_kg / plot_area * 10   # convert kg/m2 to t/ha
yield_t_ha

[1] 4.5

round(yield_t_ha, 1)

[1] 4.5


Object names are case-sensitive (Yield and yield are different objects). Use short names without spaces, such as plant_height.


1.5.2 Vectors
A vector is a set of values of the same type. It is the basic building block of R: each column of a dataset is a vector.

height <- c(92.5, 88.0, 101.3, 95.1)         # numeric
geno   <- c("M4-01", "M4-02", "Parent", "Check")  # character
is_check <- c(FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)      # logical

mean(height)

[1] 94.225

length(geno)

[1] 4

height[3]            # third element

[1] 101.3

height[height > 90]  # elements that meet a condition

[1]  92.5 101.3  95.1




1.5.3 Factors
A factor is a vector of categories. In breeding trials, genotype, replicate, block, row and column must be factors when they are used as effects in a model; otherwise R treats them as numbers (for example, it would treat replicate 3 as “three times” replicate 1).

rep <- c(1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3)
rep_f <- factor(rep)
rep_f

[1] 1 1 2 2 3 3
Levels: 1 2 3

levels(rep_f)

[1] "1" "2" "3"




1.5.4 Matrices
A matrix is a table in which all values are of the same type. Matrices appear in genetic analyses (e.g., a genotype × environment table of means).

gxe <- matrix(c(4.1, 3.8, 4.5,
                3.6, 3.9, 4.0),
              nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
              dimnames = list(c("M4-01", "Parent"), c("Env1", "Env2", "Env3")))
gxe

       Env1 Env2 Env3
M4-01   4.1  3.8  4.5
Parent  3.6  3.9  4.0

rowMeans(gxe)

   M4-01   Parent 
4.133333 3.833333 




1.5.5 Data frames
A data frame is a table in which each column is a vector and each row is an observation (in our case, a plot). It is the structure we will use for almost all field data.

df <- data.frame(
  geno  = c("M4-01", "M4-02", "Parent"),
  rep   = factor(c(1, 1, 1)),
  yield = c(4.6, 3.8, 4.3)
)
df

    geno rep yield
1  M4-01   1   4.6
2  M4-02   1   3.8
3 Parent   1   4.3

str(df)        # structure: type of each column

'data.frame':   3 obs. of  3 variables:
 $ geno : chr  "M4-01" "M4-02" "Parent"
 $ rep  : Factor w/ 1 level "1": 1 1 1
 $ yield: num  4.6 3.8 4.3

df$yield       # one column

[1] 4.6 3.8 4.3

df[2, ]        # second row

   geno rep yield
2 M4-02   1   3.8

df[df$yield > 4, ]   # rows that meet a condition

    geno rep yield
1  M4-01   1   4.6
3 Parent   1   4.3

title: 1  Getting Started with R and RStudio
text:
1.6 Importing field data

1.6.1 The practice dataset
The course repository includes a small practice dataset, data/precourse_trial.csv: a trial with 10 M4 mutant lines, the parent and a check, evaluated in a randomized complete block design with 3 replicates in Skopje. Each row is a plot. It has four traits: grain yield (t/ha), plant height (cm), days to flowering and disease score (1–9). The same data are provided in three formats so you can practice the most common situations.







File
Format




precourse_trial.csv
Comma separator, decimal point


precourse_trial_eu.csv
Semicolon separator, decimal comma (European Excel)


precourse_trial.xlsx
Excel workbook, sheet trial





1.6.2 Reading CSV files
We use the readr package (part of the tidyverse). Empty cells are read as missing values (NA). If your files use other codes for missing data (for example . or -), add them to the na argument.

library(readr)
trial <- read_csv("data/precourse_trial.csv", na = c("", "NA", "."))
trial

# A tibble: 36 × 13
   location  year generation  plot   rep   row   col geno   check yield_t_ha
   <chr>    <dbl> <chr>      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <chr>  <chr>      <dbl>
 1 Skopje    2025 M4             1     1     1     1 M4-01  no          4.6 
 2 Skopje    2025 M4             2     1     1     2 M4-10  no          3.77

1.6.3 Decimal comma and semicolon
Excel in many European countries saves CSV files with semicolons as separators and commas as decimal marks. If you read such a file with read_csv(), all values end up in one column, or numbers are read as text. Use read_csv2() instead:

trial_eu <- read_csv2("data/precourse_trial_eu.csv")

[1] 4.60 3.77 3.24 4.04 4.31 3.92


For other combinations, read_delim() lets you choose the separator and the decimal mark:

read_delim("my_file.txt", delim = "\t",
           locale = locale(decimal_mark = ",", encoding = "UTF-8"))







TipSpecial characters in names



If genotype or location names with characters such as č, š, ž or ğ appear incorrectly, the file was saved with a different encoding. Save it from Excel as CSV UTF-8, or add locale = locale(encoding = "latin1") (or "windows-1250" for Central European files).

text:
1.7 Basic data manipulation
The dplyr package provides a small set of verbs that cover most data preparation tasks. They are combined with the pipe |> (shortcut: Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + M), which reads as “and then”.



Verb
What it does




select()
keep or drop columns


filter()
keep rows that meet a condition


mutate()
create or modify columns


arrange()
sort rows


group_by() + summarise()
calculate summaries by group




# Keep design columns and yield
trial |>
  select(rep, geno, yield_t_ha) |>
  head()

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  rep   geno   yield_t_ha
  <fct> <fct>       <dbl>
1 1     M4-01        4.6 
2 1     M4-10        3.77
3 1     M4-06        3.24
4 1     M4-02        4.04
5 1     Parent       4.31
6 1     M4-09        3.92

# Plots of the parent only
trial |>
  filter(geno == "Parent")

# A tibble: 3 × 13
  location  year generation  plot rep   row   col   geno   check yield_t_ha
  <chr>    <dbl> <chr>      <dbl> <fct> <fct> <fct> <fct>  <chr>      <dbl>
1 Skopje    2025 M4             5 1     1     5     Parent yes         4.31
2 Skopje    2025 M4            15 2     2     3     Parent yes         4.38
3 Skopje    2025 M4            33 3     3     9     Parent yes         3.92
# ℹ 3 more variables: plant_height_cm <dbl>, days_to_flowering <dbl>,
#   disease_score <dbl>

# New variable: yield in kg/ha
trial <- trial |>
  mutate(yield_kg_ha = yield_t_ha * 1000)

Summaries by genotype are the first step to compare mutant lines with the parent:

geno_means <- trial |>
  group_by(geno) |>
  summarise(
    n          = sum(!is.na(yield_t_ha)),
    yield_mean = mean(yield_t_ha, na.rm = TRUE),
    height_mean = mean(plant_height_cm, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(yield_mean))

A great book for anyone starting from scratch. It provides a strong foundation and helps you progress beyond the basics. Highly recommended for learning through reading and hands-on practice.



R for data science








NoteMissing values



mean() returns NA if any value is missing. The argument na.rm = TRUE removes missing values before calculating. The column n shows that two genotypes have only two yield values, which we will need to account for in the analysis (Day 3).

title: 1  Getting Started with R and RStudio
text:
1.8 A first plot
ggplot2 builds graphs in layers following a “grammar of graphics”. Every plot needs three elements:

data: the data frame;
aesthetics (aes()): which variables go on the x and y axes, colour, etc.;
geometry (geom_...()): how the data are drawn (points, boxes, bars…).


library(ggplot2)
ggplot(trial, aes(x = geno, y = yield_t_ha, fill = geno)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(colour = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "Genotype", y = "Grain yield (t/ha)") +
  theme_minimal()








Adding a layer is as simple as adding +. Here, the relationship between plant height and yield, with the parent and check highlighted:

ggplot(trial, aes(x = plant_height_cm, y = yield_t_ha, colour = check)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Plant height (cm)", y = "Grain yield (t/ha)", colour = "Parent/check") +
  theme_minimal()








To save a figure in the output/ folder:

ggsave("part0-precourse/output/yield_boxplot.png", width = 7, height = 4, dpi = 300)

Day 1 of the course covers visualization for exploratory analysis in detail.

section: 1.9 Importing real field data: a bean trial
text:
1.9 Importing real field data: a bean trial
The practice dataset is small and clean. Real trial files are larger and usually bring problems that must be solved before any analysis. In this section we import a real common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) trial from the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT and apply the same steps.

1.9.1 The dataset
crumbs: 1  Getting Started with R and RStudio

title: 1  Getting Started with R and RStudio
text:
1.10 Dataset context
The file data/Example_Beans.csv contains data from the Dar16C_hiP common bean field trial conducted in Darién, Colombia, in 2016 under high-phosphorus conditions. The trial was associated with the Bean Breeding Program of the International Center for Tropical Agriculture (CIAT), currently part of the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT.
The experiment used an alpha-lattice design to evaluate 380 bean lines in two replicates. Each replicate contained 18 incomplete blocks of 22 plots. Each row of the dataset represents one experimental plot, whose field position is identified by row and column coordinates within a 66 × 12 layout.
crumbs: 1  Getting Started with R and RStudio

title: 1  Getting Started with R and RStudio
text:
1.11 Response variables

DF – Days to flowering: Number of days from planting until the flowering criterion was reached.
\[
DF = \text{Flowering date} - \text{Planting date}
\]
DPM – Days to physiological maturity: Number of days from planting until the plants reached physiological maturity.
\[
DPM = \text{Maturity date} - \text{Planting date}
\]
PLHA – Plants harvested: Number of plants harvested from the experimental plot.
POM_c2 – Grain moisture: Moisture content of the harvested seed, expressed as a percentage. Seed weight was adjusted to a reference moisture content of 14% using:
\[
MCF = \frac{100-POM\_c2}{100-14}
\]
SW100 – 100-seed weight: Weight of 100 seeds, expressed in grams. This variable is an indicator of seed size.
\[
SW100 =
\frac{\text{Sample weight}}{\text{Number of seeds}}
\times 100
\]
TSW – Total seed weight: Total seed weight harvested from the plot, expressed in grams.
YDHA – Yield based on plot area: Grain yield in kilograms per hectare, calculated from the total seed weight corrected to 14% moisture and a harvested plot area of \(1.20\;m^2\).
\[
YDHA =
\frac{
TSW\left(\frac{100-POM\_c2}{86}\right)\times 10
}{1.20}
\]
YDHPL – Yield based on harvested plants: Grain yield in kilograms per hectare, estimated from seed production per harvested plant and extrapolated to a reference population of 180,000 plants per hectare.
\[
YDHPL =
\frac{TSW}{PLHA}
\left(\frac{100-POM\_c2}{86}\right)
\times 180
\]
YdHa_clean – Cleaned yield: Corrected grain yield in kilograms per hectare. Based on the numerical relationship observed in the dataset, the calculation uses an effective harvested area of approximately \(2.22\;m^2\).
\[
YdHa_{clean} =
\frac{
TSW\left(\frac{100-POM\_c2}{86}\right)\times 10
}{2.22}
\]








Column
Content




dataset
trial name


unique_identifier, plot
plot identifiers


line
bean line (genotype)


rep
replicate (R1, R2)


treatment
entry code in the field book


block
incomplete block within the replicate


row, col
plot position in the field


DF, DPM, PLHA, POM_c2, SW100, TSW, YDHA, YDHPL, YdHa_clean
measured traits




1.11.1 Import and first check

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
beans <- read_csv("data/Example_Beans.csv")
dim(beans)

The design columns (rep, block, row, col, line) must be factors. row and col were read as numbers, so we convert them as well:

beans <- beans |>
  mutate(across(c(rep, block, row, col, line), as.factor))
nlevels(beans$line) # number of genos (lines)

[1] 380




1.11.2 Finding the problems
Missing values. Count them per column before doing anything else:

colSums(is.na(beans))

          dataset unique_identifier              plot              line 
                0                 0                 0                 0 
              rep         treatment             block               row 
                0                 0                 0                 0 
              col                DF               DPM              PLHA 
                0                 0                 6                 4 
           POM_c2             SW100               TSW              YDHA 
                0                 4                 3                 4 
            YDHPL        YdHa_clean 
                4                 4 


Seven traits have between 3 and 6 missing plots. They are few, but they mean that some lines do not have data in both replicates, which matters when we compare them.
Repeated lines. The trial has 396 plots per replicate but only 380 lines. Some lines appear more than once:

beans |>
  count(line, rep) |>
  filter(n > 1)

# A tibble: 32 × 3
   line    rep       n
   <fct>   <fct> <int>
 1 AFR_298 R1        2

10 DAA_153 R2        2
# ℹ 22 more rows


Sixteen lines appear twice in each replicate, under different entry codes (treatment). This is common in breeding trials: checks or lines entered twice in the field book. Sixteen lines were intentionally included twice in the treatment list as repeated checks
Balance across replicates. Each replicate should contain the same entries:

table(beans$rep)


 R1  R2 
396 396 




1.11.3 Looking at the trial as an RCBD
The original design is an alpha-lattice (replicates divided into incomplete blocks), which we study on Day 2. Because each replicate contains all the entries, we can also look at the trial as a randomized complete block design (RCBD), using the replicate as the complete block and ignoring the incomplete blocks.
Mean yield of the best lines across the two replicates:

beans |>
  group_by(line) |>
  summarise(
    n_plots = sum(!is.na(YdHa_clean)),
    yield   = mean(YdHa_clean, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(yield)) |>
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 3
   line    n_plots yield
   <fct>     <int> <dbl>

Yield distribution in each replicate (block):

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(beans, aes(x = rep, y = YdHa_clean)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "Replicate (block)", y = "YdHa_clean") +
  theme_minimal()








Because the field position of every plot is recorded, we can also draw the trial as a map. Patterns in this map are the reason to use blocks and, on Day 4, spatial models:

beans |>
  mutate(row = as.numeric(row), col = as.numeric(col)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = row, y = col, fill = YdHa_clean)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  labs(x = "Row", y = "Column", fill = "YdHa_clean") +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal()










1.11.4 When the text looks wrong: file encoding
The file data/Example_rice.csv (a rice trial with irrigation and drought treatments) was saved with a Spanish Windows encoding (Latin-1). If we read it with the default settings, the accented letters are not shown correctly:

rice <- read_csv("data/Example_rice.csv")
unique(rice$TRAT) # Spanish accent marks detected

[1] "Irrigaci\xf3n" "Sequ\xeda"    


Telling R the encoding of the file solves the problem:

rice <- read_csv("data/Example_rice.csv",
                 locale = locale(encoding = "latin1"))
unique(rice$TRAT)

[1] "Irrigación" "Sequía"    


The same happens with names that contain letters such as č, š, ž or ğ. For Central European files saved in Windows, use encoding = "windows-1250". The best long-term solution is to save files from Excel as CSV UTF-8.






NoteChecklist for any new data file




Read the file and check the dimensions with dim().
Check column names and types with glimpse().
Count missing values per column.
Convert design variables to factors.
Check repeated genotypes and the balance across replicates.
Check that names and accents are displayed correctly.

1.13 Key takeaways

Work inside an RStudio project and use relative paths; avoid setwd().
Check every dataset right after importing it with glimpse() and summary(); European CSV files need read_csv2().
Genotype, replicate, block, row and column must be factors before modelling.
Five dplyr verbs (select, filter, mutate, arrange, group_by + summarise) cover most data preparation.
A ggplot2 graph is data + aesthetics + geometry, built in layers with +.

title: 2  Preparing Your Data in Tidy Format
text:
2.2 Why data organization matters
Most of the time spent on a data analysis is not spent on the statistics, but on preparing the data. A field book that is easy to read for a person (titles, merged cells, colours, totals) is usually very hard to read for a computer. The consequences are:

Lost time: hours of copying, deleting and reshaping before any analysis.
Silent errors: a missing plot typed as 0 is analysed as a real zero yield; a replicate written as text is not recognized; a value with its unit (4.2 t/ha) turns the whole column into text.
Results that cannot be repeated: manual changes in Excel leave no record, so nobody (including you, six months later) can know exactly what was done.




The 80/20 Rule of Data Work: Preparing vs. Analyzing Data.


If the data are organized well from the moment they are recorded, the analysis in R becomes a few lines of code. That is the goal of this chapter, and the reason why every participant prepares their dataset before the course.
crumbs: 2  Preparing Your Data in Tidy Format

title: 2  Preparing Your Data in Tidy Format
text:
2.3 What messy data looks like
The file data/messy_trial.xlsx contains the same M4 mutant trial that we used in Chapter 1, but written the way many field books are written in practice:






Figure 2.1: The practice trial stored as a typical field book in Excel.



The sheet is clear for a person, but it contains seven problems that prevent R from reading it correctly:








Problem
Where in Figure 2.1
Why it is a problem




Title above the header
Row 1
R takes the title as the column name


Double header
Rows 3 and 4: replicate on top, trait below
R needs one row of column names


Merged cells
Location, and Rep 1, Rep 2, Rep 3
Only the first cell has a value; the others are read as empty


One variable spread over several columns
Yield and height repeated for each replicate
The replicate is a variable, but it is hidden in the column names


Two variables in one column
Entry: M4-01_mutant (genotype and type)
You cannot filter or group by each one separately


Units and codes inside cells
4.2 t/ha; missing plots as . and -
The column becomes text instead of numbers


Information only in colours, comments and summary rows
Red row, the comment on M4-08, the Mean row
Colours and comments are lost when reading; the mean row is read as a plot



Other frequent problems are a missing plot written as 0 (it looks like real data), dates written in different formats in the same column, several tables in one sheet, and the same genotype written in different ways (M4-01, M4 01, m4-01).






WarningNever save a course CSV file from Excel



Opening a CSV file in Excel and saving it again can change the separators and destroy the numbers (for example, 938.067907 becomes 938.067.907 with some regional settings). To look at a CSV file, open it in RStudio (View File) or close Excel without saving.

title: 2  Preparing Your Data in Tidy Format
section: 2.4 The three rules of tidy data
text:
2.4 The three rules of tidy data
In R for Data Science, Wickham, Çetinkaya-Rundel and Grolemund describe a consistent way to organize data, called tidy data. A dataset is tidy when it follows three rules:

Each variable is a column, and each column is one variable.
Each observation is a row, and each row is one observation.
Each value is a cell, and each cell contains one value.




Three rules make a dataset tidy: variables are columns, observations are rows, and values are cells.


In a field trial, the observation is usually the plot. So a tidy field book has one row per plot and one column for each variable: the design variables (location, replicate, block, row, column, genotype) and the traits.
This is the tidy version of the trial in Figure 2.1:

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
trial <- read_csv("data/precourse_trial.csv")
trial |>
  select(location, rep, row, col, geno, check, yield_t_ha, plant_height_cm) |>
  head(8)

# A tibble: 8 × 8
  location   rep   row   col geno   check yield_t_ha plant_height_cm
  <chr>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <chr>  <chr>      <dbl>           <dbl>
1 Skopje       1     1     1 M4-01  no          4.6             86.3
2 Skopje       1     1     2 M4-10  no          3.77            93.4
3 Skopje       1     1     3 M4-06  no          3.24            84.3
4 Skopje       1     1     4 M4-02  no          4.04            88.8
5 Skopje       1     1     5 Parent yes         4.31            96.5
6 Skopje       1     1     6 M4-09  no          3.92            82.8
7 Skopje       1     1     7 M4-05  no          4.2             94  
8 Skopje       1     1     8 M4-08  no         NA               85  


The replicate, which was hidden in the column names of the messy file, is now a column. The 12 genotypes × 3 replicates are 36 rows, one per plot.






NoteWhy tidy data works so well in R



dplyr, ggplot2 and the model functions (lm(), lmer(), SpATS()…) all expect one row per observation and one column per variable. With a tidy dataset, the formula of the model is written directly from the column names: yield_t_ha ~ rep + geno.


Read more in the chapter Data tidying of R for Data Science (2nd edition): https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-tidy.html

section: 2.5 From messy to tidy in R
text:
2.5 From messy to tidy in R
Sometimes you receive a messy file that you cannot correct by hand (for example, historical data). Here we fix messy_trial.xlsx step by step, with the readxl, tidyr and dplyr packages.

2.5.1 Step 1. Look at the sheet as R sees it

library(readxl)
raw <- read_excel("data/messy_trial.xlsx", col_names = FALSE,
                  .name_repair = "minimal")
raw

# A tibble: 19 × 8
   ``                                  ``    ``    ``    ``    ``    ``    ``   
   <chr>                               <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr>
 1 Mutant trial M4 - Skopje 2025 - RC… <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA> 
 2 <NA>                                <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA> 
 3 Location                            Entry Rep 1 <NA>  Rep 2 <NA>  Rep 3 <NA> 
 4 <NA>                                <NA>  Yiel… Heig… Yiel… Heig… Yiel… Heig…
 5 Skopje                              M4-0… 4.6   86.3  4.16  103.1 .     91.7 
 6 <NA>                                M4-0… 4.04  88.8  3.61  86    3.14  90.2 
 7 <NA>                                M4-0… 5.9   104.3 4.86  102.3 5.08  100.2
 8 <NA>                                M4-0… 4.75  88.0… 3.99  93.5  3.52  97.4…
 9 <NA>                                M4-0… 4.2 … 94    4.19  95.7  3.51  90.0…
10 <NA>                                M4-0… 3.24  84.3  3.14  83.5  2.93  93.0…
11 <NA>                                M4-0… 5.68  103.6 4.85  103.4 4.36  106.5
12 <NA>                                M4-0… -     85    3.62  90.8  3.42  92.7 
13 <NA>                                M4-0… 3.92  82.8  2.98  89.3  2.66  84.3 
14 <NA>                                M4-1… 3.77  93.4… 4.07  93.5  3.27  93.8 
15 <NA>                                Pare… 4.31  96.5  4.38  90.2  3.92  91.5 
16 <NA>                                Chec… 5.2   97.8  4.94  89.7  4.58  98.7 
17 <NA>                                Mean  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA> 
18 <NA>                                <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA> 
19 Red = damaged plots. Missing plots… <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA> 


The title, the empty row, the two header rows, the merged cells (shown as NA), the mean row and the note at the bottom are all visible.


2.5.2 Step 2. Read only the data, with clear column names
range reads only the block with plot data (cells A5 to H16), which leaves out the title, the headers, the mean row and the note. na declares the codes used for missing values. The column names are written once, combining the replicate and the trait.

trial_wide <- read_excel(
  "data/messy_trial.xlsx",
  range     = "A5:H16",
  col_names = c("location", "entry",     # rename colnames
                "R1_yield", "R1_height",
                "R2_yield", "R2_height",
                "R3_yield", "R3_height"),
  na        = c("", ".", "-")
)
trial_wide

# A tibble: 12 × 8
   location entry       R1_yield R1_height R2_yield R2_height R3_yield R3_height
   <chr>    <chr>       <chr>        <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
 1 Skopje   M4-01_muta… 4.6           86.3     4.16     103.     NA         91.7
 2 <NA>     M4-02_muta… 4.04          88.8     3.61      86       3.14      90.2
 3 <NA>     M4-03_muta… 5.9          104.      4.86     102.      5.08     100. 
 4 <NA>     M4-04_muta… 4.75          88.1     3.99      93.5     3.52      97.4
 5 <NA>     M4-05_muta… 4.2 t/ha      94       4.19      95.7     3.51      90.1
 6 <NA>     M4-06_muta… 3.24          84.3     3.14      83.5     2.93      93.1
 7 <NA>     M4-07_muta… 5.68         104.      4.85     103.      4.36     106. 
 8 <NA>     M4-08_muta… <NA>          85       3.62      90.8     3.42      92.7
 9 <NA>     M4-09_muta… 3.92          82.8     2.98      89.3     2.66      84.3
10 <NA>     M4-10_muta… 3.77          93.4     4.07      93.5     3.27      93.8
11 <NA>     Parent_par… 4.31          96.5     4.38      90.2     3.92      91.5
12 <NA>     Check_check 5.2           97.8     4.94      89.7     4.58      98.7








TipBuilding the names from the double header automatically





With many columns, writing the names by hand is slow. You can read the two header rows and combine them. Merged cells appear as NA, so the replicate is first filled to the right:

header <- read_excel("data/messy_trial.xlsx", range = "C3:H4",
                     col_names = FALSE, .name_repair = "minimal")

# Row 1: rep labels. Fill empty cells (from merged cells) with the value before them
rep_row   <- vctrs::vec_fill_missing(unlist(header[1, ]), direction = "down")

# Row 2: trait names
trait_row <- unlist(header[2, ])

# Join them into column names, e.g. "Rep1_height"
paste(rep_row, trait_row, sep = "_")

[1] "Rep 1_Yield (t/ha)" "Rep 1_Height (cm)"  "Rep 2_Yield (t/ha)"
[4] "Rep 2_Height (cm)"  "Rep 3_Yield (t/ha)" "Rep 3_Height (cm)" 







2.5.3 Step 3. Fill the merged cells
Only the first row has the location; the merged cells were read as NA. fill() copies the last value down:

library(tidyr)
# Show the location column before the fix (it has empty cells / NA)
trial_wide$location

 [1] "Skopje" NA       NA       NA       NA       NA       NA       NA      
 [9] NA       NA       NA       NA      

# Fill each NA with the last location above it
trial_wide <- trial_wide |>
  fill(location)

# Show the location column again (now every row has a location)
trial_wide$location

 [1] "Skopje" "Skopje" "Skopje" "Skopje" "Skopje" "Skopje" "Skopje" "Skopje"
 [9] "Skopje" "Skopje" "Skopje" "Skopje"




2.5.4 Step 4. Remove the units typed inside the cells
Because of 4.2 t/ha, the column R1_yield was read as text. parse_number() keeps only the number:

library(tidyverse)
# Check the type of R1_yield before the fix
class(trial_wide$R1_yield)

[1] "character"

# Extract only the number from each value and turn the column into numeric
trial_wide <- trial_wide |>
  mutate(R1_yield = parse_number(R1_yield))

# Check the type again (now "numeric")
class(trial_wide$R1_yield)

[1] "numeric"




2.5.5 Step 5. Separate two variables stored in one column

# Split the "entry" column into two new columns at the "_" separator
# (the original "entry" column is removed)
trial_wide <- trial_wide |>
  separate_wider_delim(entry, delim = "_", names = c("geno", "type"))

# Show only the location, geno and type columns, first 3 rows,
# to check that fill() and separate_wider_delim() worked
trial_wide |> select(location, geno, type) |> head(3)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  location geno  type  
  <chr>    <chr> <chr> 
1 Skopje   M4-01 mutant
2 Skopje   M4-02 mutant
3 Skopje   M4-03 mutant




2.5.6 Step 6. One row per plot: from wide to long
The replicate is hidden in the column names (R1_yield, R2_height…). pivot_longer() moves it into its own column. With names_sep = "_", the first part of the name (R1) goes to the column rep and the second part (yield, height) becomes a column of values (.value).

# Make the table long: one row per genotype and rep
trial_tidy <- trial_wide |>
  pivot_longer(cols      = starts_with("R"),      # columns R1_yield, R1_height, ...
               names_to  = c("rep", ".value"),    # "R1" goes to rep; yield/height stay as columns
               names_sep = "_") |>                # split names at "_"
  mutate(rep = parse_number(rep)) |>              # "R1" becomes 1
  rename(yield_t_ha = yield, plant_height_cm = height)  # add units to the names
trial_tidy

# A tibble: 36 × 6
   location geno  type     rep yield_t_ha plant_height_cm
   <chr>    <chr> <chr>  <dbl>      <dbl>           <dbl>
 1 Skopje   M4-01 mutant     1       4.6             86.3
 2 Skopje   M4-01 mutant     2       4.16           103. 
 3 Skopje   M4-01 mutant     3      NA               91.7
 4 Skopje   M4-02 mutant     1       4.04            88.8
 5 Skopje   M4-02 mutant     2       3.61            86  
 6 Skopje   M4-02 mutant     3       3.14            90.2
 7 Skopje   M4-03 mutant     1       5.9            104. 
 8 Skopje   M4-03 mutant     2       4.86           102. 
 9 Skopje   M4-03 mutant     3       5.08           100. 
10 Skopje   M4-04 mutant     1       4.75            88.1
# ℹ 26 more rows


36 rows: one per plot. This is the same information as the clean file.


2.5.7 Step 7. Check the result
Compare the tidy data with the clean file used in Session 1. No rows should differ:

# clean file used in Session 1.
clean <- trial |> select(geno, rep, yield_t_ha, plant_height_cm)

# Find rows in "clean" that are NOT in "trial_tidy" (matching on all 4 columns)
# 0 rows = our cleaned version matches the original
anti_join(clean, trial_tidy, by = c("geno", "rep", "yield_t_ha", "plant_height_cm"))

# A tibble: 0 × 4
# ℹ 4 variables: geno <chr>, rep <dbl>, yield_t_ha <dbl>, plant_height_cm <dbl>


An empty result means that the two datasets are identical.






NoteWhat about the colours and the comment?



The red row and the comment on M4-08 (damaged by hail) cannot be read by R. That information must be stored as data, for example in a column damaged with the values yes / no. Information that exists only as a colour is usually lost.




2.5.8 The opposite: from long to wide
Sometimes a wide table is useful, for example to present yield per replicate in a report. pivot_wider() does the opposite of pivot_longer():

# This is the opposite of pivot_longer(). It gives a table that's easier for people to read, 
# with each genotype's reps side by side.
trial |>
  select(geno, rep, yield_t_ha) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = rep, values_from = yield_t_ha, names_prefix = "rep_") |>
  head(4)

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  geno  rep_1 rep_2 rep_3
  <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 M4-01  4.6   4.16 NA   
2 M4-10  3.77  4.07  3.27
3 M4-06  3.24  3.14  2.93
4 M4-02  4.04  3.61  3.14


The rule is: store and analyse the data in long format; make wide tables only to present results.

2.6 The course field book template
To avoid all these problems, organize your data with the template data/template_field_book.xlsx. It has three sheets: instructions, field_book and dictionary.
The field_book sheet has one row of column names and one row per plot:









Column
Content
Example
Required

Site of the trial
Skopje
yes


year
Year of planting
2025
yes


trial
Trial name or code
M4_yield_2025
yes


generation
Generation of the mutant material
M4
yes


design
Experimental design
RCBD
yes


plot
Plot number
17
yes


rep
Replicate
2
yes


block
Incomplete block (if the design has them)
5
if any


row, col
Position of the plot in the field
3, 8
recommended


geno
Genotype, mutant line or variety
M4-07
yes


check
Is the entry a parent or check?
yes / no
yes


traits
One column per trait, with the unit in the name
yield_t_ha
yes









TipRules for the template




One table per sheet. The header in row 1 only, with no titles or empty rows above it.
No merged cells. Repeat the value in every row (for example, the location).
Only numbers in trait columns. Put the unit in the column name (yield_t_ha), not in the cell.
Leave missing values empty. Do not use ., -, NA or 0.
No colours or comments as information: add a column (damaged, notes).
No totals or means inside the data: calculate them in R.
Simple column names: lower case, no spaces or accents (plant_height_cm).
Write genotype names always the same way (M4-01, never M4 01 or m4-01).
Save the sheet as CSV UTF-8 when you send it.




2.6.1 Why the metadata matter?
The design columns are not decoration: each one becomes a term of the statistical model.







Column
Used for




rep, block
Separating environmental variation from genetic variation (Day 2 and Day 3)


row, col
Spatial analysis of field trends (Day 4)


location, year
Multi-environment trials and G×E (Day 5)


generation, check
Comparing mutant lines with the parent (Dunnett test, Day 2) and decisions on advancement (week 2)



A trial without row and col cannot be corrected for spatial trends; a trial without rep cannot be analysed as a designed experiment. Record them in the field from the beginning.

2.7 The data dictionary
A column name such as DF or SW100 is clear for the person who recorded it, but not for a colleague or for you two years later. A data dictionary describes every column of the field book: what it is, its type, its unit and its possible values. It is the dictionary sheet of the template.
This is the dictionary of the practice trial, stored in data/precourse_trial_dictionary.csv:

knitr::kable(dictionary)

section: 2.9 Digital data collection: Field Book and GridScore NEXT
text:
2.9 Digital data collection: Field Book and GridScore NEXT
Recording data directly on a phone or tablet avoids transcription errors and produces files that are already close to tidy: one row per plot, with the plot identifier and its position.




Field Book
GridScore NEXT




Developed by
PhenoApps (open source)
James Hutton Institute (open source)


Devices
Android phones and tablets
Any device with a web browser (Android, iPhone, computer); works offline


Field layout
Imported from a CSV file
Defined as a grid of rows and columns


Data export
CSV
Excel and other formats


Installation
Install Field Book app (only for Android device)
Install Gridscore NEXT


Documentation
Field Book Documentation
Gridscore Documentation



The general workflow is the same in both apps:

Generate the field layout (randomization) with FielDHub (Day 2) or your own tool, with one row per plot and the columns plot, rep, row, col and geno.
Import the layout into the app.
Define the traits with their type, unit and valid range, using the data dictionary. A valid range prevents typing errors in the field (for example, a plant height of 950 cm instead of 95.0).
Collect the data plot by plot in the field.
Export the data and read them in R. Check them with check_dataset().

title: 2  Preparing Your Data in Tidy Format
text:
2.11 Key takeaways

A tidy dataset has one column per variable, one row per observation (plot) and one value per cell.
Merged cells, double headers, units inside cells, missing-value codes, colours and summary rows are the most common problems of field books.
read_excel(range, na), fill(), parse_number(), separate_wider_delim() and pivot_longer() fix most of them in R; but it is better to record the data tidy from the beginning.
Design columns (rep, block, row, col, location, year) become terms of the statistical model: record them in the field.
A data dictionary makes your data understandable for others and for yourself in the future.
Check every file with check_dataset() before the analysis.

text:
3.1 Learning objectives
This chapter builds on Chapter 2. There we organized the data in tidy format; here we look at how the data are produced in the field and how to check that they match the experiment that was planned.
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

crumbs: 3  Collecting and Validating Field Data

title: 3  Collecting and Validating Field Data
text:
Define a trait completely: name, method, scale, unit and timing
Recognize the phenotyping challenges of mutant populations
Identify the most common errors in field data and how to prevent them
Validate a field book against the field plan in R









TipThe agridat package



agridat, by Kevin Wright, contains more than 400 datasets from published agricultural experiments, with their original references. It is used in this chapter and in Chapter 4. If it is not installed yet:

install.packages("agridat")
crumbs: 3  Collecting and Validating Field Data

title: 3  Collecting and Validating Field Data
text:
3.2 Defining a trait
A column name such as height or disease is not enough. Two people can measure “plant height” in different ways (to the tip of the leaves or to the top of the stem; one plant or the mean of five) and obtain values that cannot be compared. A trait is completely defined when we know:








Element
Question
Example: plant height




Name
What is it called in the field book?
plant_height_cm


Method
How is it measured?
From the ground to the top of the main stem


Scale or unit
In what units, or with what scale?
Centimetres


Sampling
On what part of the plot?
Mean of 5 plants in the central rows


Timing
When?
At physiological maturity



The Crop Ontology (https://cropontology.org) provides standard trait definitions for many crops, each with a unique identifier. Using them makes data comparable between programs, locations and years. For example, the cassava trait plant architecture, visual rating 1 to 5 has the identifier CO_334:0000099, and its scale is defined with photographs:






Figure 3.1: Visual scale for cassava plant architecture (1 = excellent, 5 = very bad). Source: Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT.




3.2.1 Types of scales








Type
Example
How to analyse it




Continuous
Yield (t/ha), plant height (cm)
Means, ANOVA, mixed models


Count
Number of pods, tillers
Means or count models (Poisson)


Ordinal score
Disease 1 to 9, vigour 1 to 5
The distance between scores is not equal; medians, ordinal models


Categorical
Flower colour, mutant type
Frequencies, chi-square tests


Binary
Lodged yes/no, mutant/normal
Proportions, logistic models





3.2.2 The timing matters: a real example
The dataset lee.potatoblight contains resistance scores to late blight (Phytophthora infestans) in potato, on a 1 to 9 scale, from screening trials in New Zealand (Lee, 2009). In 1999, 80 genotypes were scored on five dates:

blight <- lee.potatoblight |>
  filter(year == 1999) |>
  droplevels()
table(blight$date)


1999-12-07 1999-12-16 1999-12-30 2000-01-07 2000-01-15 
       320        320        320        320        320 



ggplot(blight, aes(x = date, y = y)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#EAD9BC") +
  labs(x = "Date of scoring", y = "Blight score (1 to 9)") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 3.2: Blight scores of 80 potato genotypes on five dates in 1999 (data: lee.potatoblight).





In this trial the scores fall as the disease advances during the season, so the same plots receive very different scores depending on the date. A score without its date cannot be interpreted, and two locations scored at different times cannot be compared. Record the date of every measurement, write down which end of the scale is healthy, and define in the protocol when each trait is scored (for example, when the susceptible check reaches a defined level of damage).
crumbs: 3  Collecting and Validating Field Data

title: 3  Collecting and Validating Field Data
text:
3.3 Phenotyping mutant populations
Mutant populations add their own challenges to field data collection:

M1 plants often show physiological damage from the mutagen (reduced germination, sterility, abnormal leaves). Most of these effects are not inherited, so M1 plants are usually not selected on their phenotype.
Chimeras: an M1 plant can be a mosaic of mutated and non-mutated tissue. The mutation appears only in the seeds of some branches, spikes or panicles. Record which part of the M1 plant each M2 family comes from.
Segregation in M2: most induced mutations are recessive and appear for the first time in the M2, segregating within families. Data are collected plant by plant or by family row, not by plot.
Off-types: a plant that looks like a mutant may come from seed admixture or outcrossing. Including the parent (non-mutagenized) regularly in the field helps to tell mutants from off-types.
Confirmation: a putative mutant must be confirmed in the next generation (M3 or later). Keep the pedigree (M1 plant, M2 family, M2 plant) so the line can be traced back.







NoteWhat to record in early generations



Besides the traits, record as columns: m1_plant, m2_family, plant (in M2), mutant (yes / no), mutant_type (for example chlorophyll, dwarf, early flowering) and notes. Each observation still occupies one row: in M2 the observation is usually the plant, not the plot.
crumbs: 3  Collecting and Validating Field Data

title: 3  Collecting and Validating Field Data
text:
3.4 Common errors in field data








Error
Example
How to prevent it




Plot recorded twice
Plot 105 entered two times
Data collection app; check duplicates in R


Plot missing
One plot skipped while walking the field
Check the number of plots against the plan


Wrong plot order
Recording in serpentine order when the field book is in straight order
Record the plot number, not only the position; use barcodes


Typing errors
103 instead of 10.3
Valid ranges in the app; range checks in R


Different names for the same genotype
Ross, ross, ROSS
Use the names from the field plan; choose from a list in the app


Changed protocol
Different people, different scale or timing
Written protocol, trained evaluators, reference photos




3.4.1 Serpentine layouts
In many trials the plots are numbered in a serpentine (zig-zag) order, following the path of the planter or of the person walking the field. The dataset kling.augmented (Kling, accessed 2022) is an augmented design of meadowfoam with 50 new genotypes in one plot each and 3 checks repeated in 6 blocks:

plan <- kling.augmented |>
  mutate(type = if_else(name %in% c("Ross", "MF183", "Starlight"), name, "New genotype"))

ggplot(plan, aes(x = col, y = row, fill = type)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = plot), size = 3) +
  scale_y_reverse(breaks = 1:6) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Ross" = "#E07B39", "MF183" = "#4F7A3A",
                               "Starlight" = "#3E6FA8", "New genotype" = "grey85")) +
  labs(x = "Column", y = "Row", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 3.3: Field layout of the augmented trial. Numbers are plot numbers; coloured plots are the checks (data: kling.augmented).





Plot 112 is at the end of row 1 and plot 113 is directly below it: the numbering goes left to right in row 1, right to left in row 2, and so on. A person who records the data in a straight order (left to right in every row) assigns half of the values to the wrong plots, and no error message appears. This is why the field book must contain the plot number and its position.
This design is similar to an early-generation mutant trial: many entries without replication, and a few checks repeated in every block to estimate the environmental variation.
crumbs: 3  Collecting and Validating Field Data

title: 3  Collecting and Validating Field Data
section: 3.5 Validating the field data against the field plan
text:
3.5 Validating the field data against the field plan
The field plan is the list of plots, with their position and genotype, produced when the experiment was designed (for example with FielDHub, Day 2). The field data are what was recorded. Before any analysis, check that the two match.
To practise, we take the field plan of the augmented trial and create a copy of the field data with five errors that are typical of real field books:

field_plan <- kling.augmented |>
  select(plot, block, row, col, name)

# Field data as recorded, with five typical errors
field_data <- kling.augmented |>
  select(plot, name, tsw) |>
  filter(plot != 152) |>                                     # 1. a plot was skipped
  bind_rows(kling.augmented |>
              filter(plot == 105) |>
              select(plot, name, tsw)) |>                    # 2. plot 105 recorded twice
  mutate(name = if_else(plot == 107, "ross", name),          # 3. a name typed differently
         tsw  = if_else(plot == 130, tsw * 10, tsw),         # 4. a decimal error
         plot = if_else(plot == 116, 216L, plot))            # 5. a wrong plot number

nrow(field_plan); nrow(field_data)

[1] 68


[1] 68


The number of rows already gives a warning: 68 plots planned, 68 rows recorded, but not the same plots. We now find each problem.

3.5.1 Duplicated plots

field_data |>
  count(plot) |>
  filter(n > 1)

  plot n
1  105 2




3.5.2 Planned plots without data, and data without a planned plot
anti_join() keeps the rows of the first table that have no match in the second:

anti_join(field_plan, field_data, by = "plot")   # planned but not recorded

  plot block row col name
1  116    B2   2   9  105
2  152    B5   5   4  123

anti_join(field_data, field_plan, by = "plot")   # recorded but not in the plan

  plot name   tsw
1  216  105 10.27


Plot 152 was never recorded, plot 116 is missing because it was typed as 216, which does not exist in the plan.


3.5.3 Genotype names that do not match the plan

field_data |>
  inner_join(field_plan, by = "plot", suffix = c("_data", "_plan")) |>
  filter(name_data != name_plan) |>
  select(plot, name_data, name_plan)

  plot name_data name_plan
1  107      ross      Ross




3.5.4 Values outside the valid range
The valid range comes from the data dictionary (Chapter 2). For thousand seed weight of meadowfoam, values between 5 and 20 g are plausible:

field_data |>
  filter(tsw < 5 | tsw > 20)

  plot name   tsw
1  130 Ross 103.2


A value of about 100 g is ten times the others: a decimal error. Look at the original field sheet before correcting it.


3.5.5 Checks in every block
In an augmented design, every block must contain every check exactly once:

field_plan |>
  filter(name %in% c("Ross", "MF183", "Starlight")) |>
  count(block, name) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = name, values_from = n)

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  block MF183  Ross Starlight
  <fct> <int> <int>     <int>
1 B1        1     1         1
2 B2        1     1         1
3 B3        1     1         1
4 B4        1     1         1
5 B5        1     1         1
6 B6        1     1         1








TipA validation routine for every trial




Same number of plots as the plan?
Any duplicated plot numbers?
Any planned plots without data, or data without a planned plot?
Do genotype names agree with the plan?
Are all values inside their valid range?
Does every block or replicate contain what the design requires?

Then run check_dataset() (Chapter 2). Never correct a value without checking the original field sheet or the app, and record every correction in a script, not by hand in Excel.
crumbs: 3  Collecting and Validating Field Data

title: 3  Collecting and Validating Field Data
text:
3.6 Exercise
The dataset stroup.nin is a wheat trial of the Nebraska Intrastate Nursery (Stroup et al., 1994), with 56 genotypes in an RCBD with 4 replicates.

How many plots have no yield (NA)?
Which genotype name do these plots have? And which replicate?
Why is this coding dangerous for the analysis?
Create a corrected version where these plots have gen as NA.







TipSolution






# 1. Plots without yield
sum(is.na(stroup.nin$yield))

[1] 18

# 2. Their genotype and replicate
stroup.nin |>
  filter(is.na(yield)) |>
  count(gen, rep)

     gen  rep  n
1 Lancer <NA> 18



The 18 plots without yield were coded with the name of a real cultivar (Lancer) and without replicate. They are positions of the field grid without data, kept so that the grid is complete for spatial analysis (the package documentation explains why). If they are not detected, Lancer appears with 22 plots instead of 4, and any count or mean per genotype is wrong.


# 4. Corrected version
nin <- stroup.nin |>
  mutate(gen = if_else(is.na(rep), NA, as.character(gen)))
nin |> count(gen == "Lancer")

  gen == "Lancer"   n
1           FALSE 220
2            TRUE   4
3              NA  18
crumbs: 3  Collecting and Validating Field Data

title: 3  Collecting and Validating Field Data
text:
3.7 Key takeaways

A trait is completely defined by its name, method, scale or unit, sampling and timing. Use the Crop Ontology when possible.
Record the date of every measurement: scores change during the season.
In mutant populations, keep the pedigree (M1 plant, M2 family, plant), include the parent regularly, and confirm mutants in the next generation.
Record the plot number and its position; serpentine numbering is a frequent source of silent errors.
Validate every field book against the field plan: duplicates, missing plots, unknown plots, names, valid ranges and the design.
