title: 4  Data Quality Control and Exploratory Analysis
text:
4.1 Learning objectives
In Chapter 3 we checked that the field book matches the field plan. Now we check the values. Quality control (QC) and exploratory data analysis (EDA) are the last steps before the statistical analysis of the next days: they do not produce results for a report, but they decide whether the results of the analysis can be trusted.
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(agridat)   # install.packages("agridat") if needed, see @sec-field-data
crumbs: 4  Data Quality Control and Exploratory Analysis

title: 4  Data Quality Control and Exploratory Analysis
text:
Detect missing values and decide what they mean
Check that values are possible and consistent between traits
Find outliers and decide whether they are errors or biology
Summarize traits by genotype and replicate, and use the CV as a quality indicator
Use plots and field maps to separate biological from technical variation
crumbs: 4  Data Quality Control and Exploratory Analysis

title: 4  Data Quality Control and Exploratory Analysis
text:
4.2 The QC workflow
The same questions are asked, in this order, for every trial:

Missing values. How many, in which traits, in which plots? Is there a pattern?
Possible values. Is every value inside the biological limits of the trait?
Consistency between traits. Do traits that depend on each other agree?
Outliers. Which values are unusual, and are they errors or real?
Summaries and plots. Means and CV by replicate and genotype, distributions, correlations and field maps.

Every decision is written in the R script, never made by hand in Excel. The raw file is not changed: corrections are made in code, so that anyone can see and repeat them.
crumbs: 4  Data Quality Control and Exploratory Analysis

title: 4  Data Quality Control and Exploratory Analysis
text:
4.3 The data
We use the common bean trial Dar16C_hiP introduced in Chapter 1: 380 lines in an alpha-lattice with 2 replicates, 792 plots in a field of 66 rows and 12 columns. Replicate R1 occupies columns 1 to 6 and R2 columns 7 to 12.

beans <- read_csv("data/Example_Beans.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

traits <- c("DF", "DPM", "PLHA", "POM_c2", "SW100", "TSW",
            "YDHA", "YDHPL", "YdHa_clean")

# one row per plot and trait: convenient for checks on all traits at once
beans_long <- beans |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(traits), names_to = "trait", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(trait = factor(trait, levels = traits))

A first overview of all traits in one table:

overview <- beans_long |>
  group_by(trait) |>
  summarise(
    n       = sum(!is.na(value)),
    missing = sum(is.na(value)),
    min     = min(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    median  = median(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    max     = max(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    cv      = 100 * sd(value, na.rm = TRUE) / mean(value, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  mutate(across(min:cv, \(x) round(x, 1)))
overview

# A tibble: 9 × 7
  trait          n missing   min median    max    cv
  <fct>      <int>   <int> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 DF           792       0  37     40     49     8  
2 DPM          786       6  77     81     86     2  
3 PLHA         788       4  17     27     47    12.7
4 POM_c2       792       0  10.9   11.6   14.2   3.3
5 SW100        788       4  22     54     79    14.6
6 TSW          789       3  31.8  295.   566.   30.5
7 YDHA         788       4 272   2493.  4752.   29.9
8 YDHPL        788       4 343   1970.  4476.   31.9
9 YdHa_clean   788       4 147   1357.  2608    30.4


This table already answers several questions: there are few missing values, no negative values, and the CV is very different between traits. We go through each point.
crumbs: 4  Data Quality Control and Exploratory Analysis

title: 4  Data Quality Control and Exploratory Analysis
text:
4.4 Missing values

4.4.1 Where are they?

beans |>
  filter(if_any(all_of(traits), is.na)) |>
  select(plot, line, rep, row, col, all_of(traits))

# A tibble: 12 × 14
    plot line       rep     row   col    DF   DPM  PLHA POM_c2 SW100   TSW  YDHA
   <dbl> <chr>      <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
 1  4540 LPA_512    R2       12     9    40    81    29   12.2    57 467.    NA 
 2  4252 DAB_607    R1       13     4    44    82    NA   11.6    NA  NA     NA 
 3  4151 SEQ_1003   R1       19     3    43    82    NA   11.6    NA 259.  2215.
 4  4506 DAN_011    R2       23     8    40    82    NA   11.6    NA  NA     NA 
 5  4625 NUA_184    R2       36    10    48    86    24   12.1    52 506.  3883.
 6  4039 DAB_053    R1       39     1    47    NA    28   11.6    58 219.  1876.
 7  4047 SAB_576    R1       47     1    46    NA    31   11.6    44 160.  1365.
 8  4051 CAL_096    R1       51     1    40    NA    28   11.8    69 246.  2106.
 9  4082 NUA_398    R1       51     2    48    NA    20   11.6    50  54.8  507.
10  4068 DAA_151    R1       65     2    42    NA    26   11.6    50  86.7  741.
11  4197 TIO_CANEL… R1       65     3    49    NA    32   12.3    22 327.  2775.
12  4463 SAB_576    R2       66     8    40    82    NA   11.6    NA  NA     NA 
# ℹ 2 more variables: YDHPL <dbl>, YdHa_clean <dbl>


Only 12 of the 792 plots have a missing value, but they are not all of the same kind:

Lost plots. Plots 4252, 4506 and 4463 have flowering and maturity dates, but no harvest data (PLHA, SW100, TSW). The plot existed in the field but was not harvested, or the harvest bag was lost.
One trait not recorded. Six plots have no DPM (days to maturity). All are in R1, columns 1 to 3, rows 39 to 65: a group of neighbouring plots, probably not visited on the day maturity was scored.
Derived trait not calculated. Plot 4540 has TSW and POM_c2 but no YDHA, and plot 4625 has no YdHa_clean. The raw data are there; the calculation was not done. These values can be recovered by calculating them again (see below).

A field map shows whether missing values are scattered or grouped:

beans_long |>
  group_by(row, col) |>
  summarise(missing = any(is.na(value)), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = row, y = col, fill = missing)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 6.5, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey85", `TRUE` = "firebrick"),
                    labels = c("complete", "with missing")) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(3.5, 9.5), labels = c("R1", "R2")) +
  labs(x = "Field row", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 4.1: Plots with at least one missing value. Each tile is a plot; R1 occupies columns 1 to 6 and R2 columns 7 to 12.







4.4.2 What to do with them

Never replace a missing value with 0. A plot that was not harvested did not yield zero; a zero would pull down the mean of the genotype. Leave the cell empty (NA).
Do not delete whole plots for one missing trait. na.omit() keeps only complete rows:


nrow(beans)

[1] 792

nrow(na.omit(beans))

[1] 780


Twelve plots are lost for all traits, although most of them have only one value missing. Remove missing values trait by trait, inside each analysis (na.rm = TRUE, or the mixed models of Chapter 7, which use all available plots).

Ask why they are missing. If missing values are linked to the genotype (for example, a mutant line that never flowered, or plants that died), they are information, not noise. Record the reason in a notes column: “not flowered” is a result; “not recorded” is not.
crumbs: 4  Data Quality Control and Exploratory Analysis

title: 4  Data Quality Control and Exploratory Analysis
text:
4.5 Possible values
Each trait has biological limits. A value outside them is an error, whatever the statistics say. The limits are set by the breeder before looking at the data:

limits <- tribble(
  ~trait,   ~low, ~high,
  "DF",       25,    70,   # days to flowering, common bean
  "DPM",      60,   110,   # days to maturity
  "PLHA",      1,    60,   # plants harvested per plot
  "POM_c2",    5,    25,   # grain moisture, %
  "SW100",    10,    90,   # g per 100 seeds
  "TSW",       0,  1500    # g per plot
)

beans_long |>
  inner_join(limits, by = "trait") |>
  filter(value < low | value > high)

# A tibble: 0 × 13
# ℹ 13 variables: dataset <chr>, unique_identifier <chr>, plot <dbl>,
#   line <chr>, rep <chr>, treatment <chr>, block <chr>, row <dbl>, col <dbl>,
#   trait <chr>, value <dbl>, low <dbl>, high <dbl>


No value is impossible. Some checks involve two traits; for example, a plant cannot mature before it flowers:

beans |> filter(DPM <= DF) |> nrow()

[1] 0

range(beans$DPM - beans$DF, na.rm = TRUE)   # days from flowering to maturity

[1] 32 45


Passing these checks does not mean that the data are correct, only that they are not impossible. A plot height of 95 cm typed as 59 cm is inside the limits; only the next checks can find it.
crumbs: 4  Data Quality Control and Exploratory Analysis

title: 4  Data Quality Control and Exploratory Analysis
text:
4.6 Consistency between traits
YDHA, YDHPL and YdHa_clean are not measured: they are calculated from TSW, POM_c2 and PLHA with the formulas given in Chapter 1. If we calculate them again, the result must be the same as the stored value:

beans_check <- beans |>
  mutate(
    mcf        = (100 - POM_c2) / 86,           # moisture correction to 14%
    YDHA_new   = TSW * mcf * 10 / 1.2,
    clean_new  = TSW * mcf * 10 / 2.22,
    ratio_YDHA = YDHA / YDHA_new,
    ratio_clean = YdHa_clean / clean_new
  )

beans_check |>
  summarise(
    YDHA_disagree  = sum(abs(ratio_YDHA - 1) > 0.02, na.rm = TRUE),
    clean_disagree = sum(abs(ratio_clean - 1) > 0.02, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  YDHA_disagree clean_disagree
          <int>          <int>
1            37              0


YdHa_clean agrees with its formula in every plot, but YDHA differs by more than 2% in 37 plots:

beans_check |>
  mutate(agrees = abs(ratio_YDHA - 1) <= 0.02) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = YDHA_new, y = YDHA, colour = agrees)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "grey60", `FALSE` = "firebrick")) +
  labs(x = "YDHA calculated again (kg/ha)", y = "YDHA stored in the file (kg/ha)",
       colour = "Agrees") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 4.2: Stored YDHA against YDHA calculated again from TSW and grain moisture. Points away from the line are plots where the stored value is inconsistent with the raw data.





Most of these plots have a stored value lower than the calculated one, as if TSW had been changed (for example, after weighing the seed again) and YDHA was not updated. We cannot know which number is right without the original field book, but the lesson is general:






ImportantDerived traits



Store the raw measurements (weights, counts, dates) and calculate derived traits in R, every time, from those measurements. A value calculated once in Excel and pasted into the file is not updated when a raw value is corrected. In this trial we use YdHa_clean, which is consistent with TSW, and leave YDHA out.
crumbs: 4  Data Quality Control and Exploratory Analysis

title: 4  Data Quality Control and Exploratory Analysis
text:
4.7 Outliers
An outlier is a value far from the others. It can be an error (a typing mistake, a wrong unit, a damaged plot) or a real value (a genotype that is truly different). In a mutant population, real outliers are exactly what we are looking for, so outliers are flagged and examined, never deleted automatically.

4.7.1 Flagging with the IQR rule
A common rule, the one used by boxplots, flags values more than 1.5 times the interquartile range (IQR) below the first quartile or above the third quartile:

flag_iqr <- function(x) {
  q   <- quantile(x, c(0.25, 0.75), na.rm = TRUE)
  iqr <- q[2] - q[1]
  x < q[1] - 1.5 * iqr | x > q[2] + 1.5 * iqr
}

beans_long |>
  group_by(trait) |>
  mutate(outlier = flag_iqr(value)) |>
  summarise(flagged = sum(outlier, na.rm = TRUE))

# A tibble: 9 × 2
  trait      flagged
  <fct>        <int>
1 DF               0
2 DPM              2
3 PLHA            18
4 POM_c2          22
5 SW100           27
6 TSW              6
7 YDHA             3
8 YDHPL           10
9 YdHa_clean       6


The rule flags dozens of values. A flag is only the start: each one must be examined in context.


4.7.2 Biology or error? Look at the other replicate
Seed size (SW100) has 27 flagged values. If a value is real, the same line should show it in the other replicate:

sw_flagged <- beans |>
  filter(flag_iqr(SW100)) |>
  distinct(line)

beans |>
  filter(line %in% sw_flagged$line) |>
  group_by(line, rep) |>
  summarise(SW100 = mean(SW100, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = rep, values_from = SW100)

# A tibble: 16 × 3
   line             R1    R2
   <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>
 1 AMADEUS        28      29
 2 DAA_014        75      59
 3 DAA_021        79      65
 4 DAA_045        74      66
 5 DAB_049        28      29
 6 DAB_052        27      26
 7 DAB_187        35      43
 8 DAB_574        72      64
 9 DAN_032        73      64
10 DOR_364        23      22
11 DOR_390        26      23
12 LPA_467        23      50
13 SEF_060        29      28
14 SEN_056        22      27
15 SER_118        32      27
16 TIO_CANELA_75  22.5    24


Almost every line is small-seeded (around 22 to 30 g, for example TIO_CANELA_75 and the DOR lines) or large-seeded (around 60 to 79 g, for example the DAA lines) in both replicates. These are real differences between genotypes: they are kept. The exception is LPA_467: 23 g in R1 and 50 g in R2. The same plot in R1 has only 17 plants and a yield of 147 kg/ha, the lowest of the trial. That plot was damaged; it is a candidate to be set to NA.


4.7.3 Look at the position in the field
Plants harvested (PLHA) has 14 values flagged as too high. Their positions:

beans |>
  filter(flag_iqr(PLHA), PLHA > median(PLHA, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  select(line, rep, row, col, PLHA) |>
  arrange(row)

# A tibble: 14 × 5
   line    rep     row   col  PLHA
   <chr>   <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
 1 AFR_735 R1        1     4    37
 2 SEN_056 R1        1     6    43
 3 NUA_365 R2        1     8    37
 4 NDZ_002 R2        1    10    37
 5 DAA_145 R2        1    11    40
 6 LPA_772 R2        5    10    38
 7 DOR_390 R1       30     4    39
 8 DAB_489 R1       31     1    36
 9 NDZ_008 R1       33     1    37
10 LPA_771 R1       36     5    36
11 DAB_938 R1       40     3    36
12 DOR_364 R1       54     2    36
13 AMADEUS R1       66     3    47
14 SER_118 R1       66     6    40


Seven of the 14 are in row 1 or row 66, the two ends of the field. Border plots often have more plants or bigger plants, because they have more space and light. This is a technical effect of the position, not of the genotype, and it is one reason for the spatial analysis of Chapter 9.


4.7.4 Deciding







What you find
Decision




Confirmed error (typing, unit, wrong plot) and the true value is known
Correct it in the script, with a comment


Confirmed error, true value unknown, or plot damaged
Set it to NA, with a comment


Real value, consistent across replicates
Keep it


Not sure
Keep it, flag it, and run the analysis with and without it




beans_qc <- beans |>
  mutate(
    # LPA_467, R1: damaged plot (17 plants, 147 kg/ha, seed weight half of R2)
    across(c(SW100, TSW, YDHPL, YdHa_clean),
           \(x) if_else(plot == 4186, NA, x))
  ) |>
  select(-YDHA)   # inconsistent with TSW, see above

After the analysis model is fitted (Days 2 and 3), outliers are checked again on the residuals: a value can look normal for the whole trial but be unusual for its genotype and block.
crumbs: 4  Data Quality Control and Exploratory Analysis

title: 4  Data Quality Control and Exploratory Analysis
text:
4.8 Summaries by replicate and genotype

4.8.1 Replicates

beans_qc |>
  group_by(rep) |>
  summarise(
    plots = sum(!is.na(YdHa_clean)),
    mean  = mean(YdHa_clean, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd    = sd(YdHa_clean, na.rm = TRUE),
    cv    = 100 * sd / mean
  )

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  rep   plots  mean    sd    cv
  <chr> <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 R1      394 1326.  430.  32.4
2 R2      393 1418.  393.  27.7


The replicates have similar means: there is no large difference between the two halves of the field. Within each replicate, the incomplete blocks also differ:

beans_qc |>
  mutate(block = factor(block, levels = paste0("B", 1:18))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = block, y = YdHa_clean)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "grey90") +
  facet_wrap(~rep, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Incomplete block", y = "Yield (kg/ha)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, size = 7))







Figure 4.3: Yield by incomplete block within each replicate.





This variation between blocks is the reason the trial was laid out as an alpha-lattice, and the blocks will be part of the model (Chapter 5).


4.8.2 The CV as a quality indicator
The coefficient of variation, \(CV = 100 \times SD / \text{mean}\), compares variability between traits measured in different units. It is a first indicator of trial quality:

overview |> select(trait, cv) |> arrange(cv)

# A tibble: 9 × 2
  trait         cv
  <fct>      <dbl>
1 DPM          2  
2 POM_c2       3.3
3 DF           8  
4 PLHA        12.7
5 SW100       14.6
6 YDHA        29.9
7 YdHa_clean  30.4
8 TSW         30.5
9 YDHPL       31.9



Days to maturity (2%) and grain moisture (3%) vary little, as expected.
Yield and total seed weight have a CV around 30%. This CV contains both the differences between genotypes and the error, so it is not yet the error CV of the ANOVA (Chapter 6), but it is high. It warns that much of the yield variation could come from the field.



4.8.3 Checks and agreement between replicates
Sixteen lines appear in 4 plots (twice in each replicate): they are the checks. Because a check is the same genotype everywhere, its variation is only field variation:

checks <- beans_qc |> count(line) |> filter(n == 4) |> pull(line)

beans_qc |>
  filter(line %in% checks) |>
  group_by(line) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(YdHa_clean, na.rm = TRUE),
            cv   = 100 * sd(YdHa_clean, na.rm = TRUE) / mean) |>
  arrange(cv)

# A tibble: 16 × 3
   line           mean    cv
   <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>
 1 SAB_686       1443.  5.74
 2 DAB_494       1359.  8.84
 3 AFR_722       1542. 10.5 
 4 CAL_096       1240. 10.7 
 5 SAB_560       1725. 13.7 
 6 SEQ_1003      1408. 17.5 
 7 DAB_295       1643. 19.1 
 8 DAB_251       1748. 21.8 
 9 TIO_CANELA_75 1924. 22.7 
10 AFR_298       1523. 23.3 
11 DAA_153       1679. 30.2 
12 SAB_659       1417. 30.5 
13 CAL_143       1068. 31.6 
14 RAA_034       1738. 39.3 
15 DAB_932       1176. 45.6 
16 DAB_614       1128. 48.1 


The same genotype varies from 6% to almost 50% depending on the check. The same idea applies to all lines: if a trait is mostly genetic, a line that is high in R1 is also high in R2.

rep_means <- beans_qc |>
  group_by(line, rep) |>
  summarise(across(c(SW100, YdHa_clean), \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_longer(c(SW100, YdHa_clean), names_to = "trait") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = rep, values_from = value)

rep_means |>
  group_by(trait) |>
  summarise(r = cor(R1, R2, use = "complete.obs"))

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  trait          r
  <chr>      <dbl>
1 SW100      0.760
2 YdHa_clean 0.284

ggplot(rep_means, aes(R1, R2)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, formula = y ~ x) +
  facet_wrap(~trait, scales = "free") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 4.4: Line means in R1 against R2. Seed size agrees well between replicates; yield much less.





The correlation between replicates is high for seed size and low for yield. This is a first, rough view of heritability (Section 7.7): for yield in this trial, a single plot says little about the genotype, and the analysis must remove as much field variation as possible.
crumbs: 4  Data Quality Control and Exploratory Analysis

title: 4  Data Quality Control and Exploratory Analysis
text:
4.9 Exploratory plots

4.9.1 Distributions

beans_qc |>
  pivot_longer(c(DF, DPM, PLHA, POM_c2, SW100, TSW, YdHa_clean),
               names_to = "trait") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~trait, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Plots") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 4.5: Distribution of each trait.





Things to look for: long tails, groups separated from the rest, spikes at round numbers (a sign of estimated rather than measured values), and two peaks. Days to flowering has two groups, around 39 and 46 days: early and late lines. In a mutant population, two peaks in a trait can be the first sign of a mutation with a large effect.


4.9.2 Correlations between traits

cor_mat <- beans_qc |>
  select(DF, DPM, PLHA, POM_c2, SW100, TSW, YdHa_clean) |>
  cor(use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

as.data.frame(as.table(cor_mat)) |>
  ggplot(aes(Var1, Var2, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(Freq, 2)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "firebrick", mid = "white", high = "steelblue",
                       limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "r") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 4.6: Correlations between traits (Pearson, plot level).





TSW and YdHa_clean have a correlation of 1: one is calculated from the other, so they are the same information. Days to flowering and to maturity go together. Correlations that are absent where biology expects them, or present where it does not, are worth a second look at the data.


4.9.3 Field maps
A field map is the most useful QC plot. It shows technical variation that no table can show:

ggplot(beans_qc, aes(x = row, y = col, fill = YdHa_clean)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 6.5, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(na.value = "white") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(3.5, 9.5), labels = c("R1", "R2")) +
  labs(x = "Field row", y = NULL, fill = "kg/ha") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 4.7: Yield of each plot in the field. White tiles are missing values.





Since genotypes are randomized, a genotype effect looks like random noise on the map. Patches, stripes or gradients are field effects: soil, water, border, management. In this trial yields are higher in some areas of the field and the lowest plots of the trial are close together in R1 (rows 51 to 56, columns 2 and 3), around the damaged plot of LPA_467 (now white). A small patch of poor soil or water damage there is more likely than several weak genotypes side by side.
A clearer example is the Nebraska wheat trial of Stroup et al. (1994), in agridat: 56 genotypes in 4 complete blocks.

ggplot(stroup.nin, aes(x = col, y = row, fill = yield)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(na.value = "white") +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Column", y = "Row", fill = "bu/ac") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 4.8: Wheat yield (bu/ac) in the Nebraska Intrastate Nursery trial. Data: Stroup et al. (1994), via agridat.





The low yields are clustered in one corner of the field. The authors explain it by a low rise in that part of the field, exposed to winter kill from wind. The genotype Buckskin, a known superior variety, was disadvantaged in this trial by the unfavourable positions of its plots. A plain RCBD analysis cannot correct this, because the patch is smaller than a block; Chapter 9 shows how spatial models do.

title: 4  Data Quality Control and Exploratory Analysis
text:
4.11 Key takeaways

QC follows a fixed order: missing values, possible values, consistency between traits, outliers, summaries and plots.
Missing values are left empty, never set to zero, and removed trait by trait, not plot by plot. Their pattern tells you why they are missing.
Calculate derived traits in R from the raw measurements; do not trust values calculated once in a spreadsheet.
Outliers are flagged and examined, not deleted. Consistency across replicates points to biology; a damaged plot, a field border or a patch points to error or field effects.
The CV, the checks and the agreement between replicates show how much of the variation is field and how much is genotype.
Always draw a field map. Technical variation is spatial, and the next days of the course show how to model it.

title: 5  Experimental Designs for Plant Breeding Trials
text:
5.1 Learning objectives
In Chapter 4 we saw that much of the variation in a trial comes from the field, not from the genotypes. This chapter is about the decisions taken before sowing that control that variation. A good design does not make the field more uniform; it arranges the plots so that the field effects can be separated from the genotype effects in the analysis (Chapter 6 and Chapter 7).
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(lme4)
library(emmeans)
library(agridat)    # install.packages("agridat") if needed
library(FielDHub)   # install.packages("FielDHub") if needed
crumbs: 5  Experimental Designs for Plant Breeding Trials

title: 5  Experimental Designs for Plant Breeding Trials
text:
Explain the three principles of design: replication, randomization and local control
Recognize the main designs used in breeding trials and when to use each one
Generate and randomize field layouts with FielDHub
Compare the precision of designs on a real field
Write the statistical model implied by a design
crumbs: 5  Experimental Designs for Plant Breeding Trials

title: 5  Experimental Designs for Plant Breeding Trials
text:
5.2 Why design matters
Three principles, proposed by R. A. Fisher in the 1920s, are the basis of every field design:








Principle
What it means
Why




Replication
Each genotype in more than one plot
Estimates the error; more plots per genotype give more precise means


Randomization
Genotypes allocated to plots at random
Avoids systematic advantages; makes the error estimate valid


Local control (blocking)
Similar plots grouped into blocks
Removes field variation from the comparison of genotypes




5.2.1 What a field looks like without genotypes
The best way to see field variation is a uniformity trial: one single variety sown over the whole field and harvested plot by plot. Every difference between plots is then field, not genotype. The barley uniformity trial of Williams and Luckett (1988) has 720 plots in 15 rows and 48 columns:

williams <- williams.barley.uniformity |>
  mutate(yield = yield / 100)   # kg/ha divided by 10, converted to t/ha

ggplot(williams, aes(x = col, y = row, fill = yield)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Column", y = "Row", fill = "t/ha") +
  theme_minimal()

williams |>
  summarise(min = min(yield), max = max(yield),
            variance = var(yield), sd = sd(yield))

   min  max   variance        sd
1 1.45 3.29 0.08360067 0.2891378








Figure 5.1: Uniformity trial of barley: one variety, 720 plots. All the variation is due to the field. Data: Williams and Luckett (1988), via agridat.





With a single variety, yield goes from 1.45 to 3.29 t/ha, with a standard deviation of 0.29 t/ha. Two genotypes that differ by 0.3 t/ha could swap positions just by the plots they happen to fall on. The map also shows that neighbouring plots are more similar than distant ones, and that the variation is not the same in both directions. There is even a systematic pattern linked to groups of three columns:

williams |>
  group_by(col) |>
  summarise(yield = mean(yield)) |>
  mutate(position = factor((col - 1) %% 3 + 1)) |>
  ggplot(aes(col, yield)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = position), size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Column", y = "Mean yield (t/ha)",
       colour = "Position in\nseeder pass") +
  theme_minimal()

williams |>
  group_by(position = (col - 1) %% 3 + 1) |>
  summarise(yield = mean(yield))

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  position yield
     <dbl> <dbl>
1        1  2.32
2        2  2.45
3        3  2.53








Figure 5.2: Mean yield of each column of the uniformity trial, coloured by the position of the column in each group of three (the width of the three-plot seeder).





The trial was sown with a three-plot seeder, and Williams noted that the yield depends on the position of the plot in each pass. Columns in the first position of each group of three yield on average about 0.1 to 0.2 t/ha less than the other two. This is extraneous variation: it comes from how the trial was managed, not from the soil. Blocks that follow the columns will capture it; large blocks will not.


5.2.2 Complications in breeding trials
Classical designs were developed for experiments with a few treatments. Breeding trials are different:

There is one factor, the genotype, with many levels (from 100 to several thousand lines).
Replication is costly, and in early generations there is often seed for only one plot.
The field is heterogeneous in more than one direction, as the uniformity trial shows.

With 300 genotypes, a complete block has 300 plots: it is too large to be uniform. The solution is incomplete blocks: blocks smaller than the number of genotypes.
crumbs: 5  Experimental Designs for Plant Breeding Trials

title: 5  Experimental Designs for Plant Breeding Trials
text:
5.3 The main designs

5.3.1 Classical designs








Design
Structure
Use in breeding




CRD, completely randomized
Genotypes allocated at random to all plots, no blocks
Uniform conditions only: growth chambers, some greenhouse trials


RCBD, randomized complete blocks
Each block contains every genotype once
Few genotypes (up to about 20 to 30), for example advanced yield trials


Augmented
New lines in one plot each; checks replicated in every block
Early generations with seed for one plot, many lines



The RCBD was used in Chapter 4 for the Nebraska wheat trial (stroup.nin): 56 genotypes in blocks of 56 plots. Its low-yield corner was smaller than a block, so the blocks could not remove it. The augmented design was introduced in Chapter 3 with kling.augmented.


5.3.2 Designs with incomplete blocks








Design
Blocks formed in
Blocks grouped in complete replicates (resolvable)




Alpha-lattice
One direction (for example columns)
Yes


Row-column
Two directions (rows and columns)
No


Resolvable row-column
Two directions (rows and columns)
Yes


Partially replicated (p-rep)
Usually analysed with rows, columns and spatial terms
No



Alpha-lattice (Patterson and Williams, 1976). Each replicate is divided into \(s\) incomplete blocks of \(k\) plots, so the number of genotypes is \(t = s \times k\). Each replicate contains all the genotypes. Pairs of genotypes occur together in a block once or never (an \(\alpha(0,1)\) design), and the allocation is chosen to give the lowest average variance of the differences between genotypes. The bean trial of this course is an alpha-lattice: 380 lines in 2 replicates of 396 plots (16 checks appear twice in each replicate), each replicate with 18 blocks of 22 plots (11 rows by 2 columns).
Row-column designs block in two directions at the same time: every row and every column is an incomplete block. In the resolvable version, the field is first divided into complete replicates, and rows and columns are blocks within each replicate. Randomization is not simple, because the design must be balanced in both directions; software such as FielDHub searches for a good allocation.
Partially replicated (p-rep) designs (Cullis et al., 2006) replicate only a fraction of the test lines (for example 20%) and sow the rest in one plot. The replicated lines provide the estimate of error, instead of repeating the same check many times.
crumbs: 5  Experimental Designs for Plant Breeding Trials

title: 5  Experimental Designs for Plant Breeding Trials
section: 5.4 Comparing designs on a real field
text:
5.4 Comparing designs on a real field
How much does each design gain? We can answer this with real data: lay each design over the uniformity trial as if 360 genotypes had been sown in 2 replicates (720 plots), and analyse the blank field with the model of each design. Because there is only one variety, the true differences between “genotypes” are zero: everything the model attributes to error is real field variation that the design did not remove.
This approach follows the course Genotype to phenotype modelling of multi-environment trials (Biometris, Wageningen University and Research, 2021), which used the same uniformity trial. There, simulated genetic effects were added on top of the field; here we do not simulate anything.

5.4.1 Generating the layouts with FielDHub
All layouts have 360 entries in 2 replicates. Replicate 1 occupies columns 1 to 24 and replicate 2 columns 25 to 48 (15 rows by 24 columns each).

nt <- 360   # number of entries

crd   <- CRD(t = nt, reps = 2, seed = 2026)
rcbd  <- RCBD(t = nt, reps = 2, seed = 2026)
alpha <- alpha_lattice(t = nt, k = 15, r = 2, seed = 2026)       # 24 blocks of 15 per rep
rowcol <- row_column(t = nt, nrows = 15, r = 2, iterations = 50, seed = 2026)

head(alpha$fieldBook)

  ID LOCATION PLOT REP IBLOCK UNIT ENTRY TREATMENT
1  1        1  101   1      1    1   344     G-344
2  2        1  102   1      1    2   162     G-162
3  3        1  103   1      1    3   133     G-133
4  4        1  104   1      1    4   131     G-131
5  5        1  105   1      1    5    63      G-63
6  6        1  106   1      1    6   237     G-237


Each design returns a field book: one row per plot, with the replicate, the block and the entry. We place the plots on the field (each incomplete block of the alpha-lattice is one column of 15 plots) and join them with the uniformity yields:

fill_columns <- function(fb) {   # plots in order, column by column within each rep
  fb |>
    group_by(REP) |>
    mutate(i = row_number(),
           col = (REP - 1) * 24 + ceiling(i / 15),
           row = (i - 1) %% 15 + 1) |>
    ungroup()
}

on_field <- function(fb) {
  fb |>
    inner_join(williams, by = c("row", "col")) |>
    mutate(across(c(REP, TREATMENT), factor),
           rowf = factor(row), colf = factor(col))
}

d_crd    <- crd$fieldBook |> mutate(REP = 1) |> fill_columns() |> on_field()  # one 15 x 48 field
d_rcbd   <- rcbd$fieldBook |> fill_columns() |> on_field()
d_alpha  <- alpha$fieldBook |>
  mutate(col = (REP - 1) * 24 + IBLOCK, row = UNIT) |>
  on_field() |> mutate(IBLOCK = factor(IBLOCK))
d_rowcol <- rowcol$fieldBook |>
  mutate(col = (REP - 1) * 24 + COLUMN, row = ROW) |>
  on_field()


ggplot(d_alpha, aes(col, row, fill = factor(as.integer(IBLOCK) %% 2))) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 24.5, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey70", "grey88"), guide = "none") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Column", y = "Row") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 5.3: The alpha-lattice laid over the uniformity trial: 2 replicates, each with 24 incomplete blocks of 15 plots (one block per column). Block colours alternate to show the boundaries.







5.4.2 Fitting the model of each design
Each design implies its own model. Genotypes are fixed here, because we want to compare their means; incomplete blocks, rows and columns are random (see Section 5.9).

fit_crd    <- lm(yield ~ TREATMENT, data = d_crd)
fit_rcbd   <- lm(yield ~ REP + TREATMENT, data = d_rcbd)
fit_alpha  <- lmer(yield ~ REP + (1 | REP:IBLOCK) + TREATMENT, data = d_alpha)
fit_rowcol <- lmer(yield ~ REP + (1 | REP:rowf) + (1 | REP:colf) + TREATMENT,
                   data = d_rowcol)

The precision of a design is measured by the standard error of the difference (SED) between two genotype means: the smaller, the smaller the differences the trial can detect. With incomplete blocks the SED is not the same for every pair (it depends on whether two genotypes shared a block), so we use the average over all pairs:

average_sed <- function(fit) {
  V <- vcov(emmeans(fit, "TREATMENT", lmer.df = "asymptotic"))  # covariance of the means
  n <- nrow(V)
  mean_var <- mean(diag(V))
  mean_cov <- (sum(V) - sum(diag(V))) / (n * (n - 1))
  sqrt(2 * (mean_var - mean_cov))   # average variance of a difference = 2 (var - cov)
}

designs <- tibble(
  design = c("CRD", "RCBD", "Alpha-lattice", "Resolvable row-column"),
  sed    = c(average_sed(fit_crd), average_sed(fit_rcbd),
             average_sed(fit_alpha), average_sed(fit_rowcol))
) |>
  mutate(LSD = 2 * sed,   # approximate least significant difference (5%)
         relative_to_RCBD = round(100 * (sed[2] / sed)^2))
designs

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  design                  sed   LSD relative_to_RCBD
  <chr>                 <dbl> <dbl>            <dbl>
1 CRD                   0.291 0.582               96
2 RCBD                  0.285 0.570              100
3 Alpha-lattice         0.256 0.512              124
4 Resolvable row-column 0.196 0.393              211


On the same field, with the same number of plots, the average SED goes from 0.285 t/ha in the RCBD to 0.256 in the alpha-lattice and 0.196 in the resolvable row-column design. The last column is the relative efficiency: the resolvable row-column design is as precise as an RCBD with about 2.1 times as many replicates, at no extra cost in land or seed.
Three lessons:

The RCBD gains nothing over the CRD here. The two halves of this field have almost the same mean yield, so the two large blocks remove almost no variation. A different randomization changes the numbers slightly, but not this conclusion.
Small blocks help. The alpha blocks follow the columns, so they capture the column-to-column variation, including the seeder pattern of Figure 5.2.
Blocking in two directions helps most, because this field varies along rows and along columns.

The Wageningen course obtained the same ranking with simulated genotypes on the same field (LSD of 0.57, 0.41 and 0.36 t/ha for RCBD, alpha and resolvable row-column). The gain of a design depends on the field: in a field without trends the incomplete blocks gain little, but they rarely lose, and the model can tell how much they helped (the block variance).

title: 5  Experimental Designs for Plant Breeding Trials
text:
5.5 Real trials and their designs

5.5.1 An alpha-lattice: the bean trial

beans <- readr::read_csv("data/Example_Beans.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

beans |>
  mutate(block_n = as.integer(sub("B", "", block))) |>
  ggplot(aes(row, col, fill = factor((block_n + (block_n - 1) %/% 6) %% 2))) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 6.5, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey70", "grey88"), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(3.5, 9.5), labels = c("R1", "R2")) +
  labs(x = "Field row", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 5.4: Incomplete blocks of the bean trial Dar16C_hiP: each block is 11 rows by 2 columns (22 plots). Colours alternate between neighbouring blocks.





The model of an alpha-lattice has replicates and blocks within replicates:
\[
y_{ijk} = \mu + R_j + b_{k(j)} + G_i + \varepsilon_{ijk},
\qquad b_{k(j)} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_b), \quad \varepsilon_{ijk} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_\varepsilon)
\]
where \(R_j\) is replicate \(j\), \(b_{k(j)}\) is block \(k\) within replicate \(j\), and \(G_i\) is genotype \(i\). Note that B1 in R1 and B1 in R2 are different blocks: the term must be written rep:block, not block.


5.5.2 A resolvable row-column design: Australian wheat
The second dataset comes from 14 wheat trials in Australia (7 locations in 2008 and 2009), each laid out as a resolvable row-column design. It was used in the Wageningen course and is used here with permission. We look at the trial WH09 (Wongan Hills, 2009):

wheat <- readr::read_csv("data/wheat_Australia_2008_2009_7loc.csv",
                         show_col_types = FALSE)
wh09 <- wheat |>
  filter(Trial == "WH09") |>
  mutate(across(c(rep, row, col, geno), factor))

wh09 |> count(rep)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  rep       n
  <fct> <int>
1 1       203
2 2       203

wh09 |> count(geno, name = "plots") |> count(plots, name = "genotypes")

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  plots genotypes
  <int>     <int>
1     1         2
2     2       178
3     4        12


The trial has 406 plots in 2 replicates; most genotypes have 2 plots, 12 have 4 and 2 have only one. Each replicate occupies 6 columns and 34 rows:

ggplot(wh09, aes(as.integer(row), as.integer(col), fill = yield)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 6.5, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  labs(x = "Row", y = "Column", fill = "t/ha") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 5.5: Yield of the wheat trial WH09 (Wongan Hills, 2009). Replicate 1 occupies columns 1 to 6 and replicate 2 columns 7 to 12.





The model of a resolvable row-column design has replicates, and rows and columns within replicates:
\[
y_{ijkm} = \mu + Rep_m + r_{j(m)} + c_{k(m)} + G_i + \varepsilon_{ijkm}
\]
Rows and columns are incomplete blocks, so they are random. If we ignore them and analyse the trial as an RCBD (replicates only), the field variation stays in the error:

m_rcbd   <- lmer(yield ~ rep + (1 | geno), data = wh09)
m_rowcol <- lmer(yield ~ rep + (1 | rep:row) + (1 | rep:col) + (1 | geno),
                 data = wh09)

print(VarCorr(m_rcbd), comp = "Variance")

 Groups   Name        Variance
 geno     (Intercept) 0.058336
 Residual             0.300582

print(VarCorr(m_rowcol), comp = "Variance")

 Groups   Name        Variance
 geno     (Intercept) 0.087010
 rep:row  (Intercept) 0.011957
 rep:col  (Intercept) 0.107317
 Residual             0.174646


With the row-column model the residual variance falls from about 0.30 to 0.17, and most of the field variation is between columns (0.107), much less between rows (0.012). The genotype variance becomes larger, because part of what looked like error was field. How this translates into heritability is the topic of Section 7.7.






Noterow or rep:row?



In WH09 the row numbers 1 to 34 are used in both replicates. (1 | row) would treat row 5 of replicate 1 and row 5 of replicate 2 as the same block, although they are in different parts of the field. In a resolvable design, rows and columns are nested within replicates: write (1 | rep:row) + (1 | rep:col), or number the rows and columns so that each one is unique in the field.

section: 5.6 Early generations: augmented and p-rep designs
text:
5.6 Early generations: augmented and p-rep designs
In M2 to M4 populations there are hundreds or thousands of lines, seed is limited, and most lines can be sown in one plot only. Two designs are used:

Augmented designs: the test lines are not replicated; a few checks (in mutation breeding, at least the parent variety) are repeated many times. The error is estimated only from the checks.
p-rep designs: a fraction of the test lines (for example 10% to 30%) is sown in two plots, the rest in one. The replicated test lines estimate the error, and no plots are spent on repeating checks (although checks can be included).


5.6.1 Both designs on the Mercer and Hall field
We compare them again on a real uniformity trial: the wheat trial of Mercer and Hall (1911) at Rothamsted, 500 plots in 20 rows and 25 columns. Both designs test 460 entries in 500 plots:

Augmented (FielDHub diagonal_arrangement()): 460 unreplicated lines plus 4 checks in 39 plots, placed on diagonals across the field.
p-rep (FielDHub partially_replicated()): 40 lines in 2 plots and 420 lines in 1 plot.


mercer <- mercer.wheat.uniformity |>
  rename(ROW = row, COLUMN = col)

prep <- partially_replicated(nrows = 20, ncols = 25,
                             repGens = c(40, 420), repUnits = c(2, 1),
                             seed = 2026)
aug  <- diagonal_arrangement(nrows = 20, ncols = 25, lines = 460,
                             checks = 4, seed = 2026)

prep$fieldBook |> count(TREATMENT, name = "plots") |> count(plots)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  plots     n
  <int> <int>
1     1   420
2     2    40

aug$fieldBook  |> count(is_check = CHECKS > 0)

  is_check   n
1    FALSE 461
2     TRUE  39



bind_rows(
  prep$fieldBook |>
    add_count(TREATMENT) |>
    transmute(ROW, COLUMN, design = "p-rep",
              type = if_else(n > 1, "replicated", "single plot")),
  aug$fieldBook |>
    transmute(ROW, COLUMN, design = "augmented",
              type = if_else(CHECKS > 0, "replicated", "single plot"))
) |>
  ggplot(aes(COLUMN, ROW, fill = type)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~design) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(replicated = "grey25", `single plot` = "grey85")) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Column", y = "Row", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 5.6: The p-rep and augmented layouts on the Mercer and Hall field (20 rows by 25 columns). Dark plots are replicated test lines (p-rep) or checks (augmented).





Both trials are analysed with the same model: entries fixed, rows and columns random. Because the field is blank, we can measure two things for the unreplicated lines:

the SED reported by the model, which is what the breeder would see;
the true SED: the true differences between entries are zero, so the observed spread of the estimated means of the unreplicated lines is pure error (\(\sqrt{2 \times \text{variance of the means}}\)).

One randomization can be lucky or unlucky, so we repeat both designs with 10 different seeds:

sed_single_plots <- function(fb) {
  d <- fb |>
    filter(TREATMENT != "Filler") |>
    inner_join(mercer, by = c("ROW", "COLUMN")) |>
    mutate(TREATMENT = factor(TREATMENT),
           rowf = factor(ROW), colf = factor(COLUMN))
  fit <- lmer(grain ~ TREATMENT + (1 | rowf) + (1 | colf), data = d)
  em  <- emmeans(fit, "TREATMENT", lmer.df = "asymptotic")
  single <- table(d$TREATMENT)[as.character(summary(em)$TREATMENT)] == 1
  V <- vcov(em)[single, single]
  n <- nrow(V)
  c(model_sed = sqrt(2 * (mean(diag(V)) - (sum(V) - sum(diag(V))) / (n * (n - 1)))),
    true_sed  = sqrt(2 * var(summary(em)$emmean[single])))
}

seeds <- 1:10
results <- bind_rows(
  lapply(seeds, \(s) sed_single_plots(
    partially_replicated(nrows = 20, ncols = 25, repGens = c(40, 420),
                         repUnits = c(2, 1), seed = s)$fieldBook)) |>
    bind_rows() |> mutate(design = "p-rep"),
  lapply(seeds, \(s) sed_single_plots(
    diagonal_arrangement(nrows = 20, ncols = 25, lines = 460,
                         checks = 4, seed = s)$fieldBook)) |>
    bind_rows() |> mutate(design = "augmented")
)

results |>
  group_by(design) |>
  summarise(across(c(model_sed, true_sed), mean))

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  design    model_sed true_sed
  <chr>         <dbl>    <dbl>
1 augmented     0.455    0.633
2 p-rep         0.557    0.644


The result is a warning more than a winner:

The true precision is the same for both designs (true SED close to 0.63 t/ha). With one plot per line, a line’s value is its single plot, whatever the design.
The augmented design reports a precision that is too optimistic. Its error is estimated from only 39 check plots, and the model SED is clearly smaller than the true SED. The p-rep design estimates the error from 40 pairs of test lines spread over the field, and its model SED is closer to the truth.
In the p-rep design the replicated plots are test lines, so 40 candidates get two observations instead of repeating 4 checks; in the augmented design the checks give information about the field, but none about the candidates.
For both designs, rows and columns remove little variation from single plots. Unreplicated trials need the spatial models of Chapter 9 to use the information of neighbouring plots.

Mutation-specific designs (how many M2 plants, how to place the parent, family structure) are developed in Chapter 14.

section: 5.7 Choosing a design by breeding stage
text:
5.7 Choosing a design by breeding stage









Stage
Entries
Seed and replicates
Recommended design




M2 to M3, early generations
Hundreds to thousands
One plot per line
Augmented with the parent as check, or p-rep if some lines have seed for 2 plots; spatial analysis


Preliminary yield trial
100 to 400
2 replicates
Alpha-lattice or resolvable row-column


Advanced yield trial
20 to 60
3 or 4 replicates
Alpha-lattice; RCBD only with few entries in a uniform field


Multi-location trials
10 to 50
2 to 4 replicates per location
Alpha-lattice or resolvable row-column at each location


Greenhouse or phenotyping platform
Any
Benches, trays, conveyor positions
Row-column: rows and columns of the bench are real blocks



Two practical rules:

Choose the block size from the field, not from the number of entries. Blocks should be small enough to be uniform: in field trials, blocks of 5 to 20 plots are common.
Write down the layout before sowing (field book with replicate, block, row and column), and keep the row and column of every plot. Without coordinates, the field effects cannot be modelled later (Chapter 9).

title: 5  Experimental Designs for Plant Breeding Trials
text:
5.8 Generating layouts with FielDHub
FielDHub (Murillo et al., 2021) generates and randomizes all the designs of this chapter, as an R package and as a Shiny app:

FielDHub::run_app()   # opens the app in the browser

The app has one tab per design. You enter the number of entries, replicates, block size or field dimensions, and it returns the layout map and the field book, which can be downloaded as a CSV file.
In R, the same is done with one function per design:







Design
FielDHub function




CRD
CRD(t, reps)


RCBD
RCBD(t, reps)


Augmented RCBD
RCBD_augmented(lines, checks, b)


Augmented, diagonal checks
diagonal_arrangement(nrows, ncols, lines, checks)


Alpha-lattice
alpha_lattice(t, k, r)


Resolvable row-column
row_column(t, nrows, r)


p-rep
partially_replicated(nrows, ncols, repGens, repUnits)



Always set seed: the same seed gives the same layout, so the randomization can be reproduced and documented. Use real names for the entries with the argument data, and give the field book the column names of the course template (Chapter 2) before taking it to the field:

entries <- data.frame(ENTRY = 1:30,
                      NAME  = c("Parent", paste0("M3-", sprintf("%03d", 1:29))))

design <- alpha_lattice(t = 30, k = 5, r = 3, seed = 2026, data = entries)

field_book <- design$fieldBook |>
  transmute(location = "Skopje", year = 2027, rep = REP, block = IBLOCK,
            plot = PLOT, geno = TREATMENT)
head(field_book)

  location year rep block plot   geno
1   Skopje 2027   1     1  101 M3-027
2   Skopje 2027   1     1  102 M3-015
3   Skopje 2027   1     1  103 M3-012
4   Skopje 2027   1     1  104 M3-020
5   Skopje 2027   1     1  105 M3-022
6   Skopje 2027   1     2  106 M3-001



plot(design)                                    # layout map
write.csv(field_book, "my_alpha_field_book.csv", row.names = FALSE)

title: 5  Experimental Designs for Plant Breeding Trials
text:
5.9 From layout to statistical model
The design determines the model. Every restriction of the randomization (replicate, block, row, column) becomes a term:

# genotypes fixed; incomplete blocks, rows and columns random
lm(y ~ geno)                                                  # CRD
lm(y ~ rep + geno)                                            # RCBD
lm(y ~ block + geno)                                          # Augmented (or rows and columns random)
lmer(y ~ rep + (1 | rep:block) + geno)                        # Alpha-lattice
lmer(y ~ (1 | row) + (1 | col) + geno)                        # Row-column
lmer(y ~ rep + (1 | rep:row) + (1 | rep:col) + geno)          # Resolvable row-column
lmer(y ~ geno + (1 | row) + (1 | col))                        # p-rep, usually with a spatial term

Three rules:

Complete blocks (replicates) can be fixed or random: every genotype is in every block, so blocks and genotypes are independent.
Incomplete blocks, rows and columns should be random. A genotype is not in every block, so part of the information about genotypes is between blocks; random blocks recover it.
Genotypes are fixed to compare and select them (BLUEs), and random to estimate the genetic variance and heritability (BLUPs). Both models are fitted, as shown in Chapter 7.

title: 5  Experimental Designs for Plant Breeding Trials
text:
5.10 Exercise
The dataset john.alpha in agridat is a real spring oats trial from Craibstone, near Aberdeen (John and Williams, 1995): 24 varieties in an alpha-lattice with 3 replicates, each with 6 incomplete blocks of 4 plots.

Check the design: how many plots per replicate, how many blocks per replicate, how many plots per block?
Fit the model of an RCBD (replicates only) and the model of the alpha-lattice (blocks within replicates, random). Compare the residual variance and the average SED of the two models.
Generate a new alpha-lattice for the same trial (24 entries, blocks of 4, 3 replicates) with FielDHub, and look at its field book.







TipSolution






# 1. Check the design
john.alpha |> count(rep)

  rep  n
1  R1 24
2  R2 24
3  R3 24

john.alpha |> count(rep, block) |> count(rep, plots_per_block = n)

  rep plots_per_block n
1  R1               4 6
2  R2               4 6
3  R3               4 6

# 2. RCBD model vs alpha model
oats_rcbd  <- lm(yield ~ rep + gen, data = john.alpha)
oats_alpha <- lmer(yield ~ rep + (1 | rep:block) + gen, data = john.alpha)

sigma(oats_rcbd)^2    # residual variance, RCBD model

[1] 0.134586

print(VarCorr(oats_alpha), comp = "Variance")

 Groups    Name        Variance
 rep:block (Intercept) 0.061944
 Residual              0.085225

average_sed_gen <- function(fit) {
  V <- vcov(emmeans(fit, "gen", lmer.df = "asymptotic"))
  n <- nrow(V)
  sqrt(2 * (mean(diag(V)) - (sum(V) - sum(diag(V))) / (n * (n - 1))))
}
c(rcbd = average_sed_gen(oats_rcbd), alpha = average_sed_gen(oats_alpha))

     rcbd     alpha 
0.2995396 0.2647806 

# 3. A new randomization of the same design
new_alpha <- alpha_lattice(t = 24, k = 4, r = 3, seed = 2026)
head(new_alpha$fieldBook)

  ID LOCATION PLOT REP IBLOCK UNIT ENTRY TREATMENT
1  1        1  101   1      1    1    12      G-12
2  2        1  102   1      1    2    19      G-19
3  3        1  103   1      1    3    11      G-11
4  4        1  104   1      1    4     1       G-1
5  5        1  105   1      2    1    22      G-22
6  6        1  106   1      2    2    20      G-20


The block variance is a large part of the field variation. With the blocks in the model, the residual variance falls from 0.135 to 0.085, and the average SED from about 0.30 to 0.26 t/ha. Analysing an alpha-lattice as an RCBD throws away the information of the blocks.

title: 5  Experimental Designs for Plant Breeding Trials
text:
5.11 Key takeaways

Replication estimates the error, randomization makes it valid, and blocking removes field variation from the comparisons.
Fields vary at short distances and in more than one direction. Breeding trials, with many entries, need incomplete blocks: alpha-lattice or row-column designs.
On a real uniformity field, the resolvable row-column design was about twice as efficient as the RCBD, with the same plots and seed.
For early generations with limited seed, augmented and p-rep designs have the same true precision, but the augmented design overstates it; analyse both with spatial models.
The design determines the model: replicates, blocks within replicates, rows and columns within replicates. Incomplete blocks are random.
Generate layouts with FielDHub, set the seed, and keep the row and column of every plot.

title: 6  ANOVA and Mean Comparison in Breeding Trials
text:
6.1 Learning objectives
In Chapter 5 we chose a design and wrote its model. This chapter fits that model with lm() and reads the result. The ANOVA answers one question: is there evidence of differences among the genotypes, once the blocks are removed? The comparison of means answers the next one: which genotypes differ, and by how much? For a breeder the second question matters most, because the aim is to decide which lines advance.
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(emmeans)
library(agridat)     # install.packages("agridat") if needed
library(agricolae)   # install.packages("agricolae") if needed
crumbs: 6  ANOVA and Mean Comparison in Breeding Trials

title: 6  ANOVA and Mean Comparison in Breeding Trials
text:
Fit and read the ANOVA of a complete block design, and rebuild its sums of squares by hand
Check the assumptions with residual diagnostics and decide when a transformation is needed
Compare genotypes with LSD, Tukey and Dunnett, and know which question each one answers
Distinguish statistical from practical significance
Extend the ANOVA to augmented designs and to several environments
Identify superior genotypes and turn statistical results into selection decisions
Recognize the most common pitfalls when interpreting a comparison of means









NotePackages in this chapter



Besides the course packages, this chapter uses only base R. Levene’s test is computed with a few lines of base R (it is an ANOVA on the absolute deviations from the group median), so no extra package is needed. The optional performance and multcomp calls are marked in the text.

title: 6  ANOVA and Mean Comparison in Breeding Trials
section: 6.2 The ANOVA of a randomized complete block design
text:
6.2 The ANOVA of a randomized complete block design
We start with a real trial of durum wheat (Triticum durum) from Algeria: 24 genotypes in 22 environments, each environment an RCBD with 4 blocks. The data were collected in the course “Genotype to phenotype modelling of multi-environment trials” (Biometris, Wageningen University and Research; see Section 6.13) and are used here with permission. In this chapter we work on one environment at a time and leave the 22 together for the end.

durum <- read_csv("data/Durum_wheat_Algeria.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(Genotype = factor(Genotype),
         Block    = factor(Block),
         GenoGroup = trimws(GenoGroup))

durum |> count(Environment) |> head(3)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  Environment     n
  <chr>       <int>
1 loc01_year1    96
2 loc01_year2    96
3 loc02_year1    96

e2 <- durum |> filter(Environment == "loc10_year1")
dim(e2)

[1] 96  8


Each environment has 96 plots: 24 genotypes in 4 blocks. The model is the one derived in Section 5.9:
yield = overall mean + block effect + genotype effect + error

fit <- lm(yield ~ Block + Genotype, data = e2)
anova(fit)

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: yield
          Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
Block      3 3.9362 1.31206 20.6185 1.205e-09 ***
Genotype  23 5.4481 0.23687  3.7223 1.233e-05 ***
Residuals 69 4.3908 0.06364                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The table partitions the total variation into three parts. The block line is the variation among the four blocks, the genotype line is the variation among the 24 genotype means, and the residual is what is left: the differences among plots of the same genotype within the same block. The residual mean square (Mean Sq of Residuals) is the estimate of the error variance, \(\sigma^2\), and every comparison of means below is built from it.

6.2.1 Rebuilding the table by hand
A balanced RCBD has a simple structure, and it is worth doing the arithmetic once. The sums of squares are the squared deviations of the block means, the genotype means and the observations from the overall mean:

y    <- e2$yield
mu   <- mean(y)
b    <- nlevels(e2$Block)       # blocks
g    <- nlevels(e2$Genotype)    # genotypes

ss_total <- sum((y - mu)^2)
ss_block <- g * sum((tapply(y, e2$Block, mean) - mu)^2)
ss_geno  <- b * sum((tapply(y, e2$Genotype, mean) - mu)^2)
ss_error <- ss_total - ss_block - ss_geno

by_hand <- data.frame(
  source = c("Block", "Genotype", "Error", "Total"),
  df     = c(b - 1, g - 1, (b - 1) * (g - 1), b * g - 1),
  SS     = c(ss_block, ss_geno, ss_error, ss_total)
)
by_hand$MS <- by_hand$SS / by_hand$df
by_hand$F  <- c(by_hand$MS[1:2] / by_hand$MS[3], NA, NA)
by_hand

    source df        SS         MS         F
1    Block  3  3.936194 1.31206452 20.618489
2 Genotype 23  5.448068 0.23687253  3.722343
3    Error 69  4.390838 0.06363534        NA
4    Total 95 13.775100 0.14500105        NA


These are the numbers of anova(fit). Three quantities summarize the trial and should always be reported:

mse <- by_hand$MS[3]                      # error variance
c(MSE = mse,
  residual_sd = sqrt(mse),
  CV_percent  = 100 * sqrt(mse) / mu)

        MSE residual_sd  CV_percent 
 0.06363534  0.25226046 15.63406080 


The coefficient of variation (CV) is the residual standard deviation as a percentage of the mean. Values of 10 to 20% are usual for yield in field trials. A CV much higher than that points to a noisy trial, and the comparisons that follow will have little power.
The F value of the genotype line is the ratio of the variance among genotype means to the error variance. If all genotypes had the same true mean, F would be close to 1. Here F is 3.7 (p < 0.001), so the differences among genotypes are larger than the plot-to-plot noise can explain. Note also the block line: F = 21. The blocks differ strongly, and without them in the model that variation would have inflated the error and hidden part of the genotype differences. This is local control at work.






ImportantA significant F does not say which genotypes differ



The F test of the genotype line is a global test: at least one genotype is different from the others. It does not identify which one. For that we need the comparisons of means in the sections below.

title: 6  ANOVA and Mean Comparison in Breeding Trials
text:
6.3 Checking the assumptions
The F test and the comparisons of means assume that the errors are independent, have the same variance for all genotypes, and are approximately normal. We check these assumptions on the residuals of the model, not on the raw data, because the raw data contain the genotype and block effects.

res <- data.frame(fitted = fitted(fit), resid = resid(fit))

p1 <- ggplot(res, aes(fitted, resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Fitted values (t/ha)", y = "Residuals (t/ha)") +
  theme_minimal()

p2 <- ggplot(res, aes(sample = resid)) +
  stat_qq() + stat_qq_line() +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Residual quantiles") +
  theme_minimal()

print(p1)
print(p2)







Figure 6.1: Residual diagnostics for durum wheat in one environment. Top: residuals against fitted values (no funnel shape, no curve). Bottom: normal QQ plot of the residuals.











Figure 6.2: Residual diagnostics for durum wheat in one environment. Top: residuals against fitted values (no funnel shape, no curve). Bottom: normal QQ plot of the residuals.






shapiro.test(resid(fit))                       # normality of residuals


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  resid(fit)
W = 0.99226, p-value = 0.8572

# Levene (median version): ANOVA of the absolute deviations from each genotype median
levene <- function(y, group) anova(lm(abs(y - ave(y, group, FUN = median)) ~ group))
levene(e2$yield, e2$Genotype)   # equal variance among genotypes

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: abs(y - ave(y, group, FUN = median))
          Df Sum Sq  Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
group     23 1.0028 0.043599  0.9837  0.496
Residuals 72 3.1913 0.044323               


How to read them:

Residuals against fitted values. A random cloud around zero is what we want. A funnel (spread growing with the mean) means the variance depends on the mean; a curve means the model is missing a term.
QQ plot. Points on the line mean normal residuals. Moderate departures in the tails matter little with 20 or more residual degrees of freedom; the F test is robust to them.
Shapiro-Wilk and Levene. The first tests normality, the second tests equal variance among genotypes. With so few plots per genotype, Levene has low power. Use the plots first and the tests as a support.
Outliers. A residual larger than about three residual standard deviations deserves a look at the field book. The reason is usually a recording error or a plot with a problem, and it should be corrected or removed with a note, never silently. This is the model-based version of the checks of Chapter 4.

The performance package gives the same panels in one call, with the model’s own tests:

# optional: install.packages("performance")
performance::check_model(fit)


6.3.1 When the variance depends on the mean: transformations
Counts and proportions often fail the equal variance assumption, because their variance grows with the mean. A real example is the count of webworms in a sugar beet field, in 13 blocks, under 4 insecticide treatments (Beall, 1940, via agridat). Each plot was recorded in 25 unit areas; to analyse one value per plot we add the counts of the 25 unit areas, so that the experimental unit is the plot and not the unit area.

worms <- beall.webworms |>
  group_by(block, trt) |>
  summarise(count = sum(y), .groups = "drop")

# variance grows with the mean
worms |>
  group_by(trt) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(count), variance = var(count))

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  trt    mean variance
  <fct> <dbl>    <dbl>
1 T1     35      216. 
2 T2     12.6     17.4
3 T3     21.3    107. 
4 T4     10.3     29.4


The treatment with the highest mean has also the highest variance (a variance more than ten times that of the treatments with low counts). The residuals of the model on the raw counts show it, and the square root of the count corrects it:

f_raw  <- lm(count ~ block + trt, data = worms)
f_sqrt <- lm(sqrt(count) ~ block + trt, data = worms)

bind_rows(
  data.frame(scale = "Raw count",    fitted = fitted(f_raw),  resid = resid(f_raw)),
  data.frame(scale = "Square root",  fitted = fitted(f_sqrt), resid = resid(f_sqrt))
) |>
  mutate(scale = factor(scale, levels = c("Raw count", "Square root"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(fitted, resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~scale, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Fitted values", y = "Residuals") +
  theme_minimal()

# correlation between |residual| and fitted: near zero when the variance is stable
c(raw  = cor(abs(resid(f_raw)),  fitted(f_raw)),
  sqrt = cor(abs(resid(f_sqrt)), fitted(f_sqrt)))

       raw       sqrt 
0.40446617 0.07382039 








Figure 6.3: Residuals against fitted values for the webworm counts. Left: raw counts, the spread grows with the mean. Right: square root of the counts, the spread is stable.





Use this table to choose the transformation:







Data
Typical transformation




Counts (insects, plants, lesions)
square root, \(\sqrt{y + 0.5}\) if there are zeros


Variance proportional to the square of the mean
logarithm, \(\log(y)\) or \(\log(y + 1)\)


Proportions (percentage of infection)
arcsine of the square root, or better a binomial model (Chapter 7)



Two cautions. First, a transformation changes the scale of the means: report the means on the transformed scale and back-transform them, or fit a model for counts directly. Second, do not transform yield to fix a single outlier; investigate the outlier.

title: 6  ANOVA and Mean Comparison in Breeding Trials
text:
6.4 Comparing the means of genotypes
The ANOVA tells us there are differences. To say which genotypes differ, we compare means. For this section we use a rice trial in which a control is present.

6.4.1 The rice trial
Example_rice.csv has 72 plots of 11 genotypes: nine lines (G1 to G9), the variety centinela and a check, under two water regimes: irrigated and drought. Each regime is an RCBD with 3 blocks. The variety centinela is the parent used as reference: it is in the field twice in every block (6 plots per regime), the rest of the genotypes once.

rice <- read_csv("data/Example_rice.csv",
                 locale = locale(encoding = "latin1"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(env  = if_else(grepl("^Irri", TRAT), "Irrigated", "Drought"),
         GEN  = relevel(factor(GEN), ref = "centinela"),
         Bloq = factor(Bloq))

irr <- rice |> filter(env == "Irrigated")
irr |> count(GEN)

# A tibble: 11 × 2
   GEN           n
   <fct>     <int>
 1 centinela     6
 2 check         3
 3 G1            3
 4 G2            3
 5 G3            3
 6 G4            3
 7 G5            3
 8 G6            3
 9 G7            3
10 G8            3
11 G9            3



fit_irr <- lm(REND ~ Bloq + GEN, data = irr)
anova(fit_irr)

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: REND
          Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
Bloq       2  1.594  0.7969  0.9977 0.3841461    
GEN       10 42.052  4.2052  5.2643 0.0004845 ***
Residuals 23 18.373  0.7988                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

c(MSE = deviance(fit_irr) / df.residual(fit_irr),
  df  = df.residual(fit_irr),
  CV  = 100 * sigma(fit_irr) / mean(irr$REND))

       MSE         df         CV 
 0.7988164 23.0000000 11.1798301 


The F test for genotypes is significant (p < 0.001). The assumptions hold:

shapiro.test(resid(fit_irr))$p.value

[1] 0.158161

levene(irr$REND, irr$GEN)$`Pr(>F)`[1]

[1] 0.9930382


(Plot the residuals as in the previous section.) The control is replicated twice per block, so the design is not balanced: the model still works, and emmeans gives the correct adjusted means.

em <- emmeans(fit_irr, ~ GEN)
em

 GEN       emmean    SE df lower.CL upper.CL
 centinela   7.93 0.365 23     7.18     8.69
 check       6.00 0.516 23     4.93     7.07
 G1          8.70 0.516 23     7.63     9.77
 G2          7.30 0.516 23     6.23     8.37
 G3          8.17 0.516 23     7.10     9.23
 G4          9.67 0.516 23     8.60    10.73
 G5          7.13 0.516 23     6.07     8.20
 G6          9.20 0.516 23     8.13    10.27
 G7          6.60 0.516 23     5.53     7.67
 G8          7.87 0.516 23     6.80     8.93
 G9          9.43 0.516 23     8.37    10.50

Results are averaged over the levels of: Bloq 
Confidence level used: 0.95 




6.4.2 The problem of multiple comparisons
With 11 genotypes there are 55 pairs of genotypes. If we test each pair at the 5% level and there were no real differences at all, we would still expect about 3 “significant” differences by chance (55 × 0.05). Every procedure below deals with this problem in a different way.








Procedure
What it controls
When to use it




LSD (Fisher)
Nothing: each comparison at 5%
Only after a significant F; few comparisons, or screening where a miss is costlier than a false positive


Duncan
Less protection than Tukey, more than LSD; no control of the error of all comparisons
Common in the literature; not recommended for selection decisions


Tukey HSD
The error of all pairwise comparisons together
Every genotype is compared with every other; the conservative choice


Dunnett
The error of the comparisons with one control
New lines against a parent or a check





6.4.3 LSD and Tukey
The LSD is the smallest difference between two means that is significant at the 5% level. With the residual mean square of the ANOVA, agricolae computes it and gives the groups:

lsd <- LSD.test(fit_irr, "GEN", console = FALSE)
lsd$statistics

    MSerror Df     Mean       CV
  0.7988164 23 7.994444 11.17983

lsd$groups

              REND groups
G4        9.666667      a
G9        9.433333      a
G6        9.200000     ab
G1        8.700000    abc
G3        8.166667   abcd
centinela 7.933333    bcd
G8        7.866667   bcde
G2        7.300000   cdef
G5        7.133333    def
G7        6.600000     ef
check     6.000000      f



tuk <- HSD.test(fit_irr, "GEN", console = FALSE)
tuk$groups

              REND groups
G4        9.666667      a
G9        9.433333      a
G6        9.200000      a
G1        8.700000     ab
G3        8.166667    abc
centinela 7.933333    abc
G8        7.866667    abc
G2        7.300000    abc
G5        7.133333    abc
G7        6.600000     bc
check     6.000000      c


Means that share a letter are not significantly different. The LSD gives more groups and more separation than Tukey. The best line, G4, is separated by the LSD from six genotypes (centinela, G8, G2, G5, G7 and the check), and by Tukey from only two (G7 and the check). The LSD separates more because it is not protected against the 55 comparisons.


6.4.4 Duncan
Duncan’s multiple range test is still very common in the agricultural literature, and agricolae runs it with the same syntax:

duncan.test(fit_irr, "GEN", console = FALSE)$groups

              REND groups
G4        9.666667      a
G9        9.433333     ab
G6        9.200000     ab
G1        8.700000    abc
G3        8.166667   abcd
centinela 7.933333    bcd
G8        7.866667    bcd
G2        7.300000    cde
G5        7.133333    cde
G7        6.600000     de
check     6.000000      e


Its groups lie between those of the LSD and those of Tukey: it separates G4 from the same six genotypes as the LSD, but G9 and G6 now share a group with lower genotypes. Duncan’s test makes the critical difference grow with the number of means between the two compared, which protects against some false positives, but it does not control the error of all the comparisons together. If a paper reports Duncan letters, read them as a screening; for decisions use Tukey (all pairs) or Dunnett (against a control).
The letters can also be obtained from an emmeans object, which works for any model, including the mixed models of Chapter 7. This needs the multcomp package (install.packages("multcomp")):

multcomp::cld(em, Letters = letters, adjust = "tukey", reversed = TRUE)







WarningLetters are a summary, not a decision



Letters hide the size of the differences and the uncertainty of the means. Two genotypes with no letter in common can differ by a small amount, and two genotypes sharing a letter can differ by a large amount that the trial could not confirm. Report the difference with its confidence interval, as in the next sections.




6.4.5 Dunnett: new lines against a control
In a breeding trial the real question is rarely “are all pairs different?”. It is: is any new line better than the parent or the check? This is a comparison of each line with one control: 10 comparisons instead of 55, and Dunnett’s test controls the error of those 10 together.

dun <- contrast(em, method = "trt.vs.ctrl", ref = 1)   # reference: centinela
dun_tab <- summary(dun, infer = TRUE)
dun_tab |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))

            contrast estimate    SE df lower.CL upper.CL t.ratio p.value
1  check - centinela   -1.933 0.632 23   -3.812   -0.054  -3.059   0.041
2     G1 - centinela    0.767 0.632 23   -1.112    2.646   1.213   0.763
3     G2 - centinela   -0.633 0.632 23   -2.512    1.246  -1.002   0.865
4     G3 - centinela    0.233 0.632 23   -1.646    2.112   0.369   0.996
5     G4 - centinela    1.733 0.632 23   -0.146    3.612   2.743   0.081
6     G5 - centinela   -0.800 0.632 23   -2.679    1.079  -1.266   0.734
7     G6 - centinela    1.267 0.632 23   -0.612    3.146   2.004   0.310
8     G7 - centinela   -1.333 0.632 23   -3.212    0.546  -2.110   0.262
9     G8 - centinela   -0.067 0.632 23   -1.946    1.812  -0.105   1.000
10    G9 - centinela    1.500 0.632 23   -0.379    3.379   2.373   0.166


Each row is the difference between a genotype and centinela, with its standard error, confidence interval and the Dunnett-adjusted p. The standard error is the same for all lines (the control is replicated 6 times and the lines 3 times). Compare with the same 10 tests without adjustment:

unadj <- summary(contrast(em, "trt.vs.ctrl", ref = 1), adjust = "none")
c(unadjusted_p_below_0.05 = sum(unadj$p.value < 0.05),
  dunnett_p_below_0.05    = sum(dun_tab$p.value < 0.05))

unadjusted_p_below_0.05    dunnett_p_below_0.05 
                      4                       1 


Without protection, 4 of the 10 lines look different from the control; Dunnett’s test confirms only one (the check, which is lower than the parent). The three extra lines with p near 0.01 to 0.05 in the unadjusted tests are the ones that the adjustment removes. They may be real, but this trial cannot confirm them.

dun_tab |>
  mutate(contrast = reorder(contrast, estimate)) |>
  ggplot(aes(estimate, contrast)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lower.CL, xmax = upper.CL)) +
  labs(x = "Difference to centinela (t/ha)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 6.4: Difference between each rice genotype and the control centinela under irrigation, with Dunnett 95% confidence intervals. Intervals that cross zero are not confirmed differences.





If the only question is whether a line is better than the control, a one-sided test is justified, but it must be decided before the trial. In the course we use two-sided intervals, because a line worse than the parent is also information.
