title: 6  ANOVA and Mean Comparison in Breeding Trials
section: 6.5 Statistically significant is not the same as useful
text:
6.5 Statistically significant is not the same as useful
A p-value says whether a difference could be due to chance. It does not say whether the difference is big enough to matter. Three numbers answer that and should be read together:

The size of the difference, in t/ha and as a percentage of the control.
The confidence interval, which gives the range of differences compatible with the data.
The smallest difference that matters to the breeder, decided before the trial (for example 10% of the yield of the parent).


ctrl_mean <- summary(em) |> filter(GEN == "centinela") |> pull(emmean)

dun_tab |>
  mutate(gain_percent = 100 * estimate / ctrl_mean) |>
  select(contrast, estimate, lower.CL, upper.CL, gain_percent, p.value) |>
  arrange(desc(estimate)) |>
  head(4) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))

        contrast estimate lower.CL upper.CL gain_percent p.value
1 G4 - centinela     1.73    -0.15     3.61        21.85    0.08
2 G9 - centinela     1.50    -0.38     3.38        18.91    0.17
3 G6 - centinela     1.27    -0.61     3.15        15.97    0.31
4 G1 - centinela     0.77    -1.11     2.65         9.66    0.76


G4 yields about 1.7 t/ha more than the parent, which is +22%. The Dunnett p is 0.08, so it is not significant at 5%, and the interval goes from about -0.1 to +3.6 t/ha. Two different conclusions are possible and both are wrong if stated alone:

“There is no difference between G4 and the parent”: wrong. The trial failed to detect a difference of the size seen; it did not show that there is none.
“G4 is 22% better”: too strong. The trial is compatible with a gain of almost nothing and with a gain of more than 3 t/ha.

The honest conclusion is that G4 is a promising line that needs more replication or more environments. The cause is the precision of the trial:

# smallest difference between two genotypes (3 plots each) detectable at 5% (LSD)
lsd_value <- qt(0.975, df.residual(fit_irr)) * sqrt(2 * sigma(fit_irr)^2 / 3)
c(LSD_t_ha = lsd_value, LSD_percent_of_mean = 100 * lsd_value / mean(irr$REND))

           LSD_t_ha LSD_percent_of_mean 
           1.509616           18.883313 


With 3 replicates and a CV of 11%, this trial cannot confirm differences smaller than about 1.5 t/ha, which is about 19% of the mean. If the breeder cares about a 10% gain, the trial is under-powered, and the options are more replicates, a design with smaller blocks (Chapter 5), or several environments (Chapter 11).
crumbs: 6  ANOVA and Mean Comparison in Breeding Trials

title: 6  ANOVA and Mean Comparison in Breeding Trials
text:
6.6 Augmented designs
In early generations there is seed for one plot per line (Chapter 5). The augmented design puts a few replicated checks in every block and the new lines once. The checks estimate the error and the block effects; the new lines are adjusted for the blocks. The model is the same as for an RCBD, fitted with lm():
The dataset kling.augmented in agridat is a real example: 50 new lines of meadowfoam (one plot each) and 3 checks (G89, G90, G91, in every block), in 6 blocks, with the response thousand-seed weight (tsw).

aug <- kling.augmented |>
  mutate(gen = droplevels(gen),
         type = if_else(gen %in% c("G89", "G90", "G91"), "check", "new"))

aug |> count(type)

   type  n
1 check 18
2   new 50

aug |> count(block, type) |> pivot_wider(names_from = type, values_from = n)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  block check   new
  <fct> <int> <int>
1 B1        3     9
2 B2        3     9
3 B3        3     9
4 B4        3     9
5 B5        3     9
6 B6        3     5



fit_aug <- lm(tsw ~ block + gen, data = aug)
anova(fit_aug)

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: tsw
          Df  Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
block      5  1.7112 0.34224  4.9028 0.0158408 *  
gen       52 27.5185 0.52920  7.5811 0.0007876 ***
Residuals 10  0.6981 0.06981                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

c(MSE = deviance(fit_aug) / df.residual(fit_aug),
  df  = df.residual(fit_aug),
  CV  = 100 * sigma(fit_aug) / mean(aug$tsw))

        MSE          df          CV 
 0.06980556 10.00000000  2.60012792 


Look at the residual: only 10 degrees of freedom. They come from the checks only: 3 checks in 6 blocks give (6 - 1) × (3 - 1) = 10. The new lines, with one plot each, contribute nothing to the error. That is the cost of the design. The error is estimated from the checks only, and with 10 df the comparisons have little power and the estimate is itself uncertain.
The adjusted means of the new lines remove the block effect:

em_aug <- emmeans(fit_aug, ~ gen)
em_df  <- as.data.frame(em_aug)

# top five lines, adjusted for blocks
em_df |>
  arrange(desc(emmean)) |>
  head(5) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))

  gen emmean  SE df lower.CL upper.CL
1 G31  12.35 0.3 10    11.68    13.01
2 G30  11.78 0.3 10    11.11    12.44
3 G11  11.75 0.3 10    11.08    12.41
4 G23  11.15 0.3 10    10.49    11.82
5 G36  11.04 0.3 10    10.37    11.70


The standard errors differ by the type of comparison: two checks, a check and a new line, and two new lines have different SEDs, because the checks are replicated and the new lines are not:

chk <- c("G89", "G90", "G91")
pw  <- as.data.frame(pairs(em_aug, adjust = "none"))
pw$a <- sub(" - .*", "", pw$contrast)
pw$b <- sub(".* - ", "", pw$contrast)
pw$type <- case_when(pw$a %in% chk & pw$b %in% chk ~ "check vs check",
                     pw$a %in% chk | pw$b %in% chk ~ "new vs check",
                     TRUE                           ~ "new vs new")
pw |> group_by(type) |> summarise(SED = mean(SE), .groups = "drop")

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  type             SED
  <chr>          <dbl>
1 check vs check 0.153
2 new vs check   0.318
3 new vs new     0.422


For selection, compare the new lines with the mean of the checks (or the best check) and consider the large SED of two unreplicated lines. In Chapter 9 and Chapter 7 we will see how a spatial or a mixed model uses all the plots to estimate the error and improves the augmented analysis.
crumbs: 6  ANOVA and Mean Comparison in Breeding Trials

title: 6  ANOVA and Mean Comparison in Breeding Trials
text:
6.7 More than one environment
Breeding decisions rely on several environments. The simplest extension of the ANOVA is to put the environments and the genotypes in the same model, with the interaction between them.

6.7.1 Two water regimes in rice
Rice under irrigation and under drought, 3 blocks in each. The block effect is nested in the environment (the blocks of one regime are not the blocks of the other):

fit_2env <- lm(REND ~ env / Bloq + GEN * env, data = rice)
anova(fit_2env)

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: REND
          Df  Sum Sq Mean Sq  F value    Pr(>F)    
env        1 228.267 228.267 390.4503 < 2.2e-16 ***
GEN       10  63.909   6.391  10.9315  3.24e-09 ***
env:Bloq   4   2.349   0.587   1.0044    0.4150    
env:GEN   10   7.789   0.779   1.3322    0.2424    
Residuals 46  26.893   0.585                       
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Environment (irrigated against drought) explains most of the variation: the drought regime reduces the yield strongly. The genotype effect is significant, and the genotype by environment interaction is not (p = 0.24): the lines keep a similar ranking in both regimes. If it were significant, the best genotype in one regime would not be the best in the other, and we would need to analyse each regime separately and decide which one matters for the target population.


6.7.2 Durum wheat in 22 environments
The Algerian durum wheat trial has 24 genotypes in 22 environments. Here the interaction is the main story:

fit_met <- lm(yield ~ Environment / Block + Genotype * Environment, data = durum)
anova(fit_met)

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: yield
                       Df Sum Sq Mean Sq  F value    Pr(>F)    
Environment            21 935.95  44.569 537.1651 < 2.2e-16 ***
Genotype               23  80.84   3.515  42.3627 < 2.2e-16 ***
Environment:Block      66 117.69   1.783  21.4909 < 2.2e-16 ***
Environment:Genotype  483 151.66   0.314   3.7845 < 2.2e-16 ***
Residuals            1518 125.95   0.083                       
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


All the terms are highly significant. The genotype by environment line (Genotype:Environment) has a mean square about 4 times the residual: the ranking of the genotypes changes across environments. Which F do we use to test the genotypes? The residual mean square (0.083) is the error between plots of the same genotype in the same environment, but the environments are a sample of the target environments. The correct denominator for genotypes is the interaction mean square:

a <- anova(fit_met)
ms <- setNames(a$`Mean Sq`, rownames(a))
F_geno <- ms["Genotype"] / ms["Environment:Genotype"]
c(F_residual = unname(ms["Genotype"] / ms["Residuals"]),
  F_interaction = unname(F_geno),
  p_value = unname(pf(F_geno, a["Genotype", "Df"], a["Environment:Genotype", "Df"], lower.tail = FALSE)))

   F_residual F_interaction       p_value 
 4.236266e+01  1.119373e+01  2.886352e-32 


The F against the interaction (11) is much smaller than the F against the residual (42), but it is still highly significant. The genotypes differ on average over the environments, in addition to the interaction.
The mean squares also give the variance components, which are the basis of heritability (Section 7.7). With \(r\) = 4 blocks and \(e\) = 22 environments, from the expected mean squares:

r <- 4; e <- 22
s2_e  <- ms["Residuals"]
s2_ge <- (ms["Environment:Genotype"] - ms["Residuals"]) / r
s2_g  <- (ms["Genotype"] - ms["Environment:Genotype"]) / (r * e)
round(c(genotype = unname(s2_g), GxE = unname(s2_ge), error = unname(s2_e)), 4)

genotype      GxE    error 
  0.0364   0.0578   0.0830 


The genotype by environment variance is larger than the genotype variance. This is why one environment is not enough to choose the genotypes, and why the next sessions model G×E (Chapter 11) and estimate the components with a mixed model (Chapter 7).
crumbs: 6  ANOVA and Mean Comparison in Breeding Trials

title: 6  ANOVA and Mean Comparison in Breeding Trials
text:
6.8 Identifying superior genotypes
The comparison of means ends in a decision: which lines advance to the next stage, which are tested again, and which are dropped. A decision rule written before looking at the results avoids choosing the criterion that gives the answer we like. For a trial with a parent (or a check) the rule has three parts:

The reference: the parent or the best check, with its adjusted mean.
The smallest gain that matters: for example 10% over the parent. A line that is better by less than this is not worth the cost of advancing it.
The evidence: the Dunnett confidence interval of the difference to the reference, which already accounts for the number of lines compared.

With these we classify every line:








Class
Rule
Decision




Confirmed superior
Dunnett interval of the difference above zero
Advance


Promising
Estimated gain at least the smallest gain that matters, but the interval includes zero
Test again with more replication or more environments


Not different
Gain smaller than the threshold, interval includes zero
Drop, or keep only for other traits


Confirmed inferior
Interval below zero
Drop




6.8.1 An example on the rice trial
The function below applies the rule to one environment. We run it on the irrigated and on the drought trial, with centinela as the reference and 10% as the smallest gain that matters.

classify <- function(d, env_name) {
  fit  <- lm(REND ~ Bloq + GEN, data = d)
  em   <- emmeans(fit, ~ GEN)
  ctrl <- summary(em)$emmean[1]                  # centinela is the reference level
  summary(contrast(em, "trt.vs.ctrl", ref = 1), infer = TRUE) |>
    mutate(env  = env_name,
           line = sub(" - centinela", "", contrast),
           pct  = 100 * estimate / ctrl,
           pct_lower = 100 * lower.CL / ctrl,
           pct_upper = 100 * upper.CL / ctrl,
           class = case_when(lower.CL > 0 ~ "confirmed superior",
                             upper.CL < 0 ~ "confirmed inferior",
                             pct >= 10    ~ "promising",
                             TRUE         ~ "not different"))
}

sel <- bind_rows(classify(filter(rice, env == "Irrigated"), "Irrigated"),
                 classify(filter(rice, env == "Drought"),   "Drought"))


sel |>
  mutate(class = factor(class, levels = c("confirmed superior", "promising",
                                          "not different", "confirmed inferior")),
         env   = factor(env, levels = c("Irrigated", "Drought"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(pct, reorder(line, pct), colour = class)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 1, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 10, linetype = 3) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = pct_lower, xmax = pct_upper)) +
  facet_wrap(~env) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("confirmed superior" = "#1b7837",
                                 "promising"          = "#e08214",
                                 "not different"      = "grey50",
                                 "confirmed inferior" = "#b2182b")) +
  labs(x = "Gain over centinela (%)", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")







Figure 6.5: Gain of each rice line over centinela, as a percentage of centinela, with Dunnett 95% intervals. The dotted line marks the smallest gain that matters (10%). Colours give the class of each line.






# Class of each line in the two regimes
sel |>
  select(line, env, class) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = env, values_from = class) |>
  arrange(Drought, Irrigated)

# A tibble: 10 × 3
   line  Irrigated          Drought           
   <chr> <chr>              <chr>             
 1 G8    not different      confirmed superior
 2 G4    promising          confirmed superior
 3 G9    promising          confirmed superior
 4 check confirmed inferior not different     
 5 G2    not different      not different     
 6 G5    not different      not different     
 7 G7    not different      not different     
 8 G1    not different      promising         
 9 G3    not different      promising         
10 G6    promising          promising         


Read the figure by rows of evidence:

G9 and G4 are promising under irrigation (+19% and +22%, interval includes zero) and confirmed superior under drought (+34% and +32%). They are the first candidates to advance: the same direction in two environments is stronger evidence than a p-value in one.
G8 is confirmed superior under drought (+43%) but equal to the parent under irrigation. It is a candidate for drought-prone sites, not a general one. Remember that the genotype by regime interaction was not significant in this trial (Section 6.7), so differences between the two regimes should not be over-interpreted with 3 blocks.
G6 is promising in both regimes, without confirmation in either: retest.
The check is confirmed inferior under irrigation. It tells us that the trial can detect a difference when it is large.



6.8.2 Is a line superior everywhere? Durum wheat in 22 environments
Two environments are a start. The Algerian durum trial has 22. We compare every genotype with WAHA in each environment separately (Dunnett, as before), and count the environments where the genotype is better, and where it is significantly better or worse.

durum_w <- durum |> mutate(Genotype = relevel(Genotype, ref = "WAHA"))

vs_waha <- durum_w |>
  group_split(Environment) |>
  lapply(function(e) {
    f  <- lm(yield ~ Block + Genotype, data = e)
    em <- emmeans(f, ~ Genotype)
    s  <- as.data.frame(summary(contrast(em, "trt.vs.ctrl", ref = 1)))
    s$Environment <- e$Environment[1]
    s$waha <- summary(em)$emmean[1]
    s
  }) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  mutate(line = gsub("[()]", "", sub(" - WAHA$", "", contrast)))

consistency <- vs_waha |>
  group_by(line) |>
  summarise(better_in          = sum(estimate > 0),
            significantly_higher = sum(p.value < 0.05 & estimate > 0),
            significantly_lower  = sum(p.value < 0.05 & estimate < 0),
            mean_gain_percent    = round(mean(100 * estimate / waha), 1),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(better_in), desc(significantly_higher))

head(consistency, 6)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  line     better_in significantly_higher significantly_lower mean_gain_percent
  <chr>        <int>                <int>               <int>             <dbl>
1 GTADUR          16                    2                   2               9.2
2 CHENS           15                    2                   1               6.8
3 SIMETO          13                    2                   3               3.2
4 SAHEL77         12                    5                   2               5.9
5 B.DUR194        12                    2                   3               4  
6 OFANTO          12                    2                   2               3.2


No genotype is better than WAHA in all environments. The best, GTADUR, is above WAHA in 16 of 22 environments, with an average gain of about 9%, and it is significantly higher in 2 and significantly lower in 2. Compare with the exercise: OFANTO was 45% above WAHA in loc07_year1, but over the 22 environments the average gain is about 3%. One environment can show a spectacular difference that the rest do not confirm.


6.8.3 The best lines of one environment are not as good elsewhere
When we choose the best lines because they were the best in a trial, their observed advantage includes a part of luck (good plots, good blocks) that will not be repeated. This is the selection bias (also called winner’s curse). We can measure it in the durum data: in each environment we select the 3 best genotypes and compare their advantage over the environment mean where they were selected and in the other 21 environments.

env_means <- durum |>
  group_by(Environment, Genotype) |>
  summarise(y = mean(yield), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(Environment) |>
  mutate(dev = y - mean(y)) |>          # deviation from the environment mean
  ungroup()

bias <- bind_rows(lapply(unique(env_means$Environment), function(en) {
  top <- env_means |> filter(Environment == en) |> slice_max(y, n = 3) |> pull(Genotype)
  data.frame(Environment = en,
             where_selected = mean(env_means$dev[env_means$Environment == en &
                                                 env_means$Genotype %in% top]),
             other_envs     = mean(env_means$dev[env_means$Environment != en &
                                                 env_means$Genotype %in% top]))
}))

colMeans(bias[, c("where_selected", "other_envs")])   # advantage in t/ha

where_selected     other_envs 
     0.4800213      0.1483397 

mean(bias$other_envs > 0)                              # share of environments with a real advantage

[1] 0.9090909


The three best genotypes of an environment are, on average, 0.48 t/ha above the environment mean where they were selected, and only 0.15 t/ha above the mean in the other environments: about two thirds of the apparent advantage disappears. The selection is not useless (in 91% of the cases the selected lines are still above average elsewhere), but the gain we will see in the next stage is smaller than the gain we saw when we selected. Three practical consequences:

Select more lines than we need at the first stage, and let the next stage decide.
Use the adjusted means and the interval, not the raw ranking.
Confirm in other environments or seasons before releasing or submitting a line.



6.8.4 A decision rule






TipFrom the trial to the decision




Fix the reference and the smallest gain that matters before the trial.
Fit the model of the design, check the residuals, and get the adjusted means.
Compare all lines with the reference (Dunnett) and classify them: confirmed superior, promising, not different, confirmed inferior.
Advance the confirmed lines and the promising lines that are in the same direction in more than one environment or season.
Retest the other promising lines; drop the rest.
Keep more lines than the final number needed, because the advantage of the selected lines shrinks in the next stage.
Report the difference, its interval and the percentage over the reference, not only the letters.
crumbs: 6  ANOVA and Mean Comparison in Breeding Trials

title: 6  ANOVA and Mean Comparison in Breeding Trials
text:
6.9 Common interpretation pitfalls








Pitfall
Why it misleads
What to do




Reading the letters as a ranking of true values
Letters hide the size of the differences and their uncertainty
Report differences with intervals


“Not significant” means “equal”
The trial may not have power to detect the difference (G4: +22%, p = 0.08)
Look at the interval and at the minimum detectable difference


Many unadjusted tests
With 55 pairs, about 3 false positives are expected by chance
Use Tukey for all pairs, Dunnett against a control


Using the wrong reference
The conclusion changes if the control is the parent, a check or the trial mean
Decide the reference before the trial


Analysing one environment only
A line that wins in one environment may not win in others (G x E)
Use several environments or seasons; look at the consistency


Selection bias
The advantage observed in the selected lines is partly luck
Select more lines than needed and confirm in the next stage


Skipping the diagnostics
A funnel in the residuals or an outlier changes the standard errors
Check the residuals before the comparisons


Transforming the data without going back
Means on the square root scale are not on the original scale
Back-transform the means, or use a model for counts


Treating subsamples as replicates
Plants in the same plot are not independent replicates (pseudoreplication)
Average the subsamples to one value per plot


Ignoring missing plots
Unbalanced data change the standard errors by genotype
Use adjusted means (emmeans), not raw means


One p-value as the decision
It says nothing about the size of the gain
Combine size, interval and the smallest gain that matters
crumbs: 6  ANOVA and Mean Comparison in Breeding Trials

title: 6  ANOVA and Mean Comparison in Breeding Trials
text:
6.10 Questions for discussion
Use these questions to connect the session with your own trials:

In your program, what is the reference against which a new line must be compared? A parent, a check, or both?
What is the smallest gain that would make you advance a line? Is it the same for yield and for disease resistance?
How many replicates and environments do you have in the first trials of a mutant population? What difference could you detect with them?
How many lines do you advance from one stage to the next, and how many would you advance knowing the selection bias?
Which of the pitfalls of the table have you met in your own data?
crumbs: 6  ANOVA and Mean Comparison in Breeding Trials

title: 6  ANOVA and Mean Comparison in Breeding Trials
text:
6.11 Exercise
Use the Algerian durum wheat data in the environment loc07_year1.

Fit the RCBD model and write the ANOVA table. What are the CV and the residual degrees of freedom?
Check the assumptions with a residual plot, a QQ plot and Levene’s test.
Calculate the LSD at 5% and the Tukey groups.
Compare all the genotypes with WAHA, a widely grown variety, using Dunnett. Which genotypes are significantly higher? How many differences would the unadjusted tests have declared?
Express the best genotype as a percentage of WAHA, with its confidence interval. Is it above 10%?







TipSolution






e5 <- durum |>
  filter(Environment == "loc07_year1") |>
  mutate(Genotype = relevel(Genotype, ref = "WAHA"))

# 1. ANOVA, CV, residual df
fit5 <- lm(yield ~ Block + Genotype, data = e5)
anova(fit5)
c(CV = 100 * sigma(fit5) / mean(e5$yield), df = df.residual(fit5))

# 2. Assumptions (the `levene` function is defined in the chapter)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2)); plot(fit5, which = 1:2); par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
levene(e5$yield, e5$Genotype)

# 3. LSD and Tukey
LSD.test(fit5, "Genotype", console = TRUE)$groups
HSD.test(fit5, "Genotype", console = TRUE)$groups

# 4. Dunnett against WAHA
em5  <- emmeans(fit5, ~ Genotype)
dun5 <- summary(contrast(em5, "trt.vs.ctrl", ref = 1), infer = TRUE)
dun5 |> arrange(desc(estimate)) |> head()
sum(summary(contrast(em5, "trt.vs.ctrl", ref = 1), adjust = "none")$p.value < 0.05)

# 5. Percentage of WAHA
waha <- summary(em5) |> filter(Genotype == "WAHA") |> pull(emmean)
dun5 |>
  slice_max(estimate, n = 1) |>
  mutate(across(c(estimate, lower.CL, upper.CL), \(x) 100 * x / waha))

In this environment the CV is 13% with 69 residual degrees of freedom, and the assumptions hold (Levene p = 0.74). Dunnett’s test finds three genotypes above WAHA: OFANTO, CHENS and SIMETO; the unadjusted tests would have declared eight. The best one, OFANTO, yields 45% more than WAHA, with a confidence interval from 12% to 77%, so even the lower limit is above the 10% that matters. Remember that this is one environment: the same genotypes may rank differently elsewhere (Chapter 11).
crumbs: 6  ANOVA and Mean Comparison in Breeding Trials

title: 6  ANOVA and Mean Comparison in Breeding Trials
text:
6.12 Key takeaways

The ANOVA partitions the variation into blocks, genotypes and error. The residual mean square is the base of every comparison; report it, the CV and the residual degrees of freedom.
A significant F says that there are differences, not where. The question that follows decides the test: LSD for screening after a significant F, Tukey for all pairs, Dunnett for lines against a control.
Check the residuals, not the raw data. Funnel shapes in the residuals call for a transformation (square root for counts, logarithm for multiplicative variance).
Statistical significance is not the same as practical value. Read the size of the difference, the confidence interval and the smallest difference that matters, and design the trial so that it can detect that difference.
In augmented designs the error comes from the checks only; the new lines are adjusted for the blocks and the comparisons among them have a large SED.
With several environments, test genotypes against the interaction, not the residual, and look at the G×E variance. When it is larger than the genotype variance, one environment is not enough.
To identify superior genotypes, decide the reference and the smallest gain that matters before the trial, classify the lines with the Dunnett intervals (confirmed, promising, not different, inferior), and prefer lines that agree in more than one environment.
The advantage of the selected lines shrinks in the next stage (in the durum data, by about two thirds). Select more lines than needed and confirm them.
Duncan’s test is common but offers little protection; use Tukey or Dunnett for decisions.

title: 7  Mixed Models, BLUEs, BLUPs and Heritability
text:
7.1 Learning objectives
In Chapter 5 we wrote the model that follows from the layout, and in Chapter 6 we fitted it as a fixed ANOVA. That works well in a complete block design. This chapter explains what changes when the design has incomplete blocks, when some plots are lost, or when we want to predict the performance of lines and measure how much of the variation is genetic.
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(lme4)
library(emmeans)
crumbs: 7  Mixed Models, BLUEs, BLUPs and Heritability

title: 7  Mixed Models, BLUEs, BLUPs and Heritability
text:
Explain why the ANOVA of Chapter 6 is not enough for incomplete block designs and for unbalanced data
Distinguish fixed and random effects, and choose them for a breeding trial
Fit a mixed model with lme4, extract the variance components and test them
Extract and compare BLUEs and BLUPs, and know which one to use
Estimate the heritability of a trial (classical and generalized) and understand what it depends on
crumbs: 7  Mixed Models, BLUEs, BLUPs and Heritability

title: 7  Mixed Models, BLUEs, BLUPs and Heritability
text:
7.2 The bean trial
We use the alpha-lattice bean trial of Chapter 5 and Chapter 4: 380 lines in 2 replicates, each replicate divided into 18 incomplete blocks of 22 plots. Sixteen lines are repeated twice in each replicate (checks), the other 364 lines appear once per replicate. The yield is YdHa_clean, the cleaned and recalculated yield of Chapter 4.

beans <- read_csv("data/Example_Beans.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(rep  = factor(rep),
         line = factor(line),
         # the labels B1 to B18 are used again in each replicate: the block is "rep:block"
         rb   = factor(paste(rep, block, sep = ":")))

n_plots <- beans |> filter(!is.na(YdHa_clean)) |> count(line, name = "n")
checks  <- n_plots |> filter(n > 2) |> pull(line)

yield <- beans |> filter(!is.na(YdHa_clean))     # 788 plots (4 plots have no yield)
c(plots = nrow(yield), lines = nlevels(droplevels(yield$line)), blocks = nlevels(yield$rb))

 plots  lines blocks 
   788    380     36 








WarningBlocks must be nested in the replicate



The block labels B1 to B18 are repeated in the two replicates. If we write (1 | block), the model treats B1 of replicate 1 and B1 of replicate 2 as the same block, which is wrong. We create rb, the block inside its replicate, and use it. This is a very common mistake in resolvable designs.
crumbs: 7  Mixed Models, BLUEs, BLUPs and Heritability

title: 7  Mixed Models, BLUEs, BLUPs and Heritability
section: 7.3 Why the ANOVA is not enough
text:
7.3 Why the ANOVA is not enough
The ANOVA of Chapter 6 can be fitted to this trial:

fit_lm <- lm(YdHa_clean ~ rep + rb + line, data = yield)
anova(fit_lm)

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: YdHa_clean
           Df   Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
rep         1  1774601 1774601 22.0750 3.693e-06 ***
rb         34 37594755 1105728 13.7546 < 2.2e-16 ***
line      379 66960815  176678  2.1978 2.613e-14 ***
Residuals 373 29985316   80390                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


It runs, and the genotype line is significant. But it has four limitations that matter in breeding:

Blocks are as important as genotypes. In a moment we will see that the variance among incomplete blocks is as large as the genetic variance. A line that happened to be sown in a good block looks better than it is.
Fixed blocks use only part of the information. With blocks as fixed effects each line is compared only within the blocks where it appears. A mixed model also uses the differences between blocks (recovery of inter-block information).
The ANOVA gives no genetic parameters. For heritability we need the variance of the genotypes, not the test of their differences.
Lines with different replication are treated alike. In this trial 16 lines have 4 plots and 364 have 2 (and 4 lines have a single plot because of lost yields). The precision of their means is different, and the ranking should take it into account.

The raw means show the problem. Compare the 20% best lines by raw mean with the 20% best lines after adjusting for the blocks:

fit_fix <- lmer(YdHa_clean ~ rep + line + (1 | rb), data = yield)
blue <- emmeans(fit_fix, ~ line, lmer.df = "asymptotic") |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  select(line, BLUE = emmean, SE_BLUE = SE)

raw <- yield |> group_by(line) |> summarise(raw_mean = mean(YdHa_clean), .groups = "drop")
cmp <- left_join(raw, blue, by = "line")

top20 <- function(x) x >= quantile(x, 0.80)
c(correlation = cor(cmp$raw_mean, cmp$BLUE),
  best_20pct_by_raw  = sum(top20(cmp$raw_mean)),
  also_best_by_BLUE  = sum(top20(cmp$raw_mean) & top20(cmp$BLUE)))

      correlation best_20pct_by_raw also_best_by_BLUE 
        0.9019176        76.0000000        61.0000000 


The correlation between the two is 0.90, but 15 of the 76 lines chosen by raw mean (one in five) would not be chosen after adjusting for the incomplete blocks. In the next section we build the model that does the adjustment.
crumbs: 7  Mixed Models, BLUEs, BLUPs and Heritability

title: 7  Mixed Models, BLUEs, BLUPs and Heritability
text:
7.4 Fixed and random effects
A factor is fixed when its levels are the ones we are interested in and we want an estimate for each of them. It is random when its levels are a sample from a larger population and we want to know how much they vary.









Factor
In the bean trial
Usual choice
Why




Replicate
2 replicates
Fixed
Only two levels; a variance would be badly estimated


Incomplete block
36 blocks
Random
Many blocks, sample of the field; we want to recover inter-block information


Genotype (compare lines)
380 lines
Fixed
We want an adjusted mean for every line: BLUE


Genotype (predict, heritability)
380 lines
Random
Lines are a sample of a breeding population; we want their variance and a prediction for each: BLUP



The same factor, the genotype, is fixed or random depending on the question. The rest of the chapter uses both.
crumbs: 7  Mixed Models, BLUEs, BLUPs and Heritability

title: 7  Mixed Models, BLUEs, BLUPs and Heritability
text:
7.5 The model
For the alpha-lattice, the yield of line \(i\) in block \(k\) of replicate \(j\) is:
yield = overall mean + replicate effect + block effect (random)
        + genotype effect + error (random)
The random effects have a variance each: \(\sigma^2_b\) for the blocks, \(\sigma^2_g\) for the genotypes (when it is random) and \(\sigma^2_e\) for the plot error. In lme4 the random terms go in parentheses:

fit_rand <- lmer(YdHa_clean ~ rep + (1 | rb) + (1 | line), data = yield)

vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(fit_rand))
vc <- data.frame(component = c("Genotype", "Incomplete block", "Residual (plot error)"),
                 variance  = round(vc$vcov),
                 percent   = round(100 * vc$vcov / sum(vc$vcov), 1))
vc

              component variance percent
1              Genotype    48762    27.8
2      Incomplete block    46942    26.8
3 Residual (plot error)    79473    45.4


The incomplete blocks carry as much variance as the genotypes (28% and 27% of the total, with 45% for the plot error). This is the reason for the large difference between raw means and adjusted means.






NoteLink with the ANOVA



In a balanced design the variance components can be obtained from the mean squares of the ANOVA (expected mean squares, as we did for the durum wheat in Chapter 6). With incomplete blocks, unbalanced data or several random terms, the mean squares do not give the components directly, and the mixed model, fitted by REML (restricted maximum likelihood), is the tool.



7.5.1 Do the variance components differ from zero?
The likelihood ratio test compares the model with and without the term. The models are fitted by maximum likelihood (REML = FALSE) for the comparison. Because a variance cannot be negative, the null hypothesis is on the boundary and the p-value of the usual chi-square is conservative: divide it by two.

m_full <- update(fit_rand, REML = FALSE)
m_nog  <- update(m_full, . ~ . - (1 | line))     # without genotype variance
m_nob  <- update(m_full, . ~ . - (1 | rb))       # without block variance

chisq <- c(anova(m_nog, m_full)$Chisq[2], anova(m_nob, m_full)$Chisq[2])
data.frame(term = c("Genotype", "Incomplete block"),
           chisq = round(chisq, 1),
           p_value_halved = format.pval(pchisq(chisq, 1, lower.tail = FALSE) / 2, eps = 1e-16))

              term chisq p_value_halved
1         Genotype  64.3     5.4318e-16
2 Incomplete block 177.8        < 1e-16


Both variances are clearly different from zero. As a check of the residuals we use the plot of the model, as in Chapter 6:

res <- data.frame(fitted = fitted(fit_rand), resid = resid(fit_rand))
ggplot(res, aes(fitted, resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Fitted values (kg/ha)", y = "Residuals") + theme_minimal()
ggplot(res, aes(sample = resid)) + stat_qq(alpha = 0.5) + stat_qq_line() +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Residual quantiles") + theme_minimal()







Figure 7.1: Residuals of the mixed model for bean yield. Left: residuals against fitted values. Right: normal QQ plot.











Figure 7.2: Residuals of the mixed model for bean yield. Left: residuals against fitted values. Right: normal QQ plot.
crumbs: 7  Mixed Models, BLUEs, BLUPs and Heritability

title: 7  Mixed Models, BLUEs, BLUPs and Heritability
text:
7.6 BLUEs and BLUPs
The two acronyms describe two kinds of estimate of the genotype value:

BLUE (best linear unbiased estimate): the genotype is fixed. The estimate is the mean of the line adjusted for blocks and replicates, with no other correction. It is the value we computed above with emmeans.
BLUP (best linear unbiased prediction): the genotype is random. The estimate is a weighted combination of the line’s own data and the population mean. Lines with little or noisy information are pulled toward the mean: they are shrunk.


mu <- fixef(fit_rand)["(Intercept)"] + fixef(fit_rand)["repR2"] / 2   # mean of the 2 replicates
blup <- tibble(line = rownames(ranef(fit_rand)$line),
               BLUP = mu + ranef(fit_rand)$line[, 1])

est <- blue |> left_join(blup, by = "line") |> left_join(n_plots, by = "line") |>
  mutate(plots = factor(n))

c(sd_BLUE = sd(est$BLUE), sd_BLUP = sd(est$BLUP), correlation = cor(est$BLUE, est$BLUP))

    sd_BLUE     sd_BLUP correlation 
296.9985284 162.6427027   0.9955397 


The BLUEs and BLUPs are almost perfectly correlated, but the BLUPs are much less spread: the standard deviation of the BLUEs includes the plot error, the BLUPs are corrected for it.

ggplot(est, aes(BLUE, BLUP, colour = plots)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "BLUE (kg/ha)", y = "BLUP (kg/ha)", colour = "Plots per line") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 7.3: BLUE against BLUP of the 380 bean lines. The dashed line is y = x. Lines with fewer plots (colour) are shrunk more toward the mean.





How much each group is shrunk can be measured as the slope of the BLUP deviations on the BLUE deviations:

est |>
  group_by(plots) |>
  summarise(lines = n(),
            shrinkage_slope = coef(lm(I(BLUP - mean(est$BLUP)) ~ 0 + I(BLUE - mean(est$BLUE))))[[1]],
            .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(shrinkage_slope = round(shrinkage_slope, 2))

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  plots lines shrinkage_slope
  <fct> <int>           <dbl>
1 1         4            0.38
2 2       360            0.54
3 4        16            0.7 


A slope of 1 would mean no shrinkage. The lines with a single plot keep only 38% of their deviation from the mean, those with two plots 54%, and those with four plots 70%. The shrinkage factor is the reliability: the part of the variation of the estimate that is genetic. It grows with the number of plots and with the heritability.






ImportantWhich one to use?











Use
BLUE
BLUP




Ranking and selecting lines in one trial
Possible, but noisy for lines with few plots
Preferred: corrects for the unequal precision


Comparison with a parent or a check (Dunnett, Chapter 6)
Yes: the genotype is fixed
No


Input to a second stage (multi-environment analysis, Chapter 11)
Yes, with its standard error as weight
Not as input (the shrinkage would be applied twice)


Heritability and genetic parameters
No
Yes (random genotype)



BLUPs rank lines more fairly, BLUEs are unbiased estimates of each line. A line with a high BLUE and little data can be a lucky line; the BLUP tells us how much to trust it.
crumbs: 7  Mixed Models, BLUEs, BLUPs and Heritability

title: 7  Mixed Models, BLUEs, BLUPs and Heritability
text:
7.7 Heritability
The broad-sense heritability is the proportion of the variance of the phenotypic values that is genetic. Its value depends on what we call a phenotypic value. For the variance components of a trial there are two common bases:
Plot basis:        H2 = Vg / (Vg + Ve)
Entry-mean basis:  H2 = Vg / (Vg + Ve / r)       r = replicates per line
The first is the heritability of a single plot, and the second is the heritability of the mean of \(r\) plots. The second is the one that matters for selecting lines on their means. In this trial \(r\) is about 2.07, the mean number of plots per line:

vcs <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(fit_rand))
Vg <- vcs$vcov[vcs$grp == "line"]; Ve <- vcs$vcov[vcs$grp == "Residual"]
r  <- nrow(yield) / nlevels(droplevels(yield$line))

c(r = r, H2_plot = Vg / (Vg + Ve), H2_mean = Vg / (Vg + Ve / r))

        r   H2_plot   H2_mean 
2.0736842 0.3802532 0.5599239 



7.7.1 Generalized heritability (Cullis)
The classical formula assumes a balanced design with the same number of plots per line, and it ignores the blocks. In an incomplete block or unbalanced trial we use the generalized heritability of Cullis et al. (2006) and Piepho and Möhring (2007), based on the precision of the BLUPs: the mean variance of the difference between two BLUPs (the PEV, prediction error variance):
H2 (Cullis) = 1 - (mean variance of a difference between two BLUPs) / (2 Vg)
lme4 does not report it directly. The function below builds it from the model matrices (the mixed model equations), for models with random intercept terms:

h2_cullis <- function(model, genotype) {
  X <- getME(model, "X"); Z <- getME(model, "Z")
  s2 <- sigma(model)^2
  vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(model))
  fl <- getME(model, "flist"); Gp <- getME(model, "Gp")
  # variance of each random effect column, in the order of Z
  v <- unlist(lapply(names(fl), function(g) rep(vc$vcov[vc$grp == g], nlevels(fl[[g]]))))
  W <- cbind(X, Z)
  C <- crossprod(W) / s2
  idx <- ncol(X) + seq_along(v)
  C[cbind(idx, idx)] <- C[cbind(idx, idx)] + 1 / v
  Cinv <- solve(as.matrix(C))
  k <- match(genotype, names(fl))
  gi <- ncol(X) + (Gp[k] + 1):Gp[k + 1]
  P <- Cinv[gi, gi]                                   # PEV matrix of the genotype BLUPs
  n <- nrow(P)
  vdiff <- 2 * (n * sum(diag(P)) - sum(P)) / (n * (n - 1))   # mean variance of a difference
  Vg <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == genotype]
  1 - vdiff / (2 * Vg)
}

h2_cullis(fit_rand, "line")

[1] 0.5424861


The Cullis value (0.54) is slightly lower than the classical one (0.56) because the unbalanced replication and the incomplete blocks are taken into account. We can check that the function is correct in a case where both must agree: a balanced RCBD, such as one durum wheat environment of Chapter 6.

durum <- read_csv("data/Durum_wheat_Algeria.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(Genotype = factor(Genotype), Block = factor(Block))

e10 <- durum |> filter(Environment == "loc10_year1")
m_e10 <- lmer(yield ~ (1 | Block) + (1 | Genotype), data = e10)
v10 <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m_e10))

c(classical = v10$vcov[v10$grp == "Genotype"] /
              (v10$vcov[v10$grp == "Genotype"] + v10$vcov[v10$grp == "Residual"] / 4),
  cullis    = h2_cullis(m_e10, "Genotype"))

classical    cullis 
0.7313521 0.7313521 




7.7.2 Heritability of each trait
The same model fitted to each trait gives the heritability of each one. This is the information needed for the selection indices of Chapter 8:

trait_h2 <- function(trait) {
  x <- beans |> filter(!is.na(.data[[trait]])) |> mutate(y = .data[[trait]])
  m <- lmer(y ~ rep + (1 | rb) + (1 | line), data = x)
  v <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m))
  data.frame(trait = trait, mean = round(mean(x$y), 1),
             Vg = round(v$vcov[v$grp == "line"], 2),
             Ve = round(v$vcov[v$grp == "Residual"], 2),
             H2_cullis = round(h2_cullis(m, "line"), 2))
}

traits <- c(yield = "YdHa_clean", flowering_days = "DF", maturity_days = "DPM",
            plant_height = "PLHA", seed_weight_100 = "SW100")
bind_rows(lapply(traits, trait_h2))

       trait   mean       Vg       Ve H2_cullis
1 YdHa_clean 1370.3 48761.81 79473.28      0.54
2         DF   41.5     4.69     5.03      0.65
3        DPM   81.6     1.09     1.17      0.64
4       PLHA   27.5     0.73    10.39      0.12
5      SW100   53.3    42.43    13.23      0.86


Seed weight is the most heritable trait (0.86), days to flowering and maturity are intermediate (0.65 and 0.64), yield is 0.54, and plant height is low (0.12): in this trial, most of the differences in plant height among lines are plot error, and selecting on it would be little better than random.
crumbs: 7  Mixed Models, BLUEs, BLUPs and Heritability

title: 7  Mixed Models, BLUEs, BLUPs and Heritability
section: 7.8 Heritability is not a property of the trait
text:
7.8 Heritability is not a property of the trait
The value of \(H^2\) belongs to a population, a set of environments and a design. The same trait gives different values in another trial. The durum wheat data show it with real numbers. In each of the 22 environments, a balanced RCBD with 4 replicates, the entry-mean heritability is:

h2_env <- durum |>
  group_by(Environment) |>
  group_modify(\(d, key) {
    a <- anova(lm(yield ~ Block + Genotype, data = d))
    tibble(H2 = 1 - a[["Mean Sq"]][3] / a[["Mean Sq"]][2])
  }) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(h2_env, aes(H2, reorder(Environment, H2))) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Heritability (entry-mean basis)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

summary(h2_env$H2)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
 0.2856  0.6697  0.7973  0.7478  0.9100  0.9783 








Figure 7.4: Heritability (entry-mean basis, 4 replicates) of durum wheat yield in the 22 environments of the Algerian trial.





The same 24 genotypes, the same design and the same crop give a heritability from 0.29 to 0.98, with a median of 0.80. An environment with a low heritability does not say that yield is “not heritable” but that in that trial the plot error was large compared with the genetic differences.

7.8.1 How the design changes the heritability
With several environments the heritability of a line mean over all of them also depends on the genotype by environment variance and on the number of environments and replicates (Chapter 11):
H2 = Vg / (Vg + Vge / e + Ve / (e r))          e = environments, r = replicates
With the variance components of the 22 environments of the durum wheat we can see what each additional replicate or environment adds. This is a planning table, calculated from the model, not new data:

m_met <- lmer(yield ~ (1 | Environment / Block) + (1 | Genotype) + (1 | Genotype:Environment),
              data = durum)
v <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m_met))
Vg_m  <- v$vcov[v$grp == "Genotype"]
Vge_m <- v$vcov[v$grp == "Genotype:Environment"]
Ve_m  <- v$vcov[v$grp == "Residual"]

expand.grid(environments = c(1, 2, 5, 10, 22), replicates = c(1, 2, 4)) |>
  mutate(H2 = round(Vg_m / (Vg_m + Vge_m / environments + Ve_m / (environments * replicates)), 2)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = replicates, values_from = H2, names_prefix = "r = ")

# A tibble: 5 × 4
  environments `r = 1` `r = 2` `r = 4`
         <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>
1            1    0.21    0.27    0.32
2            2    0.34    0.42    0.48
3            5    0.56    0.65    0.7 
4           10    0.72    0.79    0.82
5           22    0.85    0.89    0.91


A single environment with 2 replicates gives a heritability of 0.27. Moving from 2 to 4 replicates in that environment adds only 0.05 (to 0.32), while moving from 1 to 5 environments, keeping 2 replicates, adds 0.38 (to 0.65). When G×E is large, more environments are worth more than more replicates. (The variance components are those of Chapter 6: genotype 0.036, G×E 0.058, error 0.083.)






ImportantCommon misunderstandings




A high heritability does not mean that the trait is “controlled by genes” in general, but that in this trial and population the genetic differences are large compared with the error.
A low heritability does not mean that selection is impossible: with more replicates and environments the heritability of the mean increases.
Heritabilities of different trials are not comparable if the design, the number of replicates or the population differ.
The heritability is an estimate: it has a standard error that is large when there are few lines or few environments.
crumbs: 7  Mixed Models, BLUEs, BLUPs and Heritability

title: 7  Mixed Models, BLUEs, BLUPs and Heritability
text:
7.9 One stage or two stages
In a multi-environment trial there are two ways of fitting the model. In a one-stage analysis, all the plots of all the trials go in a single model. In a two-stage analysis, the first stage fits each trial separately (the model of its design, with the BLUEs of the lines), and the second stage fits the model over environments using these BLUEs. The second stage must weight the BLUEs by their precision (the weight is \(1 / sem^2\), the inverse of the squared standard error of the BLUE): without weights the residual variance is not identifiable and the result is wrong. Piepho and Möhring (2009) compared several weighting methods and found that a weighted two-stage analysis gives results close to the one-stage analysis. We use this in Chapter 11. The standard errors that we saved in blue above (SE_BLUE) are the ones used for the weights.
crumbs: 7  Mixed Models, BLUEs, BLUPs and Heritability

title: 7  Mixed Models, BLUEs, BLUPs and Heritability
text:
7.10 Exercise
Use the bean trial and the trait days to maturity (DPM).

Fit the model with random blocks (rb) and random lines. What percentage of the variance is genotype, block and residual?
Test the genotype variance with the likelihood ratio test.
Calculate the classical entry-mean heritability and the Cullis heritability. Why do they differ?
Extract the BLUPs and list the 5 earliest lines (lowest days to maturity) among the test lines (not the checks).
How many of those 5 lines are also among the 5 earliest by BLUE?







TipSolution






x <- beans |> filter(!is.na(DPM))

# 1. Variance components
m <- lmer(DPM ~ rep + (1 | rb) + (1 | line), data = x)
v <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m))
data.frame(component = v$grp, variance = round(v$vcov, 2),
           percent = round(100 * v$vcov / sum(v$vcov), 1))

# 2. LRT for genotype (p-value halved)
m_ml  <- update(m, REML = FALSE)
m_no  <- update(m_ml, . ~ . - (1 | line))
a <- anova(m_no, m_ml)
c(chisq = a$Chisq[2], p_halved = a$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2] / 2)

# 3. Heritability
r  <- nrow(x) / nlevels(droplevels(x$line))
Vg <- v$vcov[v$grp == "line"]; Ve <- v$vcov[v$grp == "Residual"]
c(classical = Vg / (Vg + Ve / r), cullis = h2_cullis(m, "line"))

# 4. Five earliest test lines by BLUP
mu <- fixef(m)["(Intercept)"] + fixef(m)["repR2"] / 2
blup_dpm <- tibble(line = rownames(ranef(m)$line), BLUP = mu + ranef(m)$line[, 1]) |>
  filter(!line %in% checks) |> arrange(BLUP)
head(blup_dpm, 5)

# 5. Same by BLUE
mf <- lmer(DPM ~ rep + line + (1 | rb), data = x)
blue_dpm <- emmeans(mf, ~ line, lmer.df = "asymptotic") |> as.data.frame() |>
  filter(!line %in% checks) |> arrange(emmean)
length(intersect(head(blup_dpm$line, 5), head(blue_dpm$line, 5)))

Genotype is 44% of the variance, incomplete blocks 8% and the residual 47%: the blocks matter much less for maturity than for yield. The genotype variance is highly significant (chi-square 112). The classical heritability is 0.66 and the Cullis heritability 0.64; the difference comes from the unequal replication (checks have 4 plots, a few lines have 1) and from the block adjustment. The five earliest test lines by BLUP are LPA_530, DAA_014, ACC_022, DAA_015 and DAB_555; four of them are also in the BLUE list (the BLUE list has DAB_489 instead of DAB_555).
crumbs: 7  Mixed Models, BLUEs, BLUPs and Heritability

title: 7  Mixed Models, BLUEs, BLUPs and Heritability
text:
7.11 Key takeaways

An incomplete block design needs the blocks as random effects; the mixed model recovers the information between blocks and gives genetic parameters. In the bean trial the block variance was as large as the genetic variance.
Blocks nested in replicates must be coded as replicate:block when their labels are repeated.
BLUE (genotype fixed) for comparing lines and as input to a second stage; BLUP (genotype random) for ranking and for heritability. BLUPs shrink the lines with little data toward the mean.
The heritability is the proportion of the variance that is genetic on a defined basis (plot or entry mean). In unbalanced or incomplete designs use the generalized (Cullis) heritability.
Heritability belongs to a trial, not to a trait: the same durum wheat gave 0.29 to 0.98 across environments. When G×E is large, more environments increase it more than more replicates.
Test variance components with the likelihood ratio test, halving the p-value.
For a multi-environment analysis in two stages, weight the BLUEs by \(1 / sem^2\).

Piepho, H. P., Möhring, J., Melchinger, A. E., & Büchse, A. (2008). BLUP for phenotypic selection in plant breeding and variety testing. Euphytica, 161, 209-228. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10681-007-9449-8

title: 8  Selection Decisions: Ranking, Expected Gain and Selection Indices
text:
8.1 Learning objectives
Chapter 7 gave us the estimates (BLUEs and BLUPs) and the heritability of each trait. This chapter uses them to decide: which lines to advance, how much gain to expect, and how to select on several traits at the same time. We continue with the bean trial and keep the same data preparation.
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(lme4)
library(emmeans)
beans <- read_csv("data/Example_Beans.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(rep = factor(rep), line = factor(line),
         rb  = factor(paste(rep, block, sep = ":")))      # block inside replicate

checks <- beans |> filter(!is.na(YdHa_clean)) |> count(line) |> filter(n > 2) |> pull(line)
crumbs: 8  Selection Decisions: Ranking, Expected Gain and Selection Indices

title: 8  Selection Decisions: Ranking, Expected Gain and Selection Indices
text:
Rank lines from BLUEs and BLUPs and compare them with the checks
Predict the genetic gain of a selection with the breeder’s equation, and compare the prediction with a realized gain
Explain why selecting on one trait is not enough and build a multi-trait selection index
Choose and justify the weights of an index, and know the limits of a base index
crumbs: 8  Selection Decisions: Ranking, Expected Gain and Selection Indices

title: 8  Selection Decisions: Ranking, Expected Gain and Selection Indices
text:
8.2 From estimates to a ranking
For each of five traits we fit the two models of Chapter 7: the model with fixed lines (BLUEs) and the model with random lines (BLUPs and the genetic standard deviation).

fit_trait <- function(trait) {
  x <- beans |> filter(!is.na(.data[[trait]])) |> mutate(y = .data[[trait]])

  m_fix <- lmer(y ~ rep + line + (1 | rb), data = x)                    # BLUE
  be <- as.data.frame(emmeans(m_fix, ~ line, lmer.df = "asymptotic"))

  m_ran <- lmer(y ~ rep + (1 | rb) + (1 | line), data = x)              # BLUP
  mu <- fixef(m_ran)["(Intercept)"] + fixef(m_ran)["repR2"] / 2

  list(blue = data.frame(line = be$line, BLUE = be$emmean),
       blup = data.frame(line = rownames(ranef(m_ran)$line),
                         BLUP = mu + ranef(m_ran)$line[, 1]),
       sd_g = sqrt(as.data.frame(VarCorr(m_ran))$vcov[1]))
}

traits <- c(Yield = "YdHa_clean", DF = "DF", DPM = "DPM", PLHA = "PLHA", SW100 = "SW100")
fits   <- lapply(traits, fit_trait)

collect <- function(what) {            # one table, one column per trait
  Reduce(\(a, b) inner_join(a, b, by = "line"),
         lapply(names(fits), \(t) setNames(fits[[t]][[what]], c("line", t))))
}
blue <- collect("blue")
blup <- collect("blup")
sd_g <- sapply(fits, `[[`, "sd_g")        # genetic standard deviation of each trait

head(blue, 3)

     line     Yield       DF      DPM     PLHA    SW100
1 ACC_002 1456.3823 39.24864 79.94415 28.51760 49.64092
2 ACC_003  908.1405 46.99363 83.32727 24.30038 48.93574
3 ACC_004  712.0953 40.28507 81.69511 23.92066 53.51706


We select among the test lines. The 16 checks are not candidates; they are the reference.

test_blue <- blue |> filter(!line %in% checks)
test_blup <- blup |> filter(!line %in% checks)
n_plots   <- beans |> filter(!is.na(YdHa_clean)) |> count(line, name = "plots")

test_blup |>
  select(line, BLUP = Yield) |>
  left_join(select(test_blue, line, BLUE = Yield), by = "line") |>
  left_join(n_plots, by = "line") |>
  arrange(desc(BLUP)) |>
  head(10) |>
  mutate(across(c(BLUP, BLUE), round))

      line BLUP BLUE plots
1  SEF_060 1936 2424     2
2  DAB_366 1855 2267     2
3  DAB_577 1817 2184     2
4  DOR_390 1783 2122     2
5  DOR_364 1772 2121     2
6  LPA_435 1721 1992     2
7  DAN_012 1704 1988     2
8  DAA_001 1671 1947     2
9  DAB_049 1668 1924     2
10 SER_118 1660 1901     2


A selection of the best 20% of the 364 test lines is 73 lines. The lists by BLUP and by BLUE share 70 of them: for a trait like yield, with similar replication in most lines, they agree. They differ in only 3 lines, those where the replication or the block makes the BLUE and the BLUP disagree.

k <- round(0.20 * nrow(test_blue))
top_blue <- test_blue$line[order(-test_blue$Yield)][1:k]
top_blup <- test_blup$line[order(-test_blup$Yield)][1:k]

c(selected = k, shared_by_BLUE_and_BLUP = length(intersect(top_blue, top_blup)))

               selected shared_by_BLUE_and_BLUP 
                     73                      70 

# the checks as reference
c(checks_mean_BLUE = mean(blue$Yield[blue$line %in% checks]),
  test_lines_mean_BLUE = mean(test_blue$Yield),
  best_check_BLUP = max(blup$Yield[blup$line %in% checks]))

    checks_mean_BLUE test_lines_mean_BLUE      best_check_BLUP 
            1516.856             1357.573             1757.469 


The mean of the checks (1517 kg/ha) is above the mean of the test lines (1358 kg/ha): the checks are good varieties, so a test line must be compared with them and not only with the trial mean. As in Chapter 6, a reference decided before the trial and the confidence interval of the difference are what turn a ranking into a decision.

title: 8  Selection Decisions: Ranking, Expected Gain and Selection Indices
text:
8.3 Expected genetic gain
How much will the next generation improve if we select the best 20%? The breeder’s equation gives the answer:
R = i × h² × σP

R   = response to selection (gain per cycle), in the units of the trait
i   = selection intensity (standardized selection differential)
h²  = heritability on the basis of the selection unit
σP  = phenotypic standard deviation of the selection unit
It is the same equation as the genetic gain equation of the Wageningen course, \(R = i \, r \, \sigma_A / t\), where \(r\) is the accuracy of selection (the square root of the heritability for a selection on means) and \(t\) the length of the cycle. The selection intensity depends only on the proportion selected:

p <- c(0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.50)
data.frame(proportion_selected = p,
           intensity_i = round(dnorm(qnorm(1 - p)) / p, 2))

  proportion_selected intensity_i
1                0.05        2.06
2                0.10        1.75
3                0.20        1.40
4                0.50        0.80


For the bean yield, with the entry-mean heritability of Chapter 7 (0.54) and the genetic standard deviation (221 kg/ha), selecting 20% gives:

i  <- dnorm(qnorm(0.80)) / 0.20             # 1.40
H2 <- 0.54                                  # Cullis heritability of yield (chapter 7)
R  <- i * sqrt(H2) * sd_g["Yield"]          # i * H2 * sigma_P = i * sqrt(H2) * sigma_g

c(gain_kg_ha = unname(R), gain_percent = unname(100 * R / mean(test_blue$Yield)))

  gain_kg_ha gain_percent 
   227.14634     16.73179 


An expected gain of about 227 kg/ha, 17% of the mean yield, in the same environment. The gain in other environments is smaller when there is G×E (Chapter 11).

8.3.1 Predicted and realized gain, with real data
We can test the equation with the data. Each test line is in two replicates. We select the best 20% by their yield in replicate 1 only, and measure how much better they are in replicate 2, which was not used for the selection. The prediction uses the heritability of a single plot:

w <- beans |> filter(!is.na(YdHa_clean)) |> group_by(line) |> filter(n() == 2) |> ungroup()
j <- inner_join(filter(w, rep == "R1") |> select(line, y1 = YdHa_clean),
                filter(w, rep == "R2") |> select(line, y2 = YdHa_clean), by = "line")

selected <- j$y1 >= quantile(j$y1, 0.80)

vcw <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(lmer(YdHa_clean ~ rep + (1 | rb) + (1 | line), data = w)))
Vg <- vcw$vcov[1]; Vb <- vcw$vcov[2]; Ve <- vcw$vcov[3]
h2_plot <- Vg / (Vg + Vb + Ve)                 # one raw plot: blocks and error are "noise"

c(lines = nrow(j),
  observed_in_selection = mean(j$y1[selected]) - mean(j$y1),
  predicted_gain        = i * h2_plot * sqrt(Vg + Vb + Ve),
  realized_gain         = mean(j$y2[selected]) - mean(j$y2))

                lines observed_in_selection        predicted_gain 
             360.0000              604.9570              166.1910 
        realized_gain 
             147.4172 


The equation predicts a gain of 166 kg/ha, and the realized gain in the independent replicate is 147 kg/ha: the prediction is close, slightly optimistic. But look at the first number: in the replicate where we selected, the chosen lines looked 605 kg/ha better than the mean. Only about a quarter of that advantage (147 kg/ha) was real. This is the selection bias of Chapter 6, now measured on one trial. A selection on a single plot overestimates the gain by a factor of four; this is why we select on BLUPs of several plots and, when we can, in several environments.

title: 8  Selection Decisions: Ranking, Expected Gain and Selection Indices
section: 8.4 Why one trait is not enough
text:
8.4 Why one trait is not enough
Breeders do not select only for yield. A line must also flower and mature at the right time, have the right seed size and the right plant type. If we select on yield alone, the other traits change as a side effect, in a direction that we did not choose.

index_traits <- c("Yield", "SW100", "DPM")
yield_only <- test_blue$line[order(-test_blue$Yield)][1:k]

# selection differential: mean of the selected lines minus mean of all test lines
diff_sel <- function(lines, vars = index_traits) {
  colMeans(test_blue[test_blue$line %in% lines, vars]) - colMeans(test_blue[, vars])
}
round(diff_sel(yield_only), 1)

Yield SW100   DPM 
415.8  -1.0  -0.2 


Selecting on yield gives 416 kg/ha more yield, and almost no change in seed weight or maturity. In this trial yield is nearly independent of the other traits, so a selection on yield alone does no harm but does not improve earliness or seed weight either. Where traits are correlated the side effects are larger: days to flowering and days to maturity have a correlation of 0.78.

round(cor(test_blue[, c("Yield", "DF", "DPM", "PLHA", "SW100")]), 2)

      Yield    DF   DPM  PLHA SW100
Yield  1.00 -0.12 -0.11  0.23 -0.03
DF    -0.12  1.00  0.78 -0.03 -0.06
DPM   -0.11  0.78  1.00 -0.06 -0.11
PLHA   0.23 -0.03 -0.06  1.00 -0.24
SW100 -0.03 -0.06 -0.11 -0.24  1.00

title: 8  Selection Decisions: Ranking, Expected Gain and Selection Indices
text:
8.5 The selection index
A selection index combines several traits in one number per line, and we select the lines with the highest value. The simplest is the base index:
I = b1 × z1 + b2 × z2 + ... + bk × zk

zj = standardized trait j  (value minus mean, divided by the standard deviation)
bj = weight of trait j
Three rules make it usable:

The sign of the weight sets the direction. Positive when higher is better (yield, seed weight), negative when lower is better (days to maturity, disease score, lodging).
Only the ratios between the weights matter. Weights of 1, 0.5 and 0.5 give the same ranking as 10, 5 and 5. They are relative importances that the breeder decides, not economic values unless we define them so.
Weights are for traits in standard deviation units. Because the traits are standardized, a trait with a large range does not dominate just because of its units.

The base index ignores the covariances among traits and the heritabilities. The Smith-Hazel index (Smith, 1936; Hazel, 1943) uses them: the weights that maximize the correlation between the index and the true breeding value are \(\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{P}^{-1}\mathbf{G}\mathbf{a}\), with \(\mathbf{P}\) the phenotypic and \(\mathbf{G}\) the genetic covariance matrix and \(\mathbf{a}\) the economic weights. It is more efficient, but it needs good estimates of \(\mathbf{G}\) and \(\mathbf{P}\), which require a multi-trait mixed model and many lines. For the first selection stages and for this course, the base index with weights that the breeder understands is the practical choice (Williams, 1962).

8.5.1 A function for the index and its PCA plot
The function below calculates the index, selects a percentage of the lines and draws a PCA that shows where the selected lines are. It has been adapted from the selection index function that we use in our own breeding work, with the following changes with respect to a basic version:

The weights are a named vector, so that a change in the column order cannot send a weight to the wrong trait.
Lines with a missing trait are reported with a warning (a line without one value cannot be ranked, and silently putting it last means it is never selected).
The index is a supplementary variable of the PCA: it is shown as an arrow, but it does not shape the axes that it is supposed to explain.
An optional sd_ref allows standardizing by a reference standard deviation (for example the genetic standard deviation) instead of the standard deviation of the data.


selIndex <- function(Y, b, scale = TRUE, sd_ref = NULL) {
  # b: named vector of weights (positive: higher is better; negative: lower is better)
  b <- b[colnames(Y)]
  if (anyNA(b)) stop("Every column of Y needs a weight in b (named vector).")
  if (!is.null(sd_ref)) {                 # standardize by a reference SD (e.g. genetic SD)
    Z <- sweep(sweep(Y, 2, colMeans(Y), "-"), 2, sd_ref[colnames(Y)], "/")
  } else if (scale) Z <- scale(Y) else Z <- Y
  drop(Z %*% b)
}

pca_index <- function(data, id, b, percentage = 0.20, sd_ref = NULL) {
  data <- as.data.frame(data)
  traits <- names(b)
  if (!all(traits %in% names(data))) stop("Some traits of b are not columns of data.")
  # lines with a missing trait cannot be ranked: report them, do not drop them silently
  miss <- !complete.cases(data[, traits])
  if (any(miss)) {
    warning(sum(miss), " line(s) with missing values were removed: ",
            paste(data[[id]][miss], collapse = ", "))
    data <- data[!miss, ]
  }
  Y <- as.matrix(data[, traits]); rownames(Y) <- data[[id]]
  res <- data.frame(Y, index = selIndex(Y, b, sd_ref = sd_ref))
  res <- res[order(-res$index), ]
  n_sel <- max(1, round(percentage * nrow(res)))
  res$selected <- factor(seq_len(nrow(res)) <= n_sel, levels = c(FALSE, TRUE),
                         labels = c("not selected", "selected"))
  # the index is a supplementary variable: it does not shape the axes
  pca <- FactoMineR::PCA(res, scale.unit = TRUE, graph = FALSE,
                         quanti.sup = which(names(res) == "index"),
                         quali.sup  = which(names(res) == "selected"))
  p1 <- factoextra::fviz_pca_var(pca, col.var = "black", repel = TRUE) + theme_minimal()
  p2 <- factoextra::fviz_pca_ind(pca, label = "none", habillage = res$selected,
                                 palette = c("#00AFBB", "#FC4E07"), addEllipses = TRUE) +
    theme_minimal()
  list(pca = pca, figure = cowplot::plot_grid(p1, p2, labels = c("A", "B")),
       results = res, selection = res[res$selected == "selected", ])
}



8.5.2 Running the index
We choose three traits: yield (weight 1), seed weight (weight 0.5) and days to maturity (weight -0.5, because earlier lines are preferred). Days to flowering are left out because they are strongly correlated with maturity (0.78): including both would count the same information twice.

b_index <- c(Yield = 1, SW100 = 0.5, DPM = -0.5)
res <- pca_index(test_blue, id = "line", b = b_index, percentage = 0.20)
res$figure







Figure 8.1: PCA of the 364 test lines for the three traits of the index. A: the traits and the index (dashed arrow, supplementary). The index points opposite to days to maturity because its weight is negative. B: the lines; the 73 selected lines (orange) are at the side of high yield and seed weight and early maturity.





The figure explains the result. In A, yield and seed weight point toward the index, and days to maturity points in the opposite direction, as it should with a negative weight. In B, the selected lines are grouped on the side where the index grows.

head(res$selection, 6) |> mutate(across(c(Yield, SW100, DPM, index), \(x) round(x, 1)))

         Yield SW100  DPM index selected
DAB_577 2183.6  66.5 81.1   3.9 selected
DAB_366 2267.1  57.4 82.0   3.2 selected
DAA_166 1817.1  62.8 80.3   2.7 selected
DAA_014 1551.8  66.4 78.8   2.7 selected
DAB_591 1853.3  56.4 79.6   2.7 selected
DAA_062 1758.6  68.7 81.2   2.6 selected


What did this selection change, compared with selecting on yield alone?

data.frame(
  trait         = index_traits,
  yield_only    = round(diff_sel(yield_only), 1),
  index_of_3    = round(diff_sel(rownames(res$selection)), 1),
  row.names     = NULL
)

  trait yield_only index_of_3
1 Yield      415.8      349.3
2 SW100       -1.0        3.7
3   DPM       -0.2       -0.8


The index gives up 67 kg/ha of yield gain (349 instead of 416) to gain 3.7 g in the weight of 100 seeds and to bring maturity forward by 0.8 days. That is the price of the other traits, and it is explicit. The mean yield of the selected lines is 1707 kg/ha, above the mean of the checks (1517 kg/ha).


8.5.3 How much do the weights matter?
The weights are a decision, so it is worth knowing how sensitive the selection is to them. We compare the lines selected by other sets of weights with the base set:

scenarios <- list(
  "base (1, 0.5, -0.5)"            = c(Yield = 1, SW100 = 0.5, DPM = -0.5),
  "base x 10 (10, 5, -5)"          = c(Yield = 10, SW100 = 5, DPM = -5),
  "equal importance (1, 1, -1)"    = c(Yield = 1, SW100 = 1, DPM = -1),
  "yield counts double (2, 0.5, -0.5)" = c(Yield = 2, SW100 = 0.5, DPM = -0.5),
  "no earliness (1, 0.5, 0)"       = c(Yield = 1, SW100 = 0.5, DPM = 0),
  "yield only (1, 0, 0)"           = c(Yield = 1, SW100 = 0, DPM = 0))

base_sel <- rownames(res$selection)
data.frame(
  weights = names(scenarios),
  shared_with_base = sapply(scenarios, \(b) {
    s <- pca_index(test_blue, id = "line", b = b, percentage = 0.20)
    length(intersect(rownames(s$selection), base_sel))
  }),
  row.names = NULL)

                             weights shared_with_base
1                base (1, 0.5, -0.5)               73
2              base x 10 (10, 5, -5)               73
3        equal importance (1, 1, -1)               62
4 yield counts double (2, 0.5, -0.5)               65
5           no earliness (1, 0.5, 0)               61
6               yield only (1, 0, 0)               53


Multiplying all the weights by 10 selects exactly the same 73 lines. Changing the ratios changes between 8 and 20 of the 73 lines. A selection that changes a few lines when the weights change slightly is robust; the lines that appear in every scenario are the safest candidates.


8.5.4 Traits with low heritability
Plant height has a heritability of only 0.12 (Chapter 7). If we give it a weight in the index with BLUEs standardized by their standard deviation, a trait that is mostly plot error gets the same importance as a trait that is mostly genetic. We can see the effect by adding plant height with the same weight as yield, and counting how many of the 73 lines chosen by yield alone remain:

b_h <- c(Yield = 1, PLHA = 1)
yield_alone <- rownames(pca_index(test_blue, id = "line", b = c(Yield = 1, PLHA = 0))$selection)

with_blue <- pca_index(test_blue, id = "line", b = b_h)                   # BLUEs, z-scores
with_blup <- pca_index(test_blup, id = "line", b = b_h, sd_ref = sd_g)    # BLUPs / genetic SD

c(BLUE_zscores = length(intersect(yield_alone, rownames(with_blue$selection))),
  BLUP_over_genetic_sd = length(intersect(yield_alone, rownames(with_blup$selection))))

        BLUE_zscores BLUP_over_genetic_sd 
                  46                   58 


With the BLUE z-scores, only 46 of the 73 lines chosen by yield alone remain: the noisy plant height reshuffles the selection. With the BLUPs divided by the genetic standard deviation, 58 remain: the BLUP of a trait of low heritability is shrunk, and it contributes less to the index, which is what we want. If a trait has a low heritability, either give it a low weight or use BLUPs.






WarningDo not standardize BLUPs by their own standard deviation



If we apply scale() to a column of BLUPs, the shrinkage is undone: the BLUPs of plant height have a standard deviation of 0.30 cm and the BLUEs of 2.5 cm, but after scale() both have a standard deviation of 1. Use the BLUEs, or standardize the BLUPs by the genetic standard deviation (sd_ref), as above.

title: 8  Selection Decisions: Ranking, Expected Gain and Selection Indices
text:
8.6 Exercise
You want an early bean line. Build an index with yield (weight 1), days to flowering (weight -0.5) and days to maturity (weight -0.5), and select the best 10% of the test lines.

How many lines are selected? Which are the five best?
What is the selection differential of each of the three traits?
How many of the lines are also in the 20% selected by the base index of this chapter?
What is the mean yield of the selected lines compared with the mean of the checks?
Days to flowering and maturity have a correlation of 0.78. What does this do to the weights of the index?







TipSolution






b_early <- c(Yield = 1, DF = -0.5, DPM = -0.5)
early <- pca_index(test_blue, id = "line", b = b_early, percentage = 0.10)

# 1. Number and five best lines
nrow(early$selection)
head(rownames(early$selection), 5)

# 2. Selection differentials
vars <- names(b_early)
round(colMeans(early$selection[, vars]) - colMeans(test_blue[, vars]), 1)

# 3. Overlap with the base index (20%)
length(intersect(rownames(early$selection), rownames(res$selection)))

# 4. Mean yield of the selected lines and of the checks
c(selected = mean(early$selection$Yield),
  checks = mean(blue$Yield[blue$line %in% checks]))

# 5. Compare with an index that uses only maturity
only_dpm <- pca_index(test_blue, id = "line", b = c(Yield = 1, DPM = -1), percentage = 0.10)
length(intersect(rownames(early$selection), rownames(only_dpm$selection)))

The 36 selected lines (10% of 364) include SEF_060, DAB_577, DAB_591, DAB_520 and DAB_366. Compared with the mean of the test lines they have +428 kg/ha of yield, 2.3 days less to flowering and 1.3 days less to maturity. Thirty-three of the 36 are also in the 20% of the base index. Their mean yield is 1786 kg/ha, against 1517 kg/ha for the checks. Because flowering and maturity are correlated, giving a negative weight to both doubles the importance of earliness in the index: the total weight on earliness (-1) is the same as the weight on yield. If earliness is meant to count half as much as yield, use weights of -0.25 for each of the two traits, or only one of them. An index with only maturity (weight -1) shares 29 of the 36 lines with this one, so using both traits does change the selection.

title: 8  Selection Decisions: Ranking, Expected Gain and Selection Indices
text:
8.7 Key takeaways

Select test lines from BLUPs (or BLUEs with their precision) and compare them with the checks, not only with the trial mean.
The breeder’s equation, \(R = i \, h^2 \, \sigma_P\), predicts the gain; in the bean trial it predicted 166 kg/ha and the realized gain was 147 kg/ha.
The advantage seen in the selected lines is mostly selection bias: 605 kg/ha observed, 147 kg/ha real. Select on BLUPs of several plots and confirm.
Selecting on one trait changes the others as a side effect. A base index combines standardized traits with weights; the sign gives the direction and only the ratios matter.
Check how sensitive the selection is to the weights, and do not give a low-heritability trait the same weight as a reliable one, unless the index uses BLUPs standardized by the genetic standard deviation.
Do not put correlated traits in the index with the same sign without thinking: the information is counted twice.
The Smith-Hazel index uses the covariance matrices and is more efficient, but it needs reliable estimates of them; for early stages the base index is the practical choice.

title: 9  Spatial Analysis and Trial Precision
text:
9.1 Learning objectives
Chapter 7 removed the variation among incomplete blocks from the comparison of lines. But a block is only a rough way of saying “these plots are close to each other”. The soil, the water and the light change gradually across a field, and a block of 22 plots can hide a lot of that change. This chapter models the position of the plots directly.
We continue with the bean trial of Chapter 7 and Chapter 8, so every result can be compared with what we already know.
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(lme4)
library(SpATS)
crumbs: 9  Spatial Analysis and Trial Precision

title: 9  Spatial Analysis and Trial Precision
text:
Recognize field heterogeneity and explain how it distorts the ranking of lines
Diagnose spatial patterns with residual maps and variograms
Fit a spatial model with SpATS (2D P-splines) and read its outputs
Quantify the gain of the spatial correction and decide when it is justified
Decide what to fix with the design and what to fix with the analysis
Run a complete single-trial analysis, from the raw file to a table ready for selection










NotePackages



SpATS is part of the course installation (R/install_packages.R). The chapter uses nothing else.
