title: 9  Spatial Analysis and Trial Precision
section: 9.2 Why the position of a plot matters
text:
9.2 Why the position of a plot matters
Every trial is laid out on land that is not uniform. Typical sources of heterogeneity are a line of trees or a road along one side of the field, a trial split by a road or a canal, a river or a drainage line crossing the field, and a slope that makes the top drier than the bottom. The figure shows four illustrative yield surfaces (they are schematic, not data) that a breeder could meet in practice.

g <- expand.grid(row = 1:60, col = 1:12)
g$`Moisture gradient`     <- -0.8 * g$row / 60 * 10
g$`Tree line (edge)`      <- -8 * exp(-(g$col - 1) / 2)
g$`Road through the trial` <- ifelse(g$row > 30, -5, 0)
g$`River (diagonal band)` <- -7 * exp(-((g$row - 5 * g$col - 5) / 6)^2)

pivot_longer(g, 3:6, names_to = "source", values_to = "effect") |>
  mutate(source = factor(source, levels = names(g)[3:6])) |>
  ggplot(aes(row, col, fill = effect)) +
  geom_tile() +
  facet_wrap(~ source, ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Row", y = "Column") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)







Figure 9.1: Four typical sources of spatial variation (schematic surfaces, not data). Darker is lower yield.





The effect on selection is simple. A line that is sown in a good patch looks better than it is; a line in a poor patch looks worse. The environmental effect is added to the genetic effect, and the ranking mixes the two. Blocks and replicates cut the field into pieces and remove the average difference among pieces, but the variation inside a block is still in the residual.
crumbs: 9  Spatial Analysis and Trial Precision

title: 9  Spatial Analysis and Trial Precision
section: 9.3 The bean trial as a map
text:
9.3 The bean trial as a map
The bean trial has a row and a column for each plot (see Chapter 4). It is a long, narrow field: 66 rows and 12 columns. The first six columns are replicate 1 and the last six are replicate 2, and each incomplete block covers 11 consecutive rows and 2 columns.

beans <- read_csv("data/Example_Beans.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(rep   = factor(rep),
         line  = factor(line),
         rb    = factor(paste(rep, block, sep = ":")),   # block inside replicate
         rowf  = factor(row),                            # row and column as factors
         colf  = factor(col),
         yield = YdHa_clean)

c(plots = nrow(beans), rows = max(beans$row), columns = max(beans$col),
  missing_yield = sum(is.na(beans$yield)))

        plots          rows       columns missing_yield 
          792            66            12             4 


Before any model, look at the raw yield on the map. This is the first diagnostic and it costs one line.

ggplot(beans, aes(row, col, fill = yield)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 6.5, linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(na.value = "grey80") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(1, 6, 7, 12)) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Row", y = "Column", fill = "Yield") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)







Figure 9.2: Raw plot yield (kg/ha) of the bean trial, drawn as the field. Columns 1 to 6 are replicate 1 and columns 7 to 12 are replicate 2.





A map of raw yield mixes genetic and environmental effects, so we look at it with care. Still, the lines were randomized, so the average of a whole column (66 plots of different lines) should be the same everywhere unless the environment changes. And the 16 checks, which are the same lines in every column, give a second reading.

check_lines <- beans |> filter(!is.na(yield)) |> count(line) |> filter(n > 2) |> pull(line)

profile <- bind_rows(
  beans |> filter(!is.na(yield)) |> group_by(col) |>
    summarise(yield = mean(yield), .groups = "drop") |> mutate(set = "All lines"),
  beans |> filter(!is.na(yield), line %in% check_lines) |> group_by(col) |>
    summarise(yield = mean(yield), .groups = "drop") |> mutate(set = "Checks only")
)

ggplot(profile, aes(col, yield)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 6.5, linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12) +
  facet_wrap(~ set) +
  labs(x = "Column", y = "Mean yield (kg/ha)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)







Figure 9.3: Mean yield by column. Left: all plots (66 per column). Right: only the plots of the 16 checks, which are the same lines everywhere. Columns 1 to 6 are replicate 1 and columns 7 to 12 are replicate 2.





The mean yield rises from 1,082 kg/ha in column 1 to 1,545 in column 6, and falls to 1,315 in column 12. That is a difference of about 463 kg/ha across the width of the field, twice the genetic standard deviation of the lines (about 220 kg/ha, Chapter 7), and it cannot be genetic because the lines are randomized. The checks show the same pattern, with 1,031 kg/ha in column 1 against 1,667 as the mean of columns 6 to 10 (each column has only 4 to 10 plots of checks, so this is a rough reading).
This is a typical edge-to-centre gradient, like the tree line of Figure 9.1: the outer columns of the trial yield less. Replicates are side by side, so each replicate sees a rising gradient (replicate 1) or a falling one (replicate 2). Next we ask whether the Day 3 model has already absorbed it.

title: 9  Spatial Analysis and Trial Precision
text:
9.4 Looking for spatial patterns
We start from the model of Chapter 7: replicate fixed, lines and incomplete blocks random.

m_block <- lmer(yield ~ rep + (1 | line) + (1 | rb), data = beans)
VarCorr(m_block)

 Groups   Name        Std.Dev.
 line     (Intercept) 220.82  
 rb       (Intercept) 216.66  
 Residual             281.91  

resid_df <- beans |> filter(!is.na(yield)) |> mutate(res = resid(m_block))


9.4.1 Residual map
If the model has captured all the structure of the field, the residuals look like random noise on the map. If not, we see patches or bands of the same sign.

ggplot(resid_df, aes(row, col, fill = res)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 6.5, linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b", midpoint = 0) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(1, 6, 7, 12)) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Row", y = "Column", fill = "Residual\n(kg/ha)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)







Figure 9.4: Residuals of the incomplete-block model (Chapter 7) drawn on the field. Patches of the same colour show variation that the blocks did not remove.





The map is not pure noise: there are more red plots near columns 6 and 7 (the boundary between the replicates) and more blue plots in columns 1 and 3. The blocks (3 per replicate, each 2 columns wide) took away most of the gradient, but not all of it. The mean residual of each column shows what is left:

col_res <- resid_df |> group_by(col) |> summarise(res = mean(res), .groups = "drop")
ggplot(col_res, aes(col, res)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 6.5, linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12) +
  labs(x = "Column", y = "Mean residual (kg/ha)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)







Figure 9.5: Mean residual of the incomplete-block model by column. Inside each block of two columns (1 and 2, 3 and 4, 5 and 6 in replicate 1) the residual goes from low in the outer column to high in the inner one.





Inside every block of replicate 1 the gradient is still there: the residual rises from -60 to 35 kg/ha (columns 1 and 2), from -74 to 76 (columns 3 and 4) and from -29 to 52 (columns 5 and 6). A block of two columns cannot remove a gradient that runs across those two columns.


9.4.2 Variogram
The eye can be fooled, so we also measure. The semivariogram compares the residuals of two plots as a function of the distance between them. If plots that are close are more alike than plots that are far, the semivariance increases with distance. If the residuals are independent it is flat.

semivariogram <- function(d, direction = c("row", "col"), max_lag = 25) {
  direction <- match.arg(direction)
  same <- if (direction == "row") outer(d$col, d$col, "==")           # same column
          else outer(d$row, d$row, "==") & outer(d$rep, d$rep, "==")  # same row and replicate
  lag  <- if (direction == "row") abs(outer(d$row, d$row, "-"))
          else abs(outer(d$col, d$col, "-"))
  half <- 0.5 * outer(d$res, d$res, "-")^2
  keep <- same & lag > 0 & lag <= max_lag & upper.tri(same)
  tibble(lag = lag[keep], gamma = half[keep]) |>
    group_by(lag) |> summarise(gamma = mean(gamma), pairs = n(), .groups = "drop")
}

vg <- bind_rows(
  mutate(semivariogram(resid_df, "row"), direction = "Along the rows (long side)"),
  mutate(semivariogram(resid_df, "col", max_lag = 5), direction = "Across the columns")
)


ggplot(vg, aes(lag, gamma)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = var(resid_df$res), linetype = 2) +
  geom_point() + geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ direction, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Distance between plots (rows or columns)", y = "Semivariance") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)







Figure 9.6: Empirical semivariograms of the residuals of the incomplete-block model. The dashed line is the variance of the residuals.





Along the rows the semivariance is 48,200 at distance 1 and reaches about 56,370 (the average of distances 5 to 9), close to the variance of the residuals, 55,507. The residuals of plots that are 1 or 2 rows apart are a little more alike than those of distant plots. The effect is weak: this trial has no strong local correlation along the rows, and the main spatial feature is the gradient across the columns that we saw in the maps. Across the columns there are only 5 possible distances, so that panel tells us little. The variogram is one piece of evidence, not a verdict.






ImportantWhen is a spatial correction justified?



Use the spatial model when at least two of these are true:

The residual map shows patches or bands.
The semivariogram increases with distance instead of being flat.
Row or column effects are large (their variance is a sizeable part of the genetic variance).
The spatial model improves the fit (AIC) or the heritability by a useful amount in the comparison of the last section.

If the residuals look random, the extra model buys nothing and costs complexity.

title: 9  Spatial Analysis and Trial Precision
text:
9.5 Spatial models with 2D P-splines
Many spatial models exist. The oldest add row and column effects, or an autoregressive correlation between neighbouring plots (AR1 x AR1; Gilmour et al. 1997, Cullis et al. 2006). The model of the SpATS package (Rodríguez-Álvarez et al. 2018) takes another route: it describes the field as a smooth surface of rows and columns, fitted with penalized splines (P-splines). It has been used for sorghum, wheat and maize trials, among others (for example Velazco et al. 2017). The idea in three sentences:

A spline is a flexible curve made of small pieces joined smoothly. The 2D version is a flexible surface.
The penalty keeps the surface smooth: it can follow a gradient or a patch, but not the noise of a single plot.
The model decides how smooth the surface should be from the data, so we do not choose a correlation structure by hand.

The surface is added to the usual mixed model, together with random row and column effects (for example for sowing or harvest direction) and the blocks of the design:

fit_spats <- function(data, trait = "yield", genotype_random = TRUE,
                      nseg = c(6, 32), random = ~ rowf + colf + rb) {
  d <- data
  d$y <- d[[trait]]
  SpATS(response = "y", genotype = "line", genotype.as.random = genotype_random,
        spatial = ~ PSANOVA(col, row, nseg = nseg, nest.div = 2),
        fixed = ~ rep, random = random, data = d,
        control = list(tolerance = 1e-03, monitoring = 0))
}

m_sp <- fit_spats(beans)

What each argument says:







Argument
Meaning in the bean trial




response
the trait, one column of the data


genotype, genotype.as.random
the lines; random gives BLUPs, fixed gives BLUEs


spatial = ~ PSANOVA(col, row, nseg)
the 2D P-spline surface over the column and row coordinates


nseg
number of spline segments in each direction (columns, rows). A good start is about half of the number of columns and rows: 6 and 32 here. Each must be a multiple of nest.div (2 by default)


fixed
fixed effects: the replicate


random
random effects: row, column and incomplete block (rowf, colf, rb, factors)









WarningRow and column must be numbers, and also factors



col and row (numeric) go inside PSANOVA(), because the surface needs the distance between plots. The factors rowf and colf go in random, to give each row and column its own effect. We create both versions from the same columns.



9.5.1 Reading the output
The print of the model shows the effective dimension of each term: how many parameters it effectively uses.

m_sp


Spatial analysis of trials with splines 

Response:                   y         
Genotypes (as random):      line      
Spatial:                    ~PSANOVA(col, row, nseg = nseg, nest.div = 2)
Fixed:                      ~rep      
Random:                     ~rowf + colf + rb


Number of observations:        788
Number of missing data:        4
Effective dimension:           303.27
Deviance:                      9835.638


The effective dimension of the lines is 244 out of 380. The smooth surface uses about 26 effective parameters, the rows 24.5 (out of 66), the columns 2.1 (out of 12) and the incomplete blocks only 1.4 (out of 36): once the surface is in the model, the blocks have little left to explain.
The estimated surface and the row effects show what was removed from the plots. The surface (left) recovers the gradient across the field: high yield in the middle, low yield in the outer columns, with a range of several hundred kg/ha. The row effects (right) are small by comparison, mostly under 100 kg/ha.

tr <- obtain.spatialtrend(m_sp)
trend <- expand.grid(col = tr$col.p, row = tr$row.p) |>
  mutate(trend = as.vector(tr$fit))

p1 <- ggplot(trend, aes(row, col, fill = trend)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b", midpoint = 0) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(1, 6, 7, 12)) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Row", y = "Column", fill = "Trend") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

row_eff <- tibble(row = 1:66, effect = m_sp$coeff[paste0("rowf", 1:66)])
p2 <- ggplot(row_eff, aes(row, effect)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Row", y = "Row effect (kg/ha)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

cowplot::plot_grid(p1, p2, nrow = 1, rel_widths = c(1.15, 1))







Figure 9.7: Spatial trend estimated by SpATS (left, kg/ha) and effect of each row (right). The trend is what the model subtracts from the plots before comparing lines.





SpATS also has its own panel with the raw data, the fitted values, the residuals, the spatial trend and the genotype predictions:

plot(m_sp, all.in.one = TRUE)







Figure 9.8: Standard SpATS plot: raw data, fitted values, residuals, spatial trend, genotype BLUPs and their histogram.







9.5.2 BLUEs and BLUPs
predict() returns the genotype means with their standard errors, as in Chapter 7. With genotype.as.random = FALSE the lines are fixed and we get BLUEs; with TRUE we get BLUPs.

blup_sp <- predict(m_sp, which = "line") |>
  select(line, BLUP = predicted.values, SE = standard.errors) |>
  mutate(BLUP = BLUP + m_sp$coeff[["repR2"]] / 2)         # centre on the mean of the two replicates

m_sp_fix <- fit_spats(beans, genotype_random = FALSE)
blue_sp <- predict(m_sp_fix, which = "line") |>
  select(line, BLUE = predicted.values, SE_BLUE = standard.errors) |>
  mutate(BLUE = BLUE + m_sp_fix$coeff[["repR2"]] / 2)

head(left_join(blue_sp, blup_sp, by = "line") |> arrange(desc(BLUP)), 5)

           line     BLUE  SE_BLUE     BLUP       SE
1       SEF_060 2242.021 180.1600 1871.757 143.9013
2       DOR_364 2114.316 181.6090 1809.103 144.3952
3       DAB_366 2036.997 178.3529 1770.903 142.6014
4 TIO_CANELA_75 1898.100 133.8103 1744.753 116.0499
5       SEN_056 1954.716 180.5070 1714.841 143.2401


As in Chapter 7, BLUEs are the input for a later stage (for example a multi-environment analysis, Chapter 11), and BLUPs are the best predictors for ranking within this trial.

title: 9  Spatial Analysis and Trial Precision
text:
9.6 Mr.Bean: spatial analysis without code
Mr.Bean is a free Shiny application developed at the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT (Aparicio et al. 2024). It has a module that fits the SpATS model of this chapter, so a breeder who does not write R can obtain the same BLUEs, BLUPs and heritability. The workflow is the same as in R:

Import the trial file. The beans file Example_Beans.csv is ready to use: it has one row per plot, with the line, the replicate, the block, the row, the column and the traits.
Tell the app which column is which: the genotype, the row and the column, the replicate and the block, and the trait to analyse.
Choose the model: spatial correction (SpATS) or the models without space for classical designs, and whether genotypes are fixed or random.
Run, inspect and download: the app shows the heritability, the variance components, the spatial trend and the residuals, and exports the BLUEs or BLUPs as a table.







NoteRunning the app



Two ways to open it, described by the authors at https://apariciojohan.github.io/MrBeanApp/: use the web version hosted on shinyapps.io (it needs an internet connection and may be slow with many users), or install it in R with remotes::install_github("AparicioJohan/MrBeanApp") and start it with library(MrBean) followed by run_app(). It is not part of the course packages. We will use it in the practical session to check that the app and the code give the same numbers.


Mr.Bean is a good way to share an analysis with colleagues who do not use R, and a good check of your own code. The limits are the usual ones of a point-and-click tool: the analysis is not stored as a script that you can rerun on the next trial.

title: 9  Spatial Analysis and Trial Precision
text:
9.7 Spatial against non-spatial
Is the spatial model better? We compare four ways of analysing the same trial, from the simplest to the most complete. All are fitted with the lines as random effects.

# generalized heritability (Cullis) from the mixed model equations, as in the heritability section of the mixed models chapter
h2_cullis <- function(model, genotype) {
  X <- getME(model, "X"); Z <- getME(model, "Z"); s2 <- sigma(model)^2
  vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(model)); fl <- getME(model, "flist"); Gp <- getME(model, "Gp")
  v <- unlist(lapply(names(fl), function(g) rep(vc$vcov[vc$grp == g], nlevels(fl[[g]]))))
  W <- cbind(X, Z); C <- crossprod(W) / s2; idx <- ncol(X) + seq_along(v)
  C[cbind(idx, idx)] <- C[cbind(idx, idx)] + 1 / v
  Cinv <- solve(as.matrix(C)); k <- match(genotype, names(fl))
  gi <- ncol(X) + (Gp[k] + 1):Gp[k + 1]; P <- Cinv[gi, gi]; n <- nrow(P)
  vdiff <- 2 * (n * sum(diag(P)) - sum(P)) / (n * (n - 1))
  1 - vdiff / (2 * vc$vcov[vc$grp == genotype])
}


m_rowcol <- lmer(yield ~ rep + (1 | line) + (1 | rb) + (1 | rowf) + (1 | colf), data = beans)
m_rc_only <- lmer(yield ~ rep + (1 | line) + (1 | rowf) + (1 | colf), data = beans)

n_lines <- nlevels(beans$line)
comp <- tibble(
  Model = c("Incomplete blocks (Day 3)", "Blocks + rows + columns",
            "Rows + columns, no blocks", "SpATS (surface + rows + columns + blocks)"),
  `Residual SD` = c(sigma(m_block), sigma(m_rowcol), sigma(m_rc_only), sqrt(m_sp$psi[1])),
  `Heritability` = c(h2_cullis(m_block, "line"), h2_cullis(m_rowcol, "line"),
                     h2_cullis(m_rc_only, "line"),
                     m_sp$eff.dim[["line"]] / (n_lines - 1)),
  AIC = c(AIC(m_block), AIC(m_rowcol), AIC(m_rc_only), NA)
)
comp |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  Model                                     `Residual SD` Heritability    AIC
  <chr>                                             <dbl>        <dbl>  <dbl>
1 Incomplete blocks (Day 3)                          282.         0.54 11510.
2 Blocks + rows + columns                            241.         0.6  11438.
3 Rows + columns, no blocks                          251.         0.59 11465.
4 SpATS (surface + rows + columns + blocks)          231.         0.64    NA 


How to read the columns:

Residual SD is the unexplained plot-to-plot variation. A smaller value means that the model took more structure out of the field.
Heritability is the generalized (Cullis) heritability of Section 7.7 for the lme4 models. For SpATS it is the effective dimension of the lines divided by their number minus one, which is the quantity that getHeritability() reports and is the same measure.
AIC compares models fitted by lme4 to the same data with the same fixed effects: the lower, the better. SpATS uses a different likelihood, so we do not compare its AIC with the others.

Adding the position of the plots lowers the residual SD from 282 to 231 kg/ha and raises the heritability of yield from 0.54 to 0.64. A simpler model with random rows and columns gets about half of that gain in heritability (0.6) and has the lowest AIC of the three lme4 models (11,438 against 11,510 for the Day 3 model).

9.7.1 Does the ranking change?
Heritability measures precision, but the breeder cares about the selection. We compare the Day 3 BLUPs with the SpATS BLUPs.

rank_cmp <- bind_cols(
  tibble(line = rownames(ranef(m_block)$line), BLUP_block = ranef(m_block)$line[, 1]),
  BLUP_spats = blup_sp$BLUP[match(rownames(ranef(m_block)$line), blup_sp$line)] - mean(blup_sp$BLUP)
)

k <- round(0.10 * nrow(rank_cmp))                       # the best 10% of the lines
top <- \(x) rank_cmp$line[order(-x)][1:k]
c(pearson  = cor(rank_cmp$BLUP_block, rank_cmp$BLUP_spats),
  spearman = cor(rank_cmp$BLUP_block, rank_cmp$BLUP_spats, method = "spearman"),
  selected = k,
  in_both  = length(intersect(top(rank_cmp$BLUP_block), top(rank_cmp$BLUP_spats))))

   pearson   spearman   selected    in_both 
 0.9433450  0.9315086 38.0000000 30.0000000 


The rankings are similar (correlation above 0.9), but not the same. Of the 38 lines selected with the Day 3 model, 30 are also selected by the spatial model; the other 8 are different lines. Which list is better?


9.7.2 A check with the other replicate
We cannot know the true genetic value, but we can ask a fair question: which model predicts better the performance of a line in a replicate it has never seen? The two replicates are in different columns, so they are independent samples of the field. We fit each model with replicate 1 only and compare its predictions with the raw means of replicate 2, and then the other way round.

check_one <- function(train, test) {
  train <- droplevels(train)
  truth <- tapply(test$yield, test$line, mean, na.rm = TRUE)

  # raw means of the training replicate
  raw <- tapply(train$yield, train$line, mean, na.rm = TRUE)

  # incomplete-block model
  m1 <- lmer(yield ~ (1 | line) + (1 | rb), data = train)
  b1 <- setNames(ranef(m1)$line[, 1], rownames(ranef(m1)$line))

  # rows and columns
  m2 <- lmer(yield ~ (1 | line) + (1 | rb) + (1 | rowf) + (1 | colf), data = train)
  b2 <- setNames(ranef(m2)$line[, 1], rownames(ranef(m2)$line))

  # SpATS (a single replicate has 6 columns)
  m3 <- SpATS(response = "yield", genotype = "line", genotype.as.random = TRUE,
              spatial = ~ PSANOVA(col, row, nseg = c(4, 32), nest.div = 2),
              random = ~ rowf + colf + rb, data = train,
              control = list(tolerance = 1e-03, monitoring = 0))
  p3 <- predict(m3, which = "line")
  b3 <- setNames(p3$predicted.values, p3$line)

  common <- Reduce(intersect, list(names(truth), names(raw), names(b1), names(b2), names(b3)))
  ok <- common[!is.na(truth[common])]
  k  <- round(0.10 * length(ok))
  out <- sapply(list(`Raw means` = raw, `Incomplete blocks` = b1,
                     `Blocks + rows + columns` = b2, SpATS = b3), function(s)
    c(correlation = cor(s[ok], truth[ok]),
      top10_yield = mean(truth[ok][order(-s[ok])][1:k])))
  as.data.frame(t(out)) |> tibble::rownames_to_column("Model")
}

r1 <- filter(beans, rep == "R1"); r2 <- filter(beans, rep == "R2")
cv <- bind_rows(mutate(check_one(r1, r2), from = "R1 to R2"),
                mutate(check_one(r2, r1), from = "R2 to R1")) |>
  group_by(Model) |>
  summarise(`Correlation with the other replicate` = mean(correlation),
            `Yield of the best 10% in the other replicate` = mean(top10_yield),
            .groups = "drop")
cv <- cv |> arrange(desc(`Correlation with the other replicate`))
cv |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  Model                   Correlation with the other re…¹ Yield of the best 10…²
  <chr>                                             <dbl>                  <dbl>
1 SpATS                                             0.367                  1608.
2 Blocks + rows + columns                           0.36                   1635.
3 Incomplete blocks                                 0.337                  1626.
4 Raw means                                         0.288                  1591.
# ℹ abbreviated names: ¹​`Correlation with the other replicate`,
#   ²​`Yield of the best 10% in the other replicate`


The correlation with the other replicate is 0.29 for the raw means, 0.34 for the incomplete-block model and 0.37 for SpATS. Adjusting for the field clearly beats the raw means, and the spatial model is slightly better than the blocks alone. The yield of the best 10% in the other replicate does not follow the same order (from 1,591 to 1,635 kg/ha), because it depends on only 38 lines. With two replicates the replicate used as “truth” is itself noisy, so we should not over-read small differences among the adjusted models.






ImportantWhat the comparison tells us



The spatial model raises the precision of the trial (smaller residual, higher heritability) and changes some selections. The check with the other replicate shows that the predictions are better than with raw means and slightly better than with the blocks alone. The cost is the time to fit and check it. For yield, which is sensitive to the field, it is worth it; the next sections show a trait where it is not.
crumbs: 9  Spatial Analysis and Trial Precision

title: 9  Spatial Analysis and Trial Precision
text:
9.8 Design or analysis?
Statistical correction is a rescue, not a plan. The cheapest way to have a precise trial is to design it well, and the two work together.








Problem
Fix with the design
Fix with the analysis




Known gradient (slope, edge)
Orient blocks across the gradient; put replicates side by side
Row or column effects, or the SpATS surface


Unknown patches
Small incomplete blocks; row-column designs (Chapter 5)
Spatial model; check residual map


Border competition
Border plots; plot size that avoids edge effect
Do not analyse border plots as data


Unreplicated or p-rep lines
Replicated checks spread over the field
Model with checks as a reference; spatial surface


Lost plots
Extra seed and reserve plots
Mixed model (it handles missing plots)


Large plot-to-plot noise
Larger plots, more replicates
Not recoverable by analysis



In the bean trial the gradient runs across the width of the field, from the outer columns to the middle. The incomplete blocks, 11 rows long and 2 columns wide, cut that gradient into three strips per replicate, and that is why the block variance is as large as the genetic variance. But each block still contains two columns with different yield levels. Blocks that are one column wide and 22 rows long would follow the contours of the gradient and be more uniform inside. Border plots in the outer columns (the lowest yield, columns 1 and 12) would remove the edge effect from the lines under evaluation. Both are design decisions that cost less than the analysis that now has to repair them.
A good rule: design for the precision you need, analyse for the heterogeneity that remains. Plan the number of replicates and the spacing of the checks before the season, because no model gives back information that the trial did not collect.
crumbs: 9  Spatial Analysis and Trial Precision

title: 9  Spatial Analysis and Trial Precision
text:
9.9 A complete single-trial workflow
Everything in the course so far is now in one path: raw file, quality control (Chapter 4), design and model (Chapter 5, Chapter 7), estimates and selection (Chapter 8). We write it as a function that takes the trial and a trait, and returns a table ready for selection.

single_trial <- function(data, trait, spatial = TRUE) {
  # 1. raw data and quality control: keep plots with a value; the outliers were handled in the QC chapter
  d <- data |> mutate(y = .data[[trait]]) |> filter(!is.na(y)) |> droplevels()

  # 2. model: spatial or incomplete blocks
  if (spatial) {
    m <- SpATS(response = "y", genotype = "line", genotype.as.random = TRUE,
               spatial = ~ PSANOVA(col, row, nseg = c(6, 32), nest.div = 2),
               fixed = ~ rep, random = ~ rowf + colf + rb, data = d,
               control = list(tolerance = 1e-03, monitoring = 0))
    p  <- predict(m, which = "line")
    sg <- m$var.comp[["line"]]
    tab <- tibble(line = as.character(p$line),
                  BLUP = p$predicted.values + m$coeff[["repR2"]] / 2,
                  SE   = p$standard.errors)
    h2 <- m$eff.dim[["line"]] / (nlevels(d$line) - 1)
  } else {
    m  <- lmer(y ~ rep + (1 | line) + (1 | rb), data = d)
    sg <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m))$vcov[1]
    pv <- as.data.frame(ranef(m, condVar = TRUE))
    tab <- tibble(line = as.character(pv$grp[pv$grpvar == "line"]),
                  BLUP = fixef(m)[1] + fixef(m)["repR2"] / 2 + pv$condval[pv$grpvar == "line"],
                  SE   = pv$condsd[pv$grpvar == "line"])
    h2 <- h2_cullis(m, "line")
  }

  # 3. selection-ready table: rank, reliability and a flag for the checks
  n_pl <- count(d, line)
  tab <- tab |>
    mutate(reliability = 1 - SE^2 / sg,
           rank = rank(-BLUP, ties.method = "first"),
           check = line %in% n_pl$line[n_pl$n > 2]) |>
    arrange(rank)

  list(model = m, table = tab, h2 = h2)
}

res <- single_trial(beans, "yield")
round(res$h2, 3)

[1] 0.644

head(res$table, 8)

# A tibble: 8 × 6
  line           BLUP    SE reliability  rank check
  <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>       <dbl> <int> <lgl>
1 SEF_060       1872.  144.       0.610     1 FALSE
2 DOR_364       1809.  144.       0.607     2 FALSE
3 DAB_366       1771.  143.       0.617     3 FALSE
4 TIO_CANELA_75 1745.  116.       0.746     4 TRUE 
5 SEN_056       1715.  143.       0.613     5 FALSE
6 DOR_390       1713.  145.       0.606     6 FALSE
7 DAB_577       1698.  144.       0.610     7 FALSE
8 AMADEUS       1672.  145.       0.606     8 FALSE


The table has what the breeder needs to decide: the BLUP, its standard error, the reliability of each line (how much we can trust its prediction, between 0 and 1) and a flag for the checks. A line with a high BLUP and low reliability is a candidate for retesting; one with a high BLUP and high reliability is a solid advance. The selection steps of Chapter 8 (expected gain, indices) start from this table.

# save the table for the next step (selection or the multi-environment analysis)
readr::write_csv(res$table, "resultados/yield_blups_spatial.csv")


9.9.1 One function, five traits
Now the same function with all the traits, with and without the spatial correction. This is the answer to “when does it pay?”.

traits <- c(Yield = "yield", `Days to flowering` = "DF", `Days to maturity` = "DPM",
            `Plant height` = "PLHA", `100-seed weight` = "SW100")

gain <- bind_rows(lapply(names(traits), function(nm) {
  a <- single_trial(beans, traits[[nm]], spatial = FALSE)$h2
  b <- single_trial(beans, traits[[nm]], spatial = TRUE)$h2
  tibble(Trait = nm, `Incomplete blocks` = a, SpATS = b, Gain = b - a)
}))
gain |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))

# A tibble: 5 × 4
  Trait             `Incomplete blocks` SpATS  Gain
  <chr>                           <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 Yield                           0.542 0.644 0.102
2 Days to flowering               0.646 0.646 0    
3 Days to maturity                0.644 0.653 0.01 
4 Plant height                    0.123 0.157 0.034
5 100-seed weight                 0.86  0.868 0.008


The gain is large for yield, the trait most affected by the soil and the water, and almost nothing for flowering, maturity and seed weight. Plant height has a very low heritability in both models and the correction does not rescue it. The spatial model is a tool for the traits that need it, not a default for all.

title: 9  Spatial Analysis and Trial Precision
text:
9.10 Exercise
Work with the same trial.

Draw the residual map of days to maturity (DPM) from the incomplete-block model. Do you see bands or patches, as in Figure 9.4?
Run single_trial() for DPM with and without space. Is the correction justified by the rule of this chapter?
How many of the 38 best lines for yield (10%) by the spatial model are among the 38 best by the Day 3 model? Which is the first line that enters the list only with the spatial model?







TipSolution






# 1. residual map of DPM
dpm <- beans |> filter(!is.na(DPM)) |> mutate(res = resid(lmer(DPM ~ rep + (1 | line) + (1 | rb), data = pick(everything()))))
ggplot(dpm, aes(row, col, fill = res)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b", midpoint = 0) +
  coord_equal() + theme_minimal(base_size = 11)







# 2. with and without space
c(blocks = single_trial(beans, "DPM", spatial = FALSE)$h2,
  spats  = single_trial(beans, "DPM", spatial = TRUE)$h2)

   blocks     spats 
0.6435511 0.6530794 

# 3. overlap for yield
a <- single_trial(beans, "yield", spatial = FALSE)$table
b <- single_trial(beans, "yield", spatial = TRUE)$table
k <- round(0.10 * nrow(a))
only_spatial <- setdiff(b$line[1:k], a$line[1:k])
c(shared = length(intersect(a$line[1:k], b$line[1:k])), selected = k)

  shared selected 
      30       38 

only_spatial[1]

[1] "DAB_090"



The residual map of DPM looks like noise: there are no bands or patches.
The heritability of DPM goes from 0.64 to 0.65, so the correction is not justified. The simpler model is enough.
Thirty of the 38 lines are shared. The first line that enters the list only with the spatial model is DAB_090.
crumbs: 9  Spatial Analysis and Trial Precision

title: 9  Spatial Analysis and Trial Precision
text:
9.11 Key takeaways

Plots that are close are more alike than plots that are far. Blocks capture part of this; the rest stays in the residual and mixes with the genetic signal.
Look before you model: a map of the raw data, a map of the residuals and a semivariogram take minutes.
SpATS fits a smooth surface of rows and columns with P-splines, plus random row, column and block effects, and returns BLUEs, BLUPs and heritability. Mr.Bean gives the same analysis without code.
The gain depends on the trait: large for yield in this trial, nearly nothing for flowering, maturity and seed weight.
A better ranking is not guaranteed by a more complex model. Check against an independent replicate and report the heritability of the model you use.
Design first, analysis second. Orient blocks, replicate the checks and protect the borders; the model repairs what remains.

title: 10  Low-Cost High-Throughput Phenotyping: Image Analysis in R
text:
10.1 Learning objectives
In the morning (Chapter 9) we saw that the quality of a trial depends on the precision of every plot value. This afternoon we look at the other end of the problem: how the plot value is measured. Counting seeds, scoring colour, measuring leaves or rating disease by eye is slow, tiring and different from person to person. A photograph and a few lines of R can do the same work for hundreds of samples, in the same way every time.
library(pliman)
library(dplyr)
All images in this chapter are the sample images installed with pliman (Olivoto 2022), so every example runs on any computer. image_pliman() reads them by name.
crumbs: 10  Low-Cost High-Throughput Phenotyping: Image Analysis in R

title: 10  Low-Cost High-Throughput Phenotyping: Image Analysis in R
text:
Explain how a photograph becomes a trait value, and where this fits in the analysis of a breeding trial
Take images that can be analysed: background, light, scale and naming
Count and measure seeds and leaves with pliman, and convert pixels to centimetres
Describe colour with vegetation indices and use it to classify seeds and leaves
Measure disease severity from a leaf image
Process a folder of images in one call and build a table with one row per plot
Check an image-based trait against a manual measurement before using it for selection








NoteInstall the image package



pliman is part of the course installation, but it also needs EBImage, a package from Bioconductor that the CRAN installer does not bring. Run this once, with internet:

if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("EBImage")

If library(pliman) prints “Package EBImage is required”, this is the step that is missing.
crumbs: 10  Low-Cost High-Throughput Phenotyping: Image Analysis in R

title: 10  Low-Cost High-Throughput Phenotyping: Image Analysis in R
section: 10.2 From a photograph to a number
text:
10.2 From a photograph to a number
An image is a table of numbers. A colour image has three tables (red, green and blue), one value per pixel. To measure something we follow the same steps every time:

Capture the image under controlled conditions.
Segment: separate the objects of interest (seeds, leaves, lesions) from the background.
Measure: count the objects, compute their size, shape and colour.
Tabulate: one row per plot, with the plot identifier.
Analyse: the table enters the same workflow as any other trait (Chapter 9, Chapter 7).

“High-throughput phenotyping” (HTP) means doing this for many samples quickly. It does not need expensive equipment. The platforms below go from the cheapest to the most expensive; the first ones are enough to start.








Platform
Typical use
Cost and effort




Smartphone with a stand and a plain tray
Seed number, size and colour; leaf area; disease on detached leaves
Very low. The same phone used for field books


Flatbed scanner
Seeds, grains, leaves, roots, with a known resolution (dpi)
Low. Scale is automatic


Fixed RGB camera on a pole or frame
Canopy cover and greenness of a plot, repeated over time
Low to medium


RGB camera modified for near infrared (NIR)
Vegetation indices that need NIR, such as NDVI
Medium


Drone with RGB or multispectral camera
Plant height, canopy cover and vigour for the whole trial
High. See the last section
crumbs: 10  Low-Cost High-Throughput Phenotyping: Image Analysis in R

title: 10  Low-Cost High-Throughput Phenotyping: Image Analysis in R
section: 10.3 Taking images that can be analysed
text:
10.3 Taking images that can be analysed
The best segmentation is the one you do not need to fix later. Most of the work of a good image analysis is done before the photograph.








Decision
What to do
What goes wrong otherwise




Background
One plain colour that the objects do not have: blue or white for green or yellow seeds, white for dark leaves
Objects and background cannot be separated


Light
Even, diffuse light, the same for all images. A box or a cloudy day, no direct sun
Shadows are read as objects, and colour changes among images


Scale
A reference object of known size in every image, or a fixed distance and a known dpi
Sizes are in pixels and cannot be compared among images


Objects
Separated, flat, not overlapping. Seeds can touch slightly
Overlapping objects are counted as one


Resolution
Enough pixels per object for its shape to be clear
Small objects become noise


File name
The plot identifier, for example plot_101.jpg
The table cannot be joined to the trial


Format
The same camera and settings in all images; keep the original files
Colour differences that are not biological



The sample image shadow.jpg shows what happens with uneven light: a dark leaf on a background that goes from light to shadow.

shadow <- image_pliman("shadow.jpg", plot = FALSE)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
plot(shadow)
bad <- analyze_objects(shadow, plot = TRUE, show_original = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)







Figure 10.1: Left: a leaf photographed with a shadow on the background. Right: the mask that the default segmentation produces. The shadow is read as part of the object and half of the leaf is lost.





No setting of the software repairs this reliably. The adaptive threshold option of analyze_objects() did not fix it with default values either: it returned 43 small fragments. The fix is a photograph with even light.
crumbs: 10  Low-Cost High-Throughput Phenotyping: Image Analysis in R

title: 10  Low-Cost High-Throughput Phenotyping: Image Analysis in R
section: 10.4 Reading an image and its colour
text:
10.4 Reading an image and its colour

soy <- image_pliman("soy_green.jpg", plot = FALSE)
dim(soy)      # height, width and three colour channels

[1] 794 410   3


A vegetation index combines the three channels in one number that highlights something. For example, the green leaf index (GLI) is high for green tissue, and the normalized green-red difference index (NGRDI) separates green from red and yellow. pliman has more than a hundred indices, listed by pliman_indexes(). image_index() draws them:

image_index(soy, index = c("R", "GLI", "NGRDI"), ncol = 3, nrow = 1)







Figure 10.2: Soybean seeds (soy_green.jpg) seen through three indices: the red channel (R), the green leaf index (GLI) and NGRDI. The two seeds that are greener than the others stand out in GLI.





The choice of index is a decision, not a default. We choose the one that separates what we want to separate, and we check it on a few images before running the whole set.
crumbs: 10  Low-Cost High-Throughput Phenotyping: Image Analysis in R

title: 10  Low-Cost High-Throughput Phenotyping: Image Analysis in R
text:
10.5 Counting and measuring seeds
analyze_objects() does the segmentation and the measurement in one call. The image soybean_touch.jpg has soybean seeds on a blue background, some of them touching.

touch <- image_pliman("soybean_touch.jpg", plot = FALSE)
seeds <- analyze_objects(touch, marker = "id", verbose = FALSE)
seeds$statistics

       stat        value
1         n 3.000000e+01
2  min_area 1.366000e+03
3 mean_area 2.051300e+03
4  max_area 2.436000e+03
5   sd_area 2.300703e+02
6  sum_area 6.153900e+04
7  coverage 1.151122e-01








Figure 10.3: Seeds detected by analyze_objects(), with their identifier. The default settings separate the touching seeds.





The first line, n, is the count: 30 seeds. We counted the labels of the figure one by one and the number is correct. This is the minimum check that every automatic count needs before it is trusted.
Each object has more than thirty measurements: area, perimeter, length, width, shape descriptors such as circularity and eccentricity.

seeds$results |>
  select(id, area, perimeter, length, width, circularity) |>
  head(5)

  id area perimeter   length    width circularity
1  1 2279  183.5097 56.57747 51.54190    14.77657
2  2 2289  178.1960 56.53366 52.36854    13.87235
3  3 2310  181.0244 57.20139 51.99249    14.18607
4  4 2436  185.6102 61.02182 51.02160    14.14250

All sizes are in pixels for now. To compare images we need a scale.

title: 10  Low-Cost High-Throughput Phenotyping: Image Analysis in R
text:
10.6 From pixels to centimetres
There are two ways to give the scale.
1. A known resolution (dpi). A flatbed scanner gives a fixed number of dots per inch. The sample image objects_300dpi.jpg was made at 300 dpi and contains a square of 10 x 10 cm.

objects <- image_pliman("objects_300dpi.jpg", plot = FALSE)
obj <- analyze_objects(objects, verbose = FALSE)







cm <- as.data.frame(unclass(get_measures(obj, dpi = 300)))
cm |> select(id, area, width, length)

  id     area    width   length
1  1 99.81199 11.10659 11.12135
2  2 24.99414  6.50271  6.51376
3  3  7.00615  2.99284  2.99197
4  4  7.93396  1.98532  3.98985


The largest object (id 1) is the square of 10 x 10 cm, and the software finds 11.11 x 11.12 cm and an area of 99.8 cm², an error of about 0.3%. This is how an image analysis is validated: measure something whose size you know.
2. A reference object in the image. With a phone there is no dpi, but we can put an object of known area in every photograph. The image la_leaves.jpg has five leaves and a square sample of 2 x 2 cm (4 cm²):

leaves <- image_pliman("la_leaves.jpg", plot = FALSE)
la <- analyze_objects(leaves, marker = "id", reference = TRUE,
                      reference_area = 4, reference_smaller = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
la$results |> select(id, area, length, width)

  id      area   length    width
1  1 43.429695 9.923322 6.320010
2  2 37.242871 8.706688 6.069490
3  3 32.920354 9.223013 5.533824
4  4 28.837758 8.217528 5.271185
5  5  8.900688 4.418591 2.839530








Figure 10.4: Leaf area with a reference object. The red square is the reference (4 cm²); the leaves are labelled.





The areas are now in cm². reference_smaller = TRUE tells the function that the reference is the smallest object; with reference_larger = TRUE it is the largest, as with the black rectangle in the flax seeds image. The same photograph, in any distance or camera, gives the same area, because the reference object travels with the sample.

10.6.1 Many small seeds
The image flax_grains.jpg has hundreds of small flax seeds and a black rectangle of 6 cm² as reference.

flax <- image_pliman("flax_grains.jpg", plot = FALSE)
fx <- analyze_objects(flax, index = "GRAY", reference = TRUE, reference_area = 6,
                      reference_larger = TRUE, show_contour = FALSE, marker = "point",
                      verbose = FALSE)
c(seeds = nrow(fx$results), mean_area_cm2 = round(mean(fx$results$area), 3))

        seeds mean_area_cm2 
      268.000         0.063 








Figure 10.5: Flax seeds with a reference rectangle (red). Seeds and reference are detected, and the sizes are in cm².











WarningA parameter can change the count



The lower_noise argument removes small objects that are probably noise. With lower_noise = 0.3 the same image gives 211 seeds instead of 268: 57 seeds disappear from the count. The parameter is useful when there is dust or small fragments, and harmful when the seeds themselves are small. Always look at the labelled image of a few samples before running a batch.
crumbs: 10  Low-Cost High-Throughput Phenotyping: Image Analysis in R

title: 10  Low-Cost High-Throughput Phenotyping: Image Analysis in R
text:
10.7 Colour as a trait
Colour is often the trait of interest: the yellow of a root or a grain as a proxy for carotenoids, the green of a leaf for chlorophyll, the brown of a seed coat. With object_index the function returns the mean value of an index inside each object.

colour <- analyze_objects(soy, marker = "id", object_index = c("R", "G", "B", "NGRDI", "GLI"),
                          verbose = FALSE)
colour$object_index |> mutate(across(-id, \(x) round(x, 3)))

  id     R     G     B  NGRDI   GLI
1  1 0.670 0.569 0.326 -0.082 0.066
2  2 0.667 0.574 0.352 -0.077 0.058
3  3 0.696 0.603 0.374 -0.071 0.060
4  4 0.672 0.580 0.362 -0.073 0.057
5  5 0.492 0.465 0.248 -0.028 0.115
6  6 0.672 0.577 0.342 -0.076 0.064
7  7 0.645 0.560 0.351 -0.072 0.058
8  8 0.647 0.551 0.319 -0.081 0.065
9  9 0.505 0.476 0.274 -0.031 0.100








Figure 10.6: Soybean seeds of soy_green.jpg. Seeds 5 and 9 are greener than the rest.





Seeds 5 and 9 have a higher GLI (0.115 and 0.100) and an NGRDI close to zero (-0.03), while the seven yellow seeds have a GLI near 0.06 and an NGRDI near -0.07. A single threshold on one of these indices classifies the seeds:

colour$object_index |>
  mutate(class = if_else(NGRDI > -0.05, "green", "yellow")) |>
  count(class)

   class n
1  green 2
2 yellow 7








ImportantThe threshold must come from data



We placed the threshold by looking at nine seeds. In a real study we would fix it on a set of seeds that were classified by an expert, and check the percentage of agreement on another set. The same applies when colour is a proxy for a trait that is expensive to measure. To use the yellow intensity of a root as a proxy for carotenoids, we first measure the carotenoids in the laboratory on a sample, build a model that predicts them from the image colour, and check the prediction on samples that were not used to build it. This is a prediction problem, and the machine learning chapter uses the same logic (Chapter 12).
crumbs: 10  Low-Cost High-Throughput Phenotyping: Image Analysis in R

title: 10  Low-Cost High-Throughput Phenotyping: Image Analysis in R
section: 10.8 Shape and leaf colour: the flax leaves
text:
10.8 Shape and leaf colour: the flax leaves
Elongated objects need one change in the settings. The image flax_leaves.jpg has 15 flax leaves, two of them yellow.

fleaves <- image_pliman("flax_leaves.jpg", plot = FALSE)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
split_default <- analyze_objects(fleaves, marker = "id", verbose = FALSE)
whole <- analyze_objects(fleaves, marker = "id", watershed = FALSE,
                         object_index = c("NGRDI", "GLI"), verbose = FALSE)
c(default = nrow(split_default$results), without_watershed = nrow(whole$results))

          default without_watershed 
               35                15 








Figure 10.7: Left: default settings, where the watershed splits each long leaf into several pieces (28 objects). Right: watershed = FALSE, 15 objects.





The default separates touching round objects (like the soybean seeds) using a watershed algorithm, and for long, thin objects it cuts them into pieces. With watershed = FALSE we get one object per leaf, and now we can measure and classify:

whole$results |>
  select(id, area, length, width) |>
  left_join(whole$object_index, by = "id") |>
  mutate(yellow = NGRDI < 0) |>
  filter(yellow)

  id area   length    width       NGRDI       GLI yellow
1 15 1779 146.8624 16.14967 -0.04648931 0.1809757   TRUE
2 17 1839 134.0336 18.95190 -0.03120197 0.1769517   TRUE


Two of the 15 leaves have an NGRDI below zero: the two yellow leaves. In a breeding trial the same logic gives a senescence score or a stay-green measure without a colour chart.

title: 10  Low-Cost High-Throughput Phenotyping: Image Analysis in R
text:
10.9 Disease severity
Severity is the percentage of leaf area with symptoms. measure_disease() needs three small images that act as colour palettes: healthy tissue, symptoms and background (here the leaf has no background).

set.seed(10)   # the palettes are sampled at random: this makes the result repeatable
leaf    <- image_pliman("sev_leaf_nb.jpg", plot = FALSE)
healthy <- image_pliman("sev_healthy.jpg", plot = FALSE)
lesions <- image_pliman("sev_sympt.jpg", plot = FALSE)

sev <- measure_disease(img = leaf, img_healthy = healthy, img_symptoms = lesions,
                       lesion_size = "large", plot = TRUE)
sev$severity

   healthy symptomatic
1 89.29372    10.70628








Figure 10.8: Soybean leaf with lesions. The software outlines the symptomatic area.





The leaf has 10.7% of symptomatic area. The palettes define what “healthy” and “symptom” mean, so the same palettes must be used for all images of a study. The software samples pixels of the palettes at random, so the percentage changes slightly from run to run unless we fix the seed, as above. In mutation breeding this is useful to screen large M2 populations for the response to a disease without rating each leaf by eye.
crumbs: 10  Low-Cost High-Throughput Phenotyping: Image Analysis in R

title: 10  Low-Cost High-Throughput Phenotyping: Image Analysis in R
text:
10.10 Many images at once
A folder of images is processed with the same call. The function looks for files whose name contains a pattern in the folder dir_original, and returns the results of all the images in one table. Here we put three sample images in a folder, named as if they were three plots:

dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "plots")
dir.create(dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
src <- system.file("tmp_images", package = "pliman")
file.copy(file.path(src, c("soybean_touch.jpg", "soy_green.jpg", "flax_grains.jpg")),
          file.path(dir, c("plot_101.jpg", "plot_102.jpg", "plot_103.jpg")))

[1] TRUE TRUE TRUE

batch <- analyze_objects(pattern = "plot_", dir_original = dir, plot = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
batch$statistics

# A tibble: 3 × 7
  img          n area_mean area_min area_max area_sum area_sd
  <chr>    <int>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>
1 plot_101    30    2051.      1366     2436    61539    230.
2 plot_102     9    7079.      5707     8370    63713    865.
3 plot_103   156      44.5        5     4679     6937    374.


(The three images are not three plots of a trial: they only show the structure of the output. The name of each file is in the column img.)
The result has one row per image, which is one row per plot when the file name is the plot identifier. The last step is to join it to the field book:

# 'trial' is the field book: one row per plot, with the column "plot"
image_traits <- batch$statistics |>
  mutate(plot = as.integer(sub("plot_", "", img))) |>
  select(plot, seed_number = n, seed_area = area_mean)

trial <- trial |> left_join(image_traits, by = "plot")

From here the image traits are traits like any other. They go to the single-trial analysis of Chapter 9 (mixed model with the design and, if justified, the spatial correction), and their heritability tells us if they are precise enough to select on.
crumbs: 10  Low-Cost High-Throughput Phenotyping: Image Analysis in R

title: 10  Low-Cost High-Throughput Phenotyping: Image Analysis in R
section: 10.11 Is the image trait good enough?
text:
10.11 Is the image trait good enough?
A trait from an image is useful only if it is precise and valid.

Valid: it measures what we want. Compare it with the manual or laboratory measurement on a subset of plots (20 to 50 is a start): correlation, and a plot of one against the other. If the correlation is low, the image trait cannot replace the manual one.
Precise: its heritability in the trial is high enough. An image trait can be perfectly valid and still not heritable (for example, the colour of a very variable environment).
Reproducible: two photographs of the same sample give the same value. Repeat 10 samples and compare.


# 'check' has one row per plot: the image value and the manual value
cor(check$seed_number_image, check$seed_number_manual)
plot(check$seed_number_manual, check$seed_number_image); abline(0, 1)

The line abline(0, 1) shows where the values would fall if the two methods agreed exactly. Systematic distance from that line is a bias that can be corrected; scatter around it is error that cannot.
crumbs: 10  Low-Cost High-Throughput Phenotyping: Image Analysis in R

title: 10  Low-Cost High-Throughput Phenotyping: Image Analysis in R
text:
10.12 Near infrared and drones, briefly
Near infrared (NIR). Healthy leaves reflect much more NIR than visible red, and stressed leaves less. An RGB camera with the infrared filter removed, or a multispectral camera, records this. With the NIR band, indices such as NDVI (normalized difference vegetation index) measure vigour and stress better than RGB indices. In pliman the functions that read a band declare it with the arguments re (red edge) and nir.
Drones. A drone takes hundreds of images that are joined in an orthomosaic. The field is then divided in plots by a shapefile, and the indices are extracted per plot. The result is again one row per plot with plant height, canopy cover or vigour. It gives the whole trial in a few minutes, but it needs a flight plan, ground control points and processing software, and the plots need to be well marked. pliman has a family of functions for orthomosaics (mosaic_*) that work with the same logic. For a programme that is starting, we suggest to learn the steps of this chapter with photographs on a tray first: the segmentation, the scale, the validation and the join with the trial are the same.
crumbs: 10  Low-Cost High-Throughput Phenotyping: Image Analysis in R

title: 10  Low-Cost High-Throughput Phenotyping: Image Analysis in R
text:
10.13 Pitfalls








Pitfall
Consequence
What to do




Uneven light or shadows
Wrong mask, wrong size and colour
Diffuse light, a box or a cloudy day; same set-up in all images


One set of parameters for all images
Counts and sizes change between images
Test the parameters on 5 to 10 images, and then keep them


No scale
Sizes in pixels, not comparable
Reference object or known dpi


Not looking at the labelled image
Wrong counts go unnoticed
Save and inspect the labelled image of a sample


Colour threshold from 9 seeds
Poor classification in a new set
Fix thresholds on a training set and check on another


Image trait without validation
We select on a number that does not measure the trait
Compare with manual measurements on a subset


Different cameras or settings between trials
Differences that are not biological
Same camera and settings; keep the originals


Overlapping objects
Several objects counted as one
Separate the objects; use watershed for round ones

title: 10  Low-Cost High-Throughput Phenotyping: Image Analysis in R
text:
10.15 Key takeaways

An image is a table of numbers. Segment, measure, tabulate and analyse: the table enters the same workflow as any other trait.
A good photograph (plain background, even light, a reference object, the plot as file name) is worth more than any software option.
pliman counts, measures size and shape, describes colour with indices, and measures severity, for one image or a folder.
Validate with something of known size, and check the labelled image before trusting a batch.
Fix colour thresholds on a training set. A colour proxy needs a laboratory calibration.
An image trait is useful only if it is valid (agrees with the manual measure) and precise (heritable).
Start with a phone and a tray; drones and NIR come after the basic steps work.

title: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction
text:
11.1 Learning objectives
Until now we compared lines inside one trial. A breeder never sells a line to one field in one year. The line will be grown on many farms and in many seasons, and a line that wins in one trial can be average in another. This chapter uses trials run in several environments to answer a different question: which lines are good on average, which are stable, and which are good only somewhere?
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(lme4)
crumbs: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction

title: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction
text:
Explain what the genotype by environment interaction (G×E) is and why one environment is not enough to choose a line
Split the variation of a multi-environment trial (MET) into genotype, environment and G×E
Estimate variance components and the heritability of a line mean across environments
Describe stability and adaptability, and compute simple stability statistics
Read a principal component analysis (PCA) of a small table, and use the same idea for the AMMI and GGE biplots
Interpret an AMMI1 biplot, a GGE “which-won-where” biplot and the mean against stability view
Combine performance and stability in a selection decision









NotePackages



The chapter uses only lme4 and ggplot2 and base R, so the AMMI and GGE biplots are built step by step and you can see what they do. At the end (Shortcuts) we show the same analyses with metan and statgenGxE, which are part of the course installation (R/install_packages.R).
crumbs: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction

title: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction
text:
11.2 Why test in several environments
Take two lines. In a good year, line A yields more than line B. In a dry year, B is better. If we had tested only in the good year, we would have kept A and lost the line that tolerates drought. That change of ranking, or of the size of the difference, from one environment to another is the genotype by environment interaction (G×E).
There are three situations, and they have different consequences for the breeder:








Situation
What it looks like
Consequence




No G×E
Lines keep the same differences everywhere
One good environment is enough to rank lines


Scale G×E (no crossing)
Differences get bigger or smaller, but the order is kept
Ranking is safe, the size of the gain changes


Crossover G×E
The order of lines changes
The best line depends on where it will be grown



The crossover case is the one that makes selection hard. We will now see how common it is in real data.
crumbs: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction

title: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction
section: 11.3 The data: durum wheat in Algeria
text:
11.3 The data: durum wheat in Algeria
We use a real multi-environment trial of durum wheat (Algeria). It is a complete and balanced data set, which makes it ideal to learn the methods.

met <- read_csv("data/Durum_wheat_Algeria.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(Genotype = factor(trimws(Genotype)),
         Env      = factor(Environment),
         Loc      = factor(Location),
         Year     = factor(Year),
         Block    = factor(Block),
         region   = factor(region),
         Group    = factor(trimws(GenoGroup)))

met |>
  summarise(plots = n(),
            genotypes = n_distinct(Genotype),
            locations = n_distinct(Loc),
            years = n_distinct(Year),
            environments = n_distinct(Env),
            blocks = n_distinct(Block),
            mean_yield = mean(yield))

# A tibble: 1 × 7
  plots genotypes locations years environments blocks mean_yield
  <int>     <int>     <int> <int>        <int>  <int>      <dbl>
1  2112        24        11     2           22      4       1.87


There are 24 genotypes, 11 locations and 2 years, which gives 22 environments (an environment is one location in one year). Each genotype appears once in each of the 4 blocks of each environment, so every line has 4 plots per environment, and the data is balanced. The locations belong to two regions (A and B), and the lines belong to two groups (A and B). Yield is in t/ha.

env_means <- met |>
  group_by(Env, region) |>
  summarise(yield = mean(yield), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(Env = reorder(Env, yield))

ggplot(env_means, aes(yield, Env, fill = region)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(A = "#c0392b", B = "#2c7fb8")) +
  labs(x = "Mean yield (t/ha)", y = NULL, fill = "Region")







Figure 11.1: Mean yield of the 22 environments. Environments are the dominant source of variation: the best environment yields almost five times more than the worst.





Mean yield goes from 0.66 to 3.24 t/ha across environments. Region does not explain this difference by itself: the two regions have almost the same mean (1.86 and 1.88 t/ha).

11.3.1 Do the lines change rank?
The next figure draws the mean of each line in each environment, with environments ordered from the poorest to the best. Each line is one grey line, and four lines are in colour. If there were no G×E, all the lines would be parallel.

gm <- met |>
  group_by(Genotype, Env) |>
  summarise(yield = mean(yield), .groups = "drop")
env_order <- gm |> group_by(Env) |> summarise(m = mean(yield)) |> arrange(m) |> pull(Env)
gm <- mutate(gm, Env = factor(Env, levels = env_order),
             hl = ifelse(Genotype %in% c("GTADUR", "O.ZENADI", "SAHEL77", "MBBACHIR"),
                         as.character(Genotype), "other"))

ggplot(gm, aes(Env, yield, group = Genotype)) +
  geom_line(data = filter(gm, hl == "other"), colour = "grey75") +
  geom_line(data = filter(gm, hl != "other"), aes(colour = hl), linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(GTADUR = "#1b9e77", O.ZENADI = "#d95f02",
                                 SAHEL77 = "#7570b3", MBBACHIR = "#e7298a")) +
  labs(x = "Environment (from poorest to best)", y = "Yield (t/ha)", colour = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 60, hjust = 1, size = 8))







Figure 11.2: Reaction of the 24 lines across the 22 environments (ordered by environment mean). Lines that are not parallel show G×E; lines that cross change their rank.





The lines are not parallel and they cross many times. The best line in the poorest environments is not always the best in the richest ones. This is G×E in real data.
crumbs: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction

title: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction
section: 11.4 How much is G×E? The analysis of variance of a MET
text:
11.4 How much is G×E? The analysis of variance of a MET
The first look at a MET is an analysis of variance that separates three sources: environments (E), genotypes (G) and their interaction (G×E). Blocks are nested in environments, because “block 1” of one location has nothing to do with “block 1” of another.

fit_met <- lm(yield ~ Env + Env:Block + Genotype + Genotype:Env, data = met)
an <- anova(fit_met)
an

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: yield
               Df Sum Sq Mean Sq  F value    Pr(>F)    
Env            21 935.95  44.569 537.1651 < 2.2e-16 ***
Genotype       23  80.84   3.515  42.3627 < 2.2e-16 ***
Env:Block      66 117.69   1.783  21.4909 < 2.2e-16 ***
Env:Genotype  483 151.66   0.314   3.7845 < 2.2e-16 ***
Residuals    1518 125.95   0.083                       
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1



data.frame(source = c("Environment", "Block within environment", "Genotype", "G×E", "Residual"),
           share_of_SS = round(pct[c("Env", "Env:Block", "Genotype", "Env:Genotype", "Residuals")], 1))

                               source share_of_SS
Env                       Environment        66.3
Env:Block    Block within environment         8.3
Genotype                     Genotype         5.7
Env:Genotype                      G×E        10.7
Residuals                    Residual         8.9


Environments explain 66 % of the total variation, genotypes only 6 %, and G×E 11 %. Two things follow:

The environment effect is huge but irrelevant for selection: the breeder cannot choose the year. What matters is the share of G and G×E, and here G×E is about twice the genotype effect.
The genotype effect cannot be tested against the residual. The environments of the trial are a sample of the environments where the line will be grown, so the right denominator is the G×E mean square.


ms <- an[["Mean Sq"]]; names(ms) <- rownames(an)
F_g <- ms["Genotype"] / ms["Env:Genotype"]
df_g <- an["Genotype", "Df"]; df_ge <- an["Env:Genotype", "Df"]
c(F = unname(F_g), p = unname(pf(F_g, df_g, df_ge, lower.tail = FALSE)))

           F            p 
1.119373e+01 2.886352e-32 


Against G×E, the genotype effect is still significant (F = 11.2), but the evidence is much weaker than the F value of 42 that we would get against the residual. This is a common mistake in published METs.

11.4.1 Where does G×E come from?
G×E can be split by the structure of the environments (a location and a year). In this data there are the same 11 locations in both years, so we can separate the part of G×E that repeats from year to year at a location from the part that does not.

fit_parts <- lm(yield ~ Env + Env:Block + Genotype + Genotype:Loc + Genotype:Year +
                  Genotype:Env, data = met)
ap <- anova(fit_parts)
ssp <- ap[["Sum Sq"]]; names(ssp) <- rownames(ap)
ge_total <- sum(ssp[c("Genotype:Loc", "Genotype:Year", "Env:Genotype")])
data.frame(part_of_GxE = c("Genotype × Location (repeatable)", "Genotype × Year", "Genotype × Location × Year (not repeatable)"),
           percent = round(100 * ssp[c("Genotype:Loc", "Genotype:Year", "Env:Genotype")] / ge_total, 0))

                                              part_of_GxE percent
Genotype:Loc             Genotype × Location (repeatable)      50
Genotype:Year                             Genotype × Year       6
Env:Genotype  Genotype × Location × Year (not repeatable)      44


About half of G×E is a genotype by location effect. This part is a property of the location, and it will appear again next year, so it is useful: we can choose lines for locations, or for groups of similar locations. The other half is genotype by location by year, which changes every season and cannot be predicted. The same logic is behind the idea of mega-environments at the end of the chapter.
crumbs: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction

title: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction
section: 11.5 Variance components and heritability across environments
text:
11.5 Variance components and heritability across environments
With the environments as a sample, genotypes, environments, G×E and blocks are all random, and we estimate their variances.

fit_vc <- lmer(yield ~ 1 + (1 | Genotype) + (1 | Env) + (1 | Genotype:Env) + (1 | Env:Block),
               data = met, REML = TRUE)
vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(fit_vc))
vc <- setNames(vc$vcov, vc$grp)
round(vc, 4)

Genotype:Env    Env:Block     Genotype          Env     Residual 
      0.0578       0.0708       0.0364       0.4433       0.0830 


The variance of G×E (0.058) is 1.6 times the genotype variance (0.036). The heritability of a line mean (the quantity that tells how well the mean of a line predicts its true value) depends on how many environments and replicates were used:
\[
H^2 = \frac{\sigma^2_G}{\sigma^2_G + \dfrac{\sigma^2_{GE}}{e} + \dfrac{\sigma^2_\varepsilon}{e\,r}}
\]
where \(e\) is the number of environments and \(r\) the number of replicates per environment.

h2_tab <- data.frame(environments = 1:22) |> mutate(H2 = H2(environments))
ggplot(h2_tab, aes(environments, H2)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2c7fb8", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = filter(h2_tab, environments %in% c(1, 4, 8, 22)), size = 2.5) +
  geom_text(data = filter(h2_tab, environments %in% c(1, 4, 8, 22)),
            aes(label = round(H2, 2)), vjust = 1.8, size = 3.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Number of environments", y = expression(H^2~"of the line mean"))







Figure 11.3: Heritability of the line mean as a function of the number of environments (4 replicates per environment). Each extra environment helps, with decreasing returns.





In a single environment the heritability is only 0.32. With 4 environments it reaches 0.65, and with the 22 environments of the trial it is 0.91. This is the quantitative argument for a MET: most of what looks like a difference between lines in one trial is G×E and error, and only repeated testing separates the genotype effect from them.






TipReplicates or environments?



Look at the formula. Adding replicates only reduces the error term (\(\sigma^2_\varepsilon / e r\)). Adding environments reduces both the G×E and the error term. When G×E is as large as here, it is almost always better to test in more environments with fewer replicates, than the opposite.
crumbs: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction

title: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction
text:
11.6 Stability and adaptability
Two words are often mixed:

Adaptability: how well a line performs in a given set of environments (its mean, or its response to the quality of the environment).
Stability: how little the line’s performance changes from one environment to another.

A line can be stable and poor (always low yield), or high yielding in good environments only. The breeder looks for lines that are high and stable, or for lines adapted to a specific group of environments.

11.6.1 Simple stability statistics
We compute three classic statistics from the table of line means by environment.

Ecovalence (Wricke): the contribution of the line to the G×E sum of squares. Low is stable.
Regression slope (Finlay and Wilkinson): the slope of the line yield on the environment mean. A slope of 1 means average response; above 1 the line responds more to good environments; below 1 it is less affected.
Coefficient of variation of the line across environments.


M <- with(met, tapply(yield, list(Genotype, Env), mean))   # genotype x environment table of means
g <- nrow(M); e <- ncol(M)
dc <- M - rowMeans(M) - matrix(colMeans(M), g, e, byrow = TRUE) + mean(M)   # G×E effects (double centred)
env_index <- colMeans(M) - mean(M)

stab <- data.frame(
  mean  = rowMeans(M),
  W     = rowSums(dc^2),                                                    # Wricke ecovalence
  slope = apply(M, 1, function(y) unname(coef(lm(y ~ env_index))[2])),      # Finlay-Wilkinson
  cv    = apply(M, 1, function(y) 100 * sd(y) / mean(y))
) |> arrange(desc(mean))
stab$rank_mean <- seq_len(g)
round(stab, 2)

         mean    W slope    cv rank_mean
GTADUR   2.17 1.05  1.20 38.59         1
CHENS    2.11 0.84  1.13 37.37         2
SAHEL77  2.10 2.77  1.07 38.55         3
BID/WAHA 2.06 0.74  1.11 37.58         4
SIMETO   2.06 2.37  1.10 39.78         5
B.DUR194 2.03 1.80  1.11 39.86         6
WAHA     2.02 1.12  1.08 37.98         7

DUILIO   1.96 1.59  1.01 37.73        10
VITRON   1.96 1.57  1.08 39.88        11
BELIKH02 1.96 1.48  1.06 39.15        12
OUMRABI9 1.95 0.95  0.98 35.88        13
EIDER    1.93 0.66  0.99 36.06        14
KEBIR    1.81 0.68  1.02 39.55        15
ARDENTE  1.78 1.67  1.11 45.21        16
INRAT69  1.77 1.16  0.99 40.44        17
HEBD/GDO 1.73 1.04  1.07 43.96        18
BIDI17   1.65 1.63  0.90 40.47        19
POLONICU 1.63 2.71  0.70 34.61        20
POLON/ZB 1.63 1.30  0.93 41.65        21
