HEBDA03  1.54 1.77  0.78 37.90        23
O.ZENADI 1.53 2.53  0.79 40.91        24


The statistics tell different stories. The line mean and the slope are strongly related (rank correlation 0.79): the lines that yield more are also the ones that respond more to good environments. The ecovalence is almost independent of the mean (-0.18), so a line can be high yielding and stable, or high and unstable. This is why no single number describes stability, and why graphical methods help.

stab$Genotype <- rownames(stab)
ggplot(stab, aes(W, mean, label = Genotype)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = median(stab$mean), linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median(stab$W), linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(colour = "#2c7fb8", size = 2) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(size = 3, max.overlaps = 30) +
  labs(x = "Wricke ecovalence (lower = more stable)", y = "Mean yield (t/ha)")







Figure 11.4: Mean yield against ecovalence. Lines in the upper left are high yielding and stable. The dashed lines are the medians.
crumbs: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction

title: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction
text:
11.7 PCA on a small example
AMMI and GGE are built on the principal component analysis (PCA) of a table of line means. We first see the idea in a table small enough to read: five lines in four environments.

small <- M[c("GTADUR", "SAHEL77", "O.ZENADI", "MBBACHIR", "CHENS"),
           c("loc01_year1", "loc14_year2", "loc05_year1", "loc07_year2")]
round(small, 2)

         loc01_year1 loc14_year2 loc05_year1 loc07_year2
GTADUR          4.12        3.51        1.29        0.88
SAHEL77         3.68        3.40        1.44        0.72
O.ZENADI        2.44        3.16        1.09        0.43
MBBACHIR        2.67        2.91        0.97        0.26
CHENS           3.75        3.63        1.50        0.90


PCA looks for the directions in which the lines differ most. First we centre the columns (subtract the environment mean), because we want differences among lines inside an environment.

pc <- prcomp(small, center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE)
if (mean(pc$rotation[, 1]) < 0) { pc$rotation[, 1] <- -pc$rotation[, 1]; pc$x[, 1] <- -pc$x[, 1] }  # the sign is arbitrary: make PC1 point to higher yield
round(pc$sdev^2 / sum(pc$sdev^2) * 100, 1)       # % of variation of each component

[1] 94.4  4.8  0.8  0.0

round(pc$x[, 1:2], 2)                             # scores of the lines

           PC1   PC2
GTADUR    0.83  0.17
SAHEL77   0.39  0.00
O.ZENADI -0.92 -0.18
MBBACHIR -0.89  0.20
CHENS     0.60 -0.20

round(pc$rotation[, 1:2], 2)                      # loadings of the environments

             PC1   PC2
loc01_year1 0.86  0.49
loc14_year2 0.31 -0.61
loc05_year1 0.23 -0.50
loc07_year2 0.33 -0.37



sc <- as.data.frame(pc$x[, 1:2]); sc$name <- rownames(sc)
ld <- as.data.frame(pc$rotation[, 1:2] * 1.3); ld$name <- short(rownames(ld))
ggplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_segment(data = ld, aes(0, 0, xend = PC1, yend = PC2), colour = "#c0392b",
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"))) +
  geom_text(data = ld, aes(PC1, PC2, label = name), colour = "#c0392b", size = 3, vjust = -0.4) +
  geom_point(data = sc, aes(PC1, PC2), size = 2.5, colour = "#2c7fb8") +
  geom_text(data = sc, aes(PC1, PC2, label = name), size = 3.3, vjust = 1.8, colour = "#2c7fb8") +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-1.2, 1.4), ylim = c(-0.9, 0.9)) + labs(x = "PC1", y = "PC2")







Figure 11.5: PCA of the small example. Lines (dots) are placed by their scores. Environments (arrows) are placed by their loadings: an arrow points to where that environment gives high yield.





In the plot, environments are named location-year (for example 01-1 is loc01_year1). How to read it:

A score says where a line is. Lines far apart differ a lot; lines close together behave similarly.
A loading says how an environment relates to the axes. Two environments with arrows in the same direction rank the lines in the same way; arrows at 90° are unrelated; opposite arrows rank the lines in the opposite way (crossover).
The first component takes the largest part of the variation; the second takes the largest part of what remains, and is perpendicular to the first.

With a few components we summarize a large table. Two special tables give the two famous biplots:



Table analysed
What is removed first
Biplot




Interaction effects only
Genotype and environment means
AMMI


Genotype + interaction
Environment means only
GGE
crumbs: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction

title: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction
text:
11.8 The AMMI model
AMMI (additive main effects and multiplicative interaction) fits the additive part (G and E) with an analysis of variance, and then fits the interaction with a PCA. We already have the double-centred table dc (the G×E effects of every line in every environment), so we apply the PCA to it. The PCA of a matrix is its singular value decomposition, svd().

sv <- svd(dc)
ipca <- data.frame(IPCA = 1:8,
                   percent_of_GxE = round(100 * sv$d[1:8]^2 / sum(sv$d^2), 1))
ipca$cumulative <- cumsum(ipca$percent_of_GxE)
ipca

  IPCA percent_of_GxE cumulative
1    1           32.9       32.9
2    2           12.1       45.0
3    3           10.8       55.8
4    4            8.3       64.1
5    5            7.5       71.6
6    6            6.7       78.3
7    7            4.6       82.9
8    8            3.9       86.8


The first interaction axis (IPCA1) captures 33 % of the G×E and the first two 45 %. G×E here is spread over many axes (the table has no “dominant” pattern), so the biplots below show only part of the story. The usual F test of each axis (Gollob) calls all the first axes significant, because it is very liberal with a large number of environments; we use the percentage and common sense instead.

11.8.1 AMMI1 biplot: mean against IPCA1
The AMMI1 biplot puts the mean on the horizontal axis and the first interaction axis on the vertical axis, for lines and for environments.

G1 <- sv$u[, 1] * sqrt(sv$d[1]); E1 <- sv$v[, 1] * sqrt(sv$d[1])
names(G1) <- rownames(M)
ammi1 <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(name = rownames(M), type = "Line", mean = rowMeans(M), ipca1 = G1),
  data.frame(name = short(colnames(M)), type = "Environment", mean = colMeans(M), ipca1 = E1))


ggplot(ammi1, aes(mean, ipca1, shape = type, colour = type, label = name)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(M), linetype = 2, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(size = 2.8, max.overlaps = 40, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Line = "#2c7fb8", Environment = "#c0392b")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(Line = 16, Environment = 17)) +
  labs(x = "Mean yield (t/ha)", y = "IPCA1", colour = NULL, shape = NULL)







Figure 11.6: AMMI1 biplot. Lines (circles) and environments (triangles, named location-year). A line close to the horizontal line (IPCA1 near 0) is stable; a line on the right has a high mean. Lines and environments on the same side of the horizontal line interact positively.





How to read it:

Horizontal position = main effect. Lines to the right of the dashed line yield more than the average.
Vertical position = interaction. Lines close to zero on IPCA1 are stable in the sense of the IPCA1 axis. Lines far from zero interact strongly.
Same side = positive interaction. A line above the horizontal line does better than expected in the environments above it, and worse than expected in those below.

On this data the lines with the highest IPCA1 are O.ZENADI, POLONICU, MBBACHIR and those with the lowest are VITRON, SAHEL77, WAHA. Lines with an above average yield and an IPCA1 close to zero (here GTADUR, B.DUR194, OFANTO, BELIKH02) are the safest candidates in this view.


11.8.2 AMMI2 biplot: the two interaction axes

G2 <- sv$u[, 1:2] %*% diag(sqrt(sv$d[1:2])); rownames(G2) <- rownames(M)
E2 <- sv$v[, 1:2] %*% diag(sqrt(sv$d[1:2])); rownames(E2) <- short(colnames(M))
gg2 <- data.frame(G2, name = rownames(G2)); ee2 <- data.frame(E2, name = rownames(E2))
ggplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_segment(data = ee2, aes(0, 0, xend = X1, yend = X2), colour = "#c0392b", alpha = 0.7,
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.15, "cm"))) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = ee2, aes(X1, X2, label = name), colour = "#c0392b", size = 2.6,
                           max.overlaps = 40) +
  geom_point(data = gg2, aes(X1, X2), colour = "#2c7fb8", size = 2) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = gg2, aes(X1, X2, label = name), colour = "#2c7fb8", size = 3,
                           max.overlaps = 40) +
  coord_equal() + labs(x = "IPCA1", y = "IPCA2")







Figure 11.7: AMMI2 biplot with the first two interaction axes. Environments (location-year) are shown as arrows from the origin: environments with arrows in the same direction rank the lines in the same way.





A line is good in an environment when it lies in the direction of the environment arrow, far from the origin. Lines near the origin have small interaction: they behave as the additive model predicts everywhere.
crumbs: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction

title: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction
text:
11.9 The GGE biplot
The GGE biplot (genotype main effect plus G×E) removes only the environment means, because the environment effect is not a property of the line. What is left is the part that matters for choosing a line: its genotype effect and its interaction. The PCA of this table gives PC1, which is mostly the genotype effect, and PC2, which is mostly G×E.

gc <- sweep(M, 2, colMeans(M))        # centre by environment
sg <- svd(gc)
Gs <- sg$u[, 1:2] %*% diag(sqrt(sg$d[1:2])); rownames(Gs) <- rownames(M)
Es <- sg$v[, 1:2] %*% diag(sqrt(sg$d[1:2])); rownames(Es) <- colnames(M)
if (mean(Es[, 1]) < 0) { Gs[, 1] <- -Gs[, 1]; Es[, 1] <- -Es[, 1] }   # PC1 positive for the average environment
gge_pct <- round(100 * sg$d[1:2]^2 / sum(sg$d^2), 1)
gge_pct

[1] 52.8  8.5


PC1 explains 52.8 % and PC2 8.5 % of G + G×E, together 61.3 %, a good representation.

11.9.1 Which-won-where
The lines at the corners of the polygon that contains all the lines are the best (or the worst) in some environments. The lines drawn perpendicular to the sides of the polygon divide the plot in sectors: the corner line of a sector is the winner for all the environments that fall in it.

gg <- data.frame(Gs, name = rownames(Gs)); ee <- data.frame(Es, name = rownames(Es))
ee$region <- env_region[ee$name, "region"]
hull <- chull(Gs)
gg$vertex <- seq_len(nrow(gg)) %in% hull
poly <- gg[c(hull, hull[1]), ]
# perpendicular sector lines through the origin
sect <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(hull), function(i) {
  p <- Gs[hull[i], ]; q <- Gs[hull[ifelse(i == length(hull), 1, i + 1)], ]
  n <- c(q[2] - p[2], -(q[1] - p[1])); if (sum(n * p) < 0) n <- -n
  n <- n / sqrt(sum(n^2)) * 3
  data.frame(x = 0, y = 0, xend = n[1], yend = n[2])
}))
ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = sect, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend), colour = "grey55", linetype = 2) +
  geom_path(data = poly, aes(X1, X2), colour = "#2c7fb8") +
  geom_point(data = gg, aes(X1, X2), colour = "#2c7fb8", size = 1.8) +
  geom_point(data = ee, aes(X1, X2, colour = region), shape = 17, size = 2.4) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = filter(gg, vertex), aes(X1, X2, label = name), colour = "#1f5f8b",
                           fontface = "bold", size = 3.4, max.overlaps = 40) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(A = "#c0392b", B = "#e08a00")) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-1.3, 1.5), ylim = c(-1.1, 1)) +
  labs(x = paste0("PC1 (", gge_pct[1], "%)"), y = paste0("PC2 (", gge_pct[2], "%)"),
       colour = "Environment region")







Figure 11.8: GGE biplot, which-won-where view. The polygon joins the lines farthest from the origin. Each sector has a winning line (the vertex) for the environments inside it.





Only the lines at the corners of the polygon are labelled; the other lines are the blue points inside. Environments are the triangles, coloured by region. Counting the environments of each sector gives:

sector_tab

         region
sector     A  B
  GTADUR   7  3
  SAHEL77  1 11


All 22 environments fall in 2 sectors, those of GTADUR and SAHEL77. The sectors are related to the regions (most environments of one sector belong to region B, and the other sector has more environments of region A), but they do not coincide with them. The environments of a sector share the same best line, so these are two candidate mega-environments. The next step is to ask whether it pays to treat them separately:

data.frame(sector_winner = sec_names,
           environments = sec_mean["n", ],
           yield_of_sector_winner = round(sec_mean["winner", ], 2),
           yield_of_overall_best = round(sec_mean["best_overall", ], 2)) |>
  mutate(gain_t_ha = round(yield_of_sector_winner - yield_of_overall_best, 2),
         gain_percent = round(100 * gain_t_ha / yield_of_overall_best, 1))

        sector_winner environments yield_of_sector_winner yield_of_overall_best
GTADUR         GTADUR           10                   2.28                  2.28
SAHEL77       SAHEL77           12                   2.17                  2.07
        gain_t_ha gain_percent
GTADUR        0.0          0.0
SAHEL77       0.1          4.8


The overall best line (GTADUR) is also the winner of one sector (gain of zero in that row). In the other sector the sector winner gives a modest gain over it. Splitting the target area in two would help in one half and give nothing in the other, so a wide-adaptation line is a reasonable choice, and the second candidate is kept as an alternative for the environments of its sector.


11.9.2 Mean performance and stability
The second view of the same biplot answers “which line is best on average and how stable is it?”. The average environment axis (AEA) is the arrow from the origin to the mean of all the environment points. The projection of a line on this axis gives its performance; the distance to the axis gives its instability.

aea <- colMeans(Es[, 1:2]); aea_u <- aea / sqrt(sum(aea^2))
perf <- as.numeric(Gs[, 1:2] %*% aea_u)
inst <- abs(Gs[, 1] * aea_u[2] - Gs[, 2] * aea_u[1])
ggplot(gg, aes(X1, X2, label = name)) +
  geom_abline(slope = aea_u[2] / aea_u[1], intercept = 0, colour = "#c0392b", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_abline(slope = -aea_u[1] / aea_u[2], intercept = 0, colour = "grey60", linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(colour = "#2c7fb8", size = 2) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(size = 3, colour = "#2c7fb8", max.overlaps = 40) +
  annotate("segment", x = 0, y = 0, xend = 1.6 * aea_u[1], yend = 1.6 * aea_u[2], colour = "#c0392b",
           linewidth = 1, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"))) +
  coord_equal() + labs(x = paste0("PC1 (", gge_pct[1], "%)"), y = paste0("PC2 (", gge_pct[2], "%)"))







Figure 11.9: GGE biplot, mean against stability. The arrow is the average environment axis: lines further along it yield more. The distance from the axis measures instability.






gge_tab <- data.frame(line = rownames(M), performance = perf, instability = inst) |>
  arrange(desc(performance))
head(gge_tab, 8) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))

             line performance instability
GTADUR     GTADUR        0.64        0.43
CHENS       CHENS        0.54        0.01
SAHEL77   SAHEL77        0.53        0.35
BID/WAHA BID/WAHA        0.43        0.06
WAHA         WAHA        0.41        0.12
SIMETO     SIMETO        0.40        0.44
OFANTO     OFANTO        0.34        0.33
BELIKH02 BELIKH02        0.29        0.36

title: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction
text:
11.10 Putting performance and stability together
A decision needs both. We gather the statistics for the best lines in one table.

decision <- stab |>
  mutate(line = rownames(stab)) |>
  left_join(gge_tab, by = "line") |>
  mutate(rank_gge = rank(-performance), rank_W = rank(W)) |>
  select(line, mean, rank_mean, slope, W, rank_W, instability) |>
  head(10)
decision |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))

       line mean rank_mean slope    W rank_W instability
1    GTADUR 2.17         1  1.20 1.05      7        0.43
2     CHENS 2.11         2  1.13 0.84      4        0.01
3   SAHEL77 2.10         3  1.07 2.77     24        0.35
4  BID/WAHA 2.06         4  1.11 0.74      3        0.06
5    SIMETO 2.06         5  1.10 2.37     21        0.44
6  B.DUR194 2.03         6  1.11 1.80     17        0.33
7      WAHA 2.02         7  1.08 1.12      8        0.12
8    OFANTO 2.02         8  0.94 1.98     18        0.33
9  MEXICALI 1.99         9  1.04 2.15     19        0.48
10   DUILIO 1.96        10  1.01 1.59     13        0.39


Among the 10 highest yielding lines, GTADUR, CHENS, BID/WAHA, WAHA have an ecovalence below the median, so they are high and stable. SAHEL77, SIMETO, B.DUR194, OFANTO, MEXICALI, DUILIO have a high mean but a high ecovalence: they are good in some environments and disappoint in others. The reading is:

High mean and stable: candidates for wide release. They make the shortlist.
High mean and unstable: candidates for a specific group of environments, only if the environments where they win can be identified and are common.
Low mean: out, however stable. Stability is not a virtue by itself.







ImportantStability does not replace the mean



Stability statistics are secondary criteria. First rank the lines by their mean across environments (a BLUP of the genotype when the data is unbalanced), and then use stability to separate lines that are close. A line that is “very stable” at a low yield is not a good variety.
crumbs: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction

title: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction
text:
11.11 Mega-environments and targeting
If the environments fall in groups where the same line wins inside a group but different lines win between groups, the target area can be divided into mega-environments, and one variety is selected for each. If the groups do not exist, the aim is a wide-adaptation line.
In our data the regions are a natural candidate. How much G×E do they explain?

fit_reg <- lm(yield ~ Env + Env:Block + Genotype + Genotype:region + Genotype:Env, data = met)
ar <- anova(fit_reg)
ge_all <- an["Env:Genotype", "Sum Sq"]
share_reg <- ar["Genotype:region", "Sum Sq"] / ge_all
cor_regions <- with(met, cor(tapply(yield[region == "A"], Genotype[region == "A"], mean),
                             tapply(yield[region == "B"], Genotype[region == "B"], mean)))
c(share_of_GxE_explained_by_region = round(share_reg, 2), correlation_of_line_means_between_regions = round(cor_regions, 2))

         share_of_GxE_explained_by_region 
                                     0.11 
correlation_of_line_means_between_regions 
                                     0.68 


The region separates only 11 % of the total G×E, and the line means in the two regions are correlated (0.68). Region is a weak mega-environment here: it changes the ranking of some lines (G×region is significant), but most of the G×E is inside the regions, between locations and years.
This is a useful negative result. Dividing the target area in two would not remove most of the G×E, so the breeding strategy should be to test in more locations and to use the stability criteria above.
crumbs: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction

title: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction
section: 11.12 Multi-environment trials in a mutation breeding programme
text:
11.12 Multi-environment trials in a mutation breeding programme
In a mutation breeding programme, the early generations (M2, M3) are grown in one environment with little seed, and the aim is only to select. The MET starts later, with the advanced mutant lines that have shown interest, in preliminary and advanced yield trials in several locations and seasons. At that stage, the methods of this chapter apply directly:

The parent and the checks are included in every environment, so that every environment is connected to the others and the mutants can be compared with the parent everywhere.
The number of environments matters more than the number of replicates, as in Figure 11.3.
A mutant with a clear advantage over the parent in most environments (and not only in the best ones) is the one to propose for release or to enter in the Mutant Variety Database.
crumbs: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction

title: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction
text:
11.13 Shortcuts: metan and statgenGxE
Both packages are part of the course installation and run the analyses of this chapter with a few lines. We show the code but do not run it here, to keep the chapter independent of package versions; check the result against the step-by-step version above.

library(metan)

# AMMI and GGE biplots
ammi_model <- performs_ammi(met, env = Env, gen = Genotype, rep = Block, resp = yield)
plot_scores(ammi_model)                       # AMMI1 and AMMI2 biplots

gge_model <- gge(met, env = Env, gen = Genotype, resp = yield)
plot(gge_model, type = 3)                     # which-won-where
plot(gge_model, type = 2)                     # mean performance and stability

# Stability indices and a combined index (WAASB)
stab_model <- waasb(met, env = Env, gen = Genotype, rep = Block, resp = yield)


library(statgenGxE)

# one data frame with columns genotype, trial, and the trait
td <- statgenSTA::createTD(data = met, genotype = "Genotype", trial = "Env")
gxe_ammi <- gxeAmmi(td, trait = "yield")
plot(gxe_ammi, plotType = "AMMI2")
gxe_fw <- gxeFw(td, trait = "yield")          # Finlay-Wilkinson

When the data is unbalanced (not every line in every environment, as is normal in breeding programmes), do not use svd() on a table with holes. Fit a mixed model with a factor analytic structure, or use the two-stage approach: first a model per trial (BLUEs, as in Chapter 9), and then a MET model with the BLUEs and their weights (Möhring and Piepho 2009). The sommer and statgenGxE packages do this.
crumbs: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction

title: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction
text:
11.14 Exercise
Use only region A (4 locations, 8 environments).

Fit the variance component model of this chapter to region A, and compute the heritability of the line mean with all its environments and with 4 replicates.
Compute the mean of each line in region A, and the ecovalence. List the three lines with the highest mean and say if they are stable.
Compare with the result of the whole trial: are the top three the same?







TipSolution






dA <- droplevels(filter(met, region == "A"))
mA <- lmer(yield ~ 1 + (1 | Genotype) + (1 | Env) + (1 | Genotype:Env) + (1 | Env:Block), data = dA)
vA <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(mA)); vA <- setNames(vA$vcov, vA$grp)
eA <- nlevels(dA$Env)
H2A <- vA[["Genotype"]] / (vA[["Genotype"]] + vA[["Genotype:Env"]] / eA + vA[["Residual"]] / (eA * n_r))

MA <- with(dA, tapply(yield, list(Genotype, Env), mean))
dcA <- MA - rowMeans(MA) - matrix(colMeans(MA), nrow(MA), ncol(MA), byrow = TRUE) + mean(MA)
tabA <- data.frame(mean = rowMeans(MA), W = rowSums(dcA^2)) |> arrange(desc(mean))
tabA$stable <- ifelse(tabA$W < median(tabA$W), "yes", "no")
head(round(tabA[, 1:2], 2), 3) |> cbind(stable = head(tabA$stable, 3))

         mean    W stable
GTADUR   2.14 0.13    yes
CHENS    2.07 0.18    yes
B.DUR194 2.06 0.27     no



In region A the variance components are 0.016 for the line and 0.022 for G×E, and the heritability of the line mean with its 8 environments is 0.74. It is lower than in the whole trial (0.91) because the lines differ less in this region (the genotype variance is smaller) and there are fewer environments.
The three best lines in region A are GTADUR, CHENS, B.DUR194. The table shows if each one has an ecovalence below the median of region A.
The top three of the whole trial are GTADUR, CHENS, SAHEL77. The best lines of a subset of environments are not necessarily the best of the whole trial: this is the practical meaning of G×E.
crumbs: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction

title: 11  Multi-Environment Trials and G×E Interaction
text:
11.15 Key takeaways

G×E is the change in the performance or in the ranking of lines across environments. In the durum wheat MET its share of the sum of squares is about twice that of the genotype effect.
Environments explain most of the variation, but the breeder works with G and G×E. Test the genotype effect against G×E, not against the residual.
Heritability of the line mean grows with the number of environments: from 0.32 in one environment to 0.91 in 22. When G×E is large, add environments before adding replicates.
About half of the G×E is repeatable across years at a location; the rest is not predictable.
AMMI (interaction only) and GGE (genotype plus interaction) are PCA of the table of means. Use AMMI1 for mean against interaction, which-won-where for mega-environments and the average environment axis for mean against stability.
Select first by the mean across environments and then use stability to choose between similar lines. Stability without yield is not a goal.

title: 12  Machine Learning for Prediction in Plant Breeding
text:
12.1 Learning objectives
Most of this course uses models to explain a trial: is there a difference between lines, how large is it, how sure are we? ML is used for another goal: to predict a value for a new sample, such as a plant that was only photographed or scanned. We do not need to understand every step of the model if it predicts well; but we do need to know how well it predicts in the situation where we will use it. This chapter is about that question.
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(glmnet)    # ridge, lasso, elastic net
library(pls)       # partial least squares
library(ranger)    # random forest
library(gbm)       # gradient boosting
library(e1071)     # support vector machines
crumbs: 12  Machine Learning for Prediction in Plant Breeding

title: 12  Machine Learning for Prediction in Plant Breeding
text:
Decide when machine learning (ML) improves a prediction and when a classical model is enough
Describe the main ML models used in breeding: penalized regression, PLS, random forest, gradient boosting and support vector machines
Build a prediction model from near-infrared (NIR) spectra and compare it with a baseline
Validate a model honestly: training, validation and test sets, cross-validation by groups and data leakage
Recognize why a model that works in one population or season can fail in the next
Explain the limits of ML and the role of breeder knowledge









NotePackages



This chapter needs glmnet, pls, gbm and e1071 in addition to ranger, which is in the course installation. If any is missing, run install.packages(c("glmnet", "pls", "gbm", "e1071")) once. The Day 6 practical uses the same packages.
crumbs: 12  Machine Learning for Prediction in Plant Breeding

title: 12  Machine Learning for Prediction in Plant Breeding
text:
12.2 Prediction against explanation
A mixed model or an ANOVA answers questions about parameters: which genotype effect, which variance component. ML models answer questions about new observations: given the spectrum, the image or the weather of a plot, what will its value be? The practical differences are:









Classical statistics (ANOVA, mixed models)
Machine learning




Main goal
Explain, estimate effects, test hypotheses
Predict new observations


Data
Designed experiments, few explanatory variables
Many variables, often more variables than samples


Model
Specified by the analyst from the design
Learned from the data, often nonlinear


Output
Effects with their uncertainty
A prediction and an error estimate


Main risk
Wrong model structure
Overfitting and a model that does not transfer



They are not rivals. The design and the mixed model give clean phenotypes, and ML turns cheap measurements (images, spectra, sensors, markers) into predictions of expensive ones (laboratory analysis, yield, disease scores).
crumbs: 12  Machine Learning for Prediction in Plant Breeding

title: 12  Machine Learning for Prediction in Plant Breeding
section: 12.3 Where ML pays in a breeding programme
text:
12.3 Where ML pays in a breeding programme
ML is useful when there are many predictors, when the relation with the trait is not a simple straight line, or when we need to measure thousands of samples quickly.








Application
Predictors
Target




Chemical composition
NIR spectra
Protein, oil, starch, carotenoids


Disease and vigour
Image features (Chapter 10)
Severity score, biomass


Yield and traits
Drone and sensor indices
Yield, plant height


Genomic prediction
Thousands of markers
Breeding value


G×E prediction
Environmental covariates (Chapter 11)
Performance in a new environment



In a mutation breeding programme, the large M2 and M3 populations have thousands of plants that cannot be measured one by one in the laboratory. A prediction from an image or a spectrum can rank every plant, so that the laboratory measures only the promising ones. The prediction does not replace the measurement: it decides where to spend it.
crumbs: 12  Machine Learning for Prediction in Plant Breeding

title: 12  Machine Learning for Prediction in Plant Breeding
section: 12.4 The data: NIR spectra of cassava breeding samples
text:
12.4 The data: NIR spectra of cassava breeding samples
We use a real data set from the CIAT cassava breeding programme (Davrieux et al. 2016), published with the rchemo package. It is a small part of a large calibration database built to predict carotenoids in fresh cassava roots, a trait of the biofortification programme, because the laboratory method (HPLC) can analyse only a few samples per day. Near-infrared spectra were measured between 400 and 2498 nm every 2 nm (1050 variables). For each sample, the concentration of a pigment was measured with the reference laboratory method (the data documentation names the target “pigment concentration”), and the aim is to predict it from the spectrum, which is much cheaper and faster.

nir <- read_csv("data/cassava_nir.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
wl_cols <- grep("^w", names(nir))
wl <- as.numeric(sub("w", "", names(nir)[wl_cols]))
X  <- as.matrix(nir[, wl_cols])
y  <- nir$pigment
is_cal <- nir$set == "calibration"

nir |>
  group_by(set, year) |>
  summarise(samples = n(), mean_pigment = mean(pigment), sd = sd(pigment), .groups = "drop")

# A tibble: 5 × 5
  set          year samples mean_pigment    sd
  <chr>       <dbl>   <int>        <dbl> <dbl>
1 calibration  2009      42         4.62  2.21
2 calibration  2010      47         6.19  2.90
3 calibration  2011      40         4.70  3.65
4 calibration  2012      71         6.33  2.84
5 test         2013      80         8.50  3.82


There are 200 samples from 2009 to 2012 (the calibration set, which we use to build models) and 80 samples from 2013 (the test set, which we keep untouched until the end and which plays the role of the next season). The table has 1050 predictors and 200 samples, so there are many more variables than samples; a standard multiple regression cannot be fitted.

set.seed(1)
show <- sample(which(is_cal), 60)
grp <- cut(y, quantile(y[is_cal], c(0, 1/3, 2/3, 1)), labels = c("low", "medium", "high"), include.lowest = TRUE)
long <- data.frame(sample = rep(show, each = length(wl)), wavelength = rep(wl, times = length(show)),
                   absorbance = as.vector(t(X[show, ])), pigment = rep(grp[show], each = length(wl)))
ggplot(long, aes(wavelength, absorbance, group = sample, colour = pigment)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(low = "#1b9e77", medium = "#e6ab02", high = "#d95f02")) +
  labs(x = "Wavelength (nm)", y = "Absorbance", colour = "Pigment")







Figure 12.1: NIR spectra of 60 samples from the calibration set, coloured by pigment concentration (low, medium and high thirds). The spectra look alike and the differences are small.






ggplot(nir, aes(factor(year), pigment, fill = set)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, size = 0.8, alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(calibration = "#9ecae1", test = "#fdae6b")) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Pigment concentration", fill = NULL)







Figure 12.2: Pigment concentration by year. The test year (2013) has a higher mean than the calibration years: the breeding population is evolving.





This figure is the most important one of the chapter. The mean of the test year is 8.5, while the calibration years have a mean of 5.6, and the test year has samples above the maximum of the calibration set (15.4 against 12.3). The breeding programme has improved the trait, so the next season is not like the previous ones. In the full CIAT database the mean carotenoid content rose by more than 80% between 2009 and 2014 (Davrieux et al. 2016), and the authors link the limits of PLS to this change. We will see what it does to the predictions.
crumbs: 12  Machine Learning for Prediction in Plant Breeding

title: 12  Machine Learning for Prediction in Plant Breeding
text:
12.5 Preparing the spectra
Raw spectra differ mainly in the baseline (how much light the sample scatters) and not in chemistry. Two standard treatments are applied to each spectrum separately:

Standard normal variate (SNV): subtract the mean of the spectrum and divide by its standard deviation. It removes differences in overall level and scale.
First derivative (after a light smoothing): it removes the slope of the baseline and sharpens the absorption peaks.


snv <- function(X) t(apply(X, 1, function(s) (s - mean(s)) / sd(s)))

first_derivative <- function(X, k = 5) {
  Xs <- t(apply(X, 1, function(s) stats::filter(s, rep(1 / k, k), sides = 2)))   # moving average
  Xs <- Xs[, !apply(Xs, 2, anyNA), drop = FALSE]
  t(apply(Xs, 1, diff))
}

prep <- function(X) {
  Z <- first_derivative(snv(X))
  colnames(Z) <- paste0("v", seq_len(ncol(Z)))
  Z
}
Z <- prep(X)
wl_d <- (wl[3:(length(wl) - 3)] + wl[4:(length(wl) - 2)]) / 2    # wavelength of each derivative variable
c(variables = ncol(Z), wavelengths = length(wl_d))

  variables wavelengths 
       1045        1045 



i15 <- show[1:15]
mk <- function(M, w, lab) data.frame(sample = rep(i15, each = length(w)), wavelength = rep(w, times = 15),
                                     value = as.vector(t(M[i15, ])), step = lab)
bind_rows(mk(X, wl, "1. Raw"), mk(snv(X), wl, "2. SNV"), mk(Z, wl_d, "3. SNV + first derivative")) |>
  ggplot(aes(wavelength, value, group = sample)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.6, colour = "#2c7fb8") +
  facet_wrap(~ step, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Wavelength (nm)", y = NULL)







Figure 12.3: The same 15 calibration spectra, raw (top), after SNV (middle) and after SNV and first derivative (bottom).





The treatment is a choice that can change the result, and it must be decided with the calibration set only. SNV and the derivative work on one spectrum at a time, so they do not use information from other samples. Treatments that compute a mean or a variance across samples (scaling variables, for example) must be learned in the training samples and then applied to new samples with the same numbers.
crumbs: 12  Machine Learning for Prediction in Plant Breeding

title: 12  Machine Learning for Prediction in Plant Breeding
text:
12.6 Measuring prediction quality
The quality of a prediction is measured on samples that the model has not seen.

RMSE (root mean squared error): the typical size of the error, in the units of the trait. Lower is better.
R² of the prediction: the share of the variation of the new samples that the prediction explains.
Bias: the mean of (prediction minus observed). It should be near zero; a bias shows that the model is systematically high or low.
RPD (ratio of performance to deviation): the standard deviation of the observed values divided by the RMSE. It is common in NIR work; values above 2 are usually taken as a useful model for screening.

Every model must be compared with a baseline. The simplest baseline predicts the mean of the calibration set for every new sample.

rmse <- function(o, p) sqrt(mean((o - p)^2))
r2   <- function(o, p) 1 - sum((o - p)^2) / sum((o - mean(o))^2)
metrics <- function(o, p) c(RMSE = rmse(o, p), R2 = r2(o, p), bias = mean(p - o), RPD = sd(o) / rmse(o, p))

A <- Z[is_cal, ];  yA <- y[is_cal]       # calibration
B <- Z[!is_cal, ]; yB <- y[!is_cal]      # test (the next season)
baseline <- metrics(yB, rep(mean(yA), length(yB)))
round(baseline, 2)

 RMSE    R2  bias   RPD 
 4.76 -0.58 -2.88  0.80 


Predicting the calibration mean gives an RMSE of 4.76 on the test year: this is the number to beat.
crumbs: 12  Machine Learning for Prediction in Plant Breeding

title: 12  Machine Learning for Prediction in Plant Breeding
text:
12.7 The models
We fit the main families of models to the same data. Each model has a tuning parameter that controls how flexible it is. A model that is too flexible learns the noise of the calibration samples (overfitting); one that is too rigid misses the signal. Tuning parameters are chosen by cross-validation inside the calibration set, never with the test set.










Model
Idea
Tuning parameter
Main strength
Main weakness




Ridge
Linear model that shrinks all coefficients
Amount of shrinkage
Stable with correlated variables
Keeps all variables


Lasso
Shrinks and sets many coefficients to zero
Amount of shrinkage
Selects a few variables
Unstable with correlated variables


Elastic net
Mix of ridge and lasso
Shrinkage and the mix
Selects groups of related variables
Two parameters


PLS
Builds a few components that covary with the trait
Number of components
Standard for spectra
Linear


Random forest
Average of many decision trees
Variables per split
Nonlinear, few assumptions
Cannot predict outside the range of the data


Gradient boosting
Trees built one after the other, each correcting the errors of the last
Number of trees, learning rate, depth
Often very accurate
Many parameters, can overfit


Support vector machine
Flexible curve fitted with a margin of tolerance
Cost and kernel width
Good with small samples
Hard to interpret



We write one function that fits any of these models to a training set and predicts a new set, with the tuning included.

fit_predict <- function(model, A, y, B) {
  switch(model,
    PLS = {
      d <- data.frame(y = y); d$X <- I(A)
      set.seed(1)
      m <- plsr(y ~ X, ncomp = 15, data = d, validation = "CV", segments = 10)
      nc <- which.min(RMSEP(m)$val[1, 1, -1])                 # components chosen by cross-validation
      as.numeric(predict(m, ncomp = nc, newdata = data.frame(X = I(B))))
    },
    Ridge = { set.seed(1); cv <- cv.glmnet(A, y, alpha = 0);   as.numeric(predict(cv, B, s = "lambda.min")) },
    Lasso = { set.seed(1); cv <- cv.glmnet(A, y, alpha = 1);   as.numeric(predict(cv, B, s = "lambda.min")) },
    ENet  = { set.seed(1); cv <- cv.glmnet(A, y, alpha = 0.5); as.numeric(predict(cv, B, s = "lambda.min")) },
    RF = {
      set.seed(1)
      predict(ranger(x = A, y = y, num.trees = 500), B)$predictions
    },
    GBM = {
      set.seed(1)
      d <- as.data.frame(A); d$y <- y
      g <- gbm(y ~ ., data = d, distribution = "gaussian", n.trees = 1500, shrinkage = 0.02,
               interaction.depth = 3, cv.folds = 5, verbose = FALSE)
      nt <- gbm.perf(g, method = "cv", plot.it = FALSE)       # number of trees chosen by cross-validation
      predict(g, as.data.frame(B), n.trees = nt)
    },
    SVM = {
      tu <- tune.svm(A, y, gamma = 10^(-4:-2), cost = c(1, 10, 100), tunecontrol = tune.control(cross = 5))
      predict(tu$best.model, B)
    })
}


models <- c("PLS", "Ridge", "Lasso", "ENet", "RF", "GBM", "SVM")
pred_test <- sapply(models, function(m) fit_predict(m, A, yA, B))
perf <- t(apply(pred_test, 2, function(p) metrics(yB, p))) |> as.data.frame()
perf$model <- rownames(perf)
perf |> arrange(RMSE) |> select(model, RMSE, R2, bias, RPD) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))

      model RMSE   R2  bias  RPD
Lasso Lasso 1.51 0.84 -1.10 2.52
ENet   ENet 1.52 0.84 -1.09 2.51
SVM     SVM 1.56 0.83 -1.11 2.45
PLS     PLS 1.61 0.82 -1.05 2.37
GBM     GBM 1.83 0.77 -1.28 2.09
RF       RF 2.22 0.66 -1.40 1.72
Ridge Ridge 2.27 0.64 -1.48 1.68


All models beat the baseline (4.76), and the best are the lasso, the elastic net and the support vector machine, with an RMSE near 1.5. The table has two lessons.

There is no model that is best for every problem. The linear models with a good penalty and the SVM are at the top here; the ridge, which keeps every variable, and the random forest are at the bottom. The order would be different in another data set, so the comparison must always be done with your data.
Every model has a negative bias. All of them predict values that are, on average, 1.2 units too low in the test year. We look at why below.


po <- as.data.frame(pred_test) |> mutate(observed = yB) |>
  pivot_longer(-observed, names_to = "model", values_to = "predicted") |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = models))
ggplot(po, aes(observed, predicted)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = min(yA), ymax = max(yA), fill = "grey85", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_abline(linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(colour = "#2c7fb8", alpha = 0.7, size = 1.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ model, nrow = 2) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Observed pigment", y = "Predicted pigment")







Figure 12.4: Predicted against observed pigment in the test year (2013). The dashed line is the 1:1 line; the shaded band is the range of the calibration set.





The points lie below the 1:1 line for the high values. The highest observed values of the test year are above anything in the calibration set, and the models do not follow them. The random forest shows it clearly: a tree predicts an average of the training values, so it can never predict above the maximum it has seen. A linear model can extrapolate, but only if the relation stays the same outside the range. This is the practical meaning of “transfer”: a model is reliable inside the range and the conditions where it was built.

12.7.1 What the lasso selected
Penalized regression has a bonus: the lasso gives a short list of spectral variables that matter.

set.seed(1)
cv_l <- cv.glmnet(A, yA, alpha = 1)
b <- as.matrix(coef(cv_l, s = "lambda.min"))[-1, 1]
sel <- data.frame(wavelength = wl_d[b != 0], coefficient = b[b != 0])
ggplot(sel, aes(wavelength, coefficient)) +
  geom_col(width = 6, fill = "#2c7fb8") +
  labs(x = "Wavelength (nm)", y = "Lasso coefficient")







Figure 12.5: Coefficients of the lasso (non-zero only). Each bar is a spectral variable (first derivative of the SNV spectrum) at its wavelength.





The lasso keeps 30 of the 1045 variables. A short list helps interpretation and a cheaper instrument (a few filters instead of the full spectrum) is possible if the important regions are known. But with correlated variables the selection is not unique: neighbouring wavelengths can replace each other, so do not read the list as “the only wavelengths that matter”.
crumbs: 12  Machine Learning for Prediction in Plant Breeding

title: 12  Machine Learning for Prediction in Plant Breeding
section: 12.8 Validation: how to know if the number is honest
text:
12.8 Validation: how to know if the number is honest
The estimate of the error is only valid if the samples used to evaluate the model were not used in any way to build it. There are three levels.








Set
Used for
Rule




Training
Fit the model
Many samples


Validation (or cross-validation folds)
Choose the tuning parameters and the model
Taken from the training data


Test
Report the final error
Used once, at the end




12.8.1 Cross-validation
In k-fold cross-validation the calibration set is divided in k parts; the model is fitted k times, each time leaving one part out and predicting it. The prediction errors of the left-out parts estimate the error for new samples.
How the parts are made is the most important decision. If the samples are not independent (the same genotype in several plots, the same plant measured several times, the same field and year), a random split puts very similar samples in the training and in the validation part, and the error looks smaller than it will be. The honest split follows the question you want to answer: a new year needs a split by year, a new genotype needs a split by genotype, a new location needs a split by location.
We compare both ways with three models.

set.seed(2)
fold_random <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = nrow(A)))
yr_cal <- nir$year[is_cal]

cv_error <- function(model, groups) {
  p <- numeric(nrow(A))
  for (g in unique(groups)) {
    i <- groups == g
    p[i] <- fit_predict(model, A[!i, , drop = FALSE], yA[!i], A[i, , drop = FALSE])
  }
  rmse(yA, p)
}

cv_tab <- data.frame(model = c("PLS", "ENet", "SVM"))
cv_tab$random_10_fold <- sapply(cv_tab$model, cv_error, groups = fold_random)
cv_tab$leave_one_year_out <- sapply(cv_tab$model, cv_error, groups = yr_cal)
cv_tab$test_2013 <- perf$RMSE[match(cv_tab$model, perf$model)]
cv_tab |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))

  model random_10_fold leave_one_year_out test_2013
1   PLS           0.98               1.71      1.61
2  ENet           0.88               1.62      1.52
3   SVM           0.89               1.47      1.56



cv_tab |>
  pivot_longer(-model, names_to = "validation", values_to = "RMSE") |>
  mutate(validation = factor(validation, levels = c("random_10_fold", "leave_one_year_out", "test_2013"),
                             labels = c("Random 10-fold", "Leave one year out", "Test year 2013"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(model, RMSE, fill = validation)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#9ecae1", "#4292c6", "#08519c")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "RMSE", fill = NULL)







Figure 12.6: Error of three models estimated by random 10-fold cross-validation, by leaving one year out, and on the real test year. Random cross-validation is too optimistic.





Random cross-validation reports an error of about 0.9, while leaving a year out gives 1.6 and the real test year 1.6. The error for a new year is 75 % larger than the random split reports, because samples of the same year share conditions (the growing season, the batch, the laboratory run) that the model learns. The leave-one-year-out error is a good forecast of the real error in the next season, and this is the number to report.


12.8.2 Data leakage
Leakage is any way in which information from the validation or test samples reaches the model before the evaluation. It always makes the error look smaller, and it is common in practice:

The same genotype, plant or sample (or its replicates) in training and test sets.
Choosing the variables (the best wavelengths, the best markers) with all the data and then cross-validating only the model. The selection must be repeated inside each fold.
Scaling or transforming variables with means computed on all the samples.
Tuning the model on the test set and reporting the same test set.
A variable in the predictors that is a consequence of the target (for example, a score that is derived from the trait).


# WRONG: variables are chosen with all the samples, the folds only see a "clean" problem
top <- order(-abs(cor(A, yA)))[1:30]
cv_error_wrong <- cross_validate(model, A[, top], yA)

# RIGHT: inside each fold, choose the variables with the training part only
for (k in 1:10) {
  train <- fold != k
  top <- order(-abs(cor(A[train, ], yA[train])))[1:30]
  fit <- fit_model(A[train, top], yA[train])
  pred[!train] <- predict(fit, A[!train, top])
}

A rule that avoids most leakage: every step that learns something from the data belongs inside the cross-validation loop.
crumbs: 12  Machine Learning for Prediction in Plant Breeding

title: 12  Machine Learning for Prediction in Plant Breeding
section: 12.9 When the next season is different
text:
12.9 When the next season is different
The model has an error of about 1.5 units in the test year, mostly because of the bias: the population moved. The practical solution is not a more complex model but a model that is updated: add to the calibration a few samples of the new population (with their laboratory value) and refit.

i_test <- which(!is_cal); i_cal <- which(is_cal)
upd <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0, 10, 20, 40), function(n) {
  r <- sapply(1:12, function(s) {
    set.seed(s)
    add <- if (n > 0) sample(i_test, n) else integer(0)
    trn <- c(i_cal, add); tst <- setdiff(i_test, add)
    p <- fit_predict("ENet", Z[trn, ], y[trn], Z[tst, ])
    c(rmse(y[tst], p), mean(p - y[tst]))
  })
  data.frame(added = n, RMSE = mean(r[1, ]), bias = mean(r[2, ]))
}))
ggplot(upd, aes(added, RMSE)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2c7fb8") + geom_point(size = 2.5, colour = "#2c7fb8") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 10, 20, 40)) +
  labs(x = "Samples of 2013 added to the calibration", y = "RMSE on the rest of 2013")







Figure 12.7: Error in the test year when 0, 10, 20 or 40 samples of 2013 are added to the calibration (elastic net). Each point is the mean of 12 random choices of the added samples; the error is computed on the 2013 samples that were not added.





With no new sample the error is 1.52; adding only 20 laboratory measurements of the new year lowers it to 1.14, and the bias goes from -1.09 to -0.62. In a breeding programme this is routine work: a calibration is a living tool, checked each season with a few reference samples and updated when it drifts.
crumbs: 12  Machine Learning for Prediction in Plant Breeding

title: 12  Machine Learning for Prediction in Plant Breeding
section: 12.10 Other uses in a breeding programme
text:
12.10 Other uses in a breeding programme
The same workflow (predictors, calibration set, models tuned by cross-validation, an honest test) applies to the other cases of the agenda.

Image features (Chapter 10): the area, colour indices and shape of the objects in a photograph are the predictors, and a laboratory or visual score is the target. The question to ask is the same one: how well does the model predict a new plant, in a new season?
Markers (genomic prediction): thousands of markers against a few hundred lines. Ridge regression is the model behind GBLUP, and the elastic net and random forest are alternatives. The validation by genotype and by environment decides if the prediction will help.
G×E prediction (Chapter 11): to predict a line in a new environment, the model needs a description of the environment (soil, weather, management). Without covariates, the best prediction for a new environment is the mean of the line, as in Chapter 11.
Early generations of mutant populations: predictions from images or spectra of thousands of M2 plants, followed by a laboratory or field check of the best ones. The prediction model is built on a subset that is measured by both ways, and checked by generation.
crumbs: 12  Machine Learning for Prediction in Plant Breeding

title: 12  Machine Learning for Prediction in Plant Breeding
text:
12.11 Limitations

Small data sets. With a few hundred samples, the error estimate itself is uncertain, and a complex model can look good by luck. Report the validation error with how many samples it comes from, and prefer simple models when the sample is small.
Overfitting. The more flexible the model, the more the calibration error understates the real error. This is why the test set is used once.
Interpretability. A random forest or boosting model does not give effects that can be explained to a farmer or a regulator. Ask if the decision needs an explanation.
Transfer. A model works inside the range and conditions where it was built: other crop, other season, other instrument, other laboratory. Verify before use and monitor after.
Label quality. The model learns from the reference measurements. If the laboratory values are noisy or biased, the best possible prediction is limited by them.
Garbage in, garbage out. Spectra from different instruments, images with different light, or sensors without calibration produce models that do not transfer.







ImportantBreeder knowledge remains essential



ML does not know the biology. The breeder knows if a prediction makes sense for the crop, which samples are unusual, when a population has changed and which errors matter. The best systems use ML for the volume (thousands of samples) and the breeder for the decision: a plant predicted as promising still has to be confirmed before it is advanced.
crumbs: 12  Machine Learning for Prediction in Plant Breeding

title: 12  Machine Learning for Prediction in Plant Breeding
text:
12.12 Exercise
Use the cassava NIR data of this chapter.

Use only the samples of 2009, 2010 and 2011 as calibration, and the samples of 2012 as validation (a “next season” that is different from the one used above).
Fit PLS and the elastic net, and compute RMSE and bias on the 2012 samples.
Compare the RMSE with the one from random 10-fold cross-validation inside 2009 to 2011. Which one would you report as the expected error for next season?







TipSolution






i_a <- is_cal & nir$year <= 2011
i_b <- is_cal & nir$year == 2012
set.seed(5)
folds <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = sum(i_a)))

one_model <- function(m) {
  p_next <- fit_predict(m, Z[i_a, ], y[i_a], Z[i_b, ])
  p_cv <- numeric(sum(i_a))
  for (k in 1:10) {
    j <- folds == k
    p_cv[j] <- fit_predict(m, Z[i_a, ][!j, ], y[i_a][!j], Z[i_a, ][j, , drop = FALSE])
  }
  c(RMSE_random_cv = rmse(y[i_a], p_cv), RMSE_2012 = rmse(y[i_b], p_next), bias_2012 = mean(p_next - y[i_b]))
}
sol <- t(sapply(c("PLS", "ENet"), one_model))
round(sol, 2)

     RMSE_random_cv RMSE_2012 bias_2012
PLS            0.97      2.18     -1.89
ENet           0.86      2.34     -2.03


The error in 2012 (2.18 for PLS and 2.34 for the elastic net) is larger than the random cross-validation error (0.97 and 0.86). The number to report is the 2012 error, because the question is “how well will this model predict next year?”, and only a split by year imitates that question.
crumbs: 12  Machine Learning for Prediction in Plant Breeding

title: 12  Machine Learning for Prediction in Plant Breeding
text:
12.13 Key takeaways

ML is for prediction: it turns cheap measurements (spectra, images, sensors, markers) into estimates of expensive ones. It does not replace the experimental design or the mixed model.
Compare every model with a baseline and with a classical model. There is no best model in general: here penalized regression and the SVM were at the top, and the random forest could not follow values beyond its training range.
The honest error comes from data that the model never saw, split the way the model will be used: by year, by genotype or by location. The error for a new year was about 75 % larger than random cross-validation reported.
Avoid leakage: every step that learns from the data (variable selection, scaling, tuning) belongs inside the validation loop.
A calibration drifts when the population evolves. Check it each season with a few reference samples and update it: 20 new samples reduced the error from 1.52 to 1.14.
The breeder decides. A prediction ranks and prioritizes, and the promising lines are confirmed before they are advanced.
